blocks.h: 1. The Convention and where it applies

blocks.p: The instrument the stem refers to is the Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007, adopted on 18 May 2007 and in force since 14 April 2015. It operates in the Convention area — the exclusive economic zone of a State Party, or an equivalent zone not extending beyond 200 nautical miles (Article 1(1)). A State Party may extend it to its own territorial sea by declaration under Article 3(2). Domestically at the date of this examination the governing Indian statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

blocks.h: 2. What "wreck" means - the four categories

blocks.p: Article 1(4) defines a wreck as something arising following upon a maritime casualty. Four categories are identified:

ul: a sunken or stranded ship;
any part of a sunken or stranded ship, including any object that is or has been on board;
any object lost at sea from a ship that is stranded, sunken or adrift at sea;
a ship that is about, or may reasonably be expected, to sink or to strand, where effective measures to assist the ship or property in danger are not already being taken.

blocks.p: Two points are commonly lost. First, the phrase "following upon a maritime casualty" is part of the definition, not scene-setting: a ship deliberately abandoned, or an object thrown overboard in the ordinary course, is not a wreck under this Convention. Second, the fourth category is anticipatory — a ship that has not yet sunk is already a wreck for these purposes if she may reasonably be expected to sink or strand and effective assistance is not already under way. That is what allows a coastal State to act before the casualty completes itself, which is usually the only cheap moment to act at all.

blocks.h: 3. Hazard - the switch that turns the Convention on

blocks.p: A wreck engages the removal machinery only if it is a hazard — Article 1(5): a condition or threat that poses a danger or impediment to navigation, or that may reasonably be expected to result in major harmful consequences to the marine environment or damage to coastal and related interests. Article 6 gives the criteria the affected State applies:

ul: the size, type and construction of the wreck, and the depth of water over it;
proximity to shipping routes, port approaches and anchorages, and the density and frequency of traffic;
the type and quantity of cargo, and the quantity and type of oil — bunkers included — on board;
the tidal range, currents and prevailing weather, and the vulnerability of port facilities;
the proximity of offshore installations, pipelines and telecommunication cables, and of areas of particular environmental sensitivity;
whether the wreck is likely to shift or deteriorate materially, and any damage already suffered.

blocks.p: The determination is therefore a reasoned assessment, not a reflex. A wreck lying deep, clear of routes, with negligible bunkers and stable structure may properly be left in place — and the Convention imposes no removal duty on its owner at all.

blocks.h: 4. Objectives and key provisions

blocks.p: The Convention was written to close a gap. UNCLOS gave coastal States rights in the exclusive economic zone but no removal machinery, so a hazardous wreck beyond the territorial sea could sit there with nobody clearly obliged to move it and no guarantee that anyone solvent would pay. States were left choosing between an unfunded removal and a permanent danger. The objectives are therefore:

ul: a uniform international rule for the prompt, effective and proportionate removal of hazardous wrecks beyond the territorial sea;
cost recovery from the owner and the owner's insurer rather than from the coastal State's public funds — the polluter-pays principle applied to obstruction as well as to pollution;
legal certainty: owners and insurers know the extent of the exposure, States know the powers they hold, and both know the time limits;
financial security that is real — compulsory insurance with a right of direct action, so the remedy does not evaporate with a single-ship company.

blocks.p: The operative provisions then run as a sequence, and it is worth learning them in that order because it is the order in which a real casualty unfolds:

rows: Report the wreck - position, type, size, nature of cargo and oil on board
Master and operator, to the affected State
Determine whether the wreck is a hazard, on the listed criteria
Locate - warn mariners, issue notices, and use all practicable means to establish the precise position
Mark, in accordance with the internationally accepted system of buoyage, and promulgate the particulars
Remove within a reasonable deadline set by the State; the State may intervene if the owner fails, or immediately where the hazard is severe

blocks.p: Behind that sequence stand the financial provisions — strict liability (Art 10), compulsory insurance with direct action (Art 12) and the time bar (Art 13). Article 9 also preserves the owner's right to contract with any salvor or contractor of his choice, subject to the State's conditions, which keeps commercial salvage inside the regime rather than displacing it.

blocks.h: 5. The shipowner - strict liability and its limits

blocks.p: Article 10 makes the registered owner strictly liable for the costs of locating, marking and removing the wreck. Fault need not be shown. The exceptions are narrow: act of war or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party acting with intent; or wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids. Article 11 stands the Convention down where CLC 1992, the HNS, Bunkers or nuclear regimes govern the same damage.

Liability is backed by Article 12: ships of 300 GT and above must maintain insurance or other financial security, carry a certificate to that effect, and the claim may be brought directly against the insurer. The security must be at least equal to the limits of liability under the applicable limitation regime, and an insurer sued directly may invoke the defences the owner could have invoked — but not the owner's insolvency or winding up. The practical consequence is that the coastal State need not find the owner, prove negligence, or hope a single-ship company still exists: it establishes the hazard, sets the deadline and, failing compliance, removes and claims against a certified insurer whose identity it already holds. Article 10(2) preserves the owner's right to limit liability under the applicable limitation regime, and Article 13 bars claims brought more than three years after the hazard was determined, and in no case later than six years after the casualty.

blocks.h: 6. The coastal State - judgement, notice and intervention

blocks.p: The affected State decides whether the wreck is a hazard on the Article 6 criteria; informs the flag State and the registered owner; warns mariners; sets a reasonable deadline for removal and may attach conditions; and, if the owner fails to act — or immediately, where the hazard is severe — may remove the wreck itself and recover the cost. Those powers are not unlimited: measures must be proportionate to the hazard and exercised consistently with international law, and the State may not interfere with the rights of other States beyond what removal requires. Where the wreck lies in the territorial sea of a State that has not opted in under Article 3(2), the Convention does not govern and the State acts under its own domestic law — in India, the wreck and salvage provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, administered through the Receiver of Wreck.

The division is therefore clean and should be written that way: the State supplies the judgement and the compulsion; the owner supplies the work and the money. The State does not become the remover of first resort, and the owner does not decide whether the wreck is dangerous.

blocks.h: 7. Environmental implications, and what the regime does not reach

blocks.p: A wreck is a continuing environmental source rather than a single event, and that is what distinguishes it from a spill:

ul: Progressive release. Bunkers, lubricating and hydraulic oils and cargo escape as tanks corrode, sometimes years after the casualty and long after the response has stood down.
Cargo hazards. Chemicals, packaged dangerous goods and containers that break free and drift, each becoming an object within category three of the definition.
Structural contaminants. Antifouling coatings, refrigerants, batteries and other hazardous materials built into the ship.
Physical damage. Smothering and scouring of the seabed, reefs and fishing grounds; obstruction of ports, approaches and fairways; risk to fishing gear and to cables and pipelines.
Navigational risk feeding back into environmental risk. An unmarked wreck causes the next casualty, which is why marking under Article 8 sits inside an environmental instrument at all.

blocks.p: The Convention's contribution to all of this is essentially financial and procedural: strict liability plus compulsory insurance is what converts an environmental risk into a funded removal, promptly and without first litigating fault. It changes who pays and how quickly, rather than changing the physics of the casualty.

Its reach is bounded. It applies only to wrecks that are hazards, only within the Convention area unless a State has opted in for its territorial sea, and the owner's liability remains subject to the applicable limitation regime — so an exceptionally costly removal can still exceed the available fund and leave a residue for the coastal State to carry.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The limbs carry 5, 5 and 6 marks and the six-mark limb names two actors. Splitting sections 5 and 6 by actor is therefore not a stylistic choice — it is what makes both halves of the largest limb visible to the examiner. Sections 1 to 3 build the definition in the order the Convention itself uses: instrument, then definition, then trigger. Answering "define wreck" without "hazard" produces a technically correct definition that explains nothing about how the Convention works.

Note also that this sitting lifts the convention into a stem lead-in rather than naming it inside limb (a). That changes where you write the instrument's full title, not whether you write it: supply Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 once, in section 1, because the printed stem does not name it.

blocks.h: The two-part definition, and why it is two parts

blocks.p: Article 1(4) tells you what a wreck is. Article 1(5) tells you when anyone has to do anything about it. Most of the Convention — reporting, locating, marking, removal, liability — hangs off the hazard determination in Article 6, not off the definition. A wreck in deep water clear of routes, with no cargo of consequence, may be left where it is.

blocks.h: Strict liability, and the word that must be used carefully

blocks.p: Strict liability means liability without proof of fault — it does not mean absolute liability, because Article 10 admits three defences. Note the contrast with the Bunkers Convention, where the liable "shipowner" is defined widely to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally, and only the insurance duty falls on the registered owner alone. Under Nairobi and under CLC the registered owner is the correct focus; under Bunkers it is not, and that distinction has been examined.

blocks.h: Two different ways the owner escapes - and they are not the same thing

blocks.p: Candidates blur Article 10 with Article 11. They do different work.

rows: The Convention applies, but the owner is not liable on these facts
The Convention stands down because another liability regime governs

Act of war or hostilities; an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party acting with intent; damage wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids
The costs are recoverable under CLC 1992, the HNS Convention, the Bunkers Convention, or the nuclear liability conventions
The State may still act, but recovers nothing from this owner under this Convention
The State recovers under the other regime instead, and is not left uncovered

blocks.p: The word to be careful with in Article 10 is wholly. Partial contribution by a third party does not release the owner; the defence requires the damage to have been caused entirely by that act or omission.

blocks.h: Wreck removal is not salvage, and the difference is examinable

rows: Voluntary service to property in danger
Compulsory duty imposed on the registered owner
The salvor offers; the master or owner accepts
The affected State determines a hazard and sets a deadline
Reward, on the no-cure-no-pay principle, with special compensation for environmental effort
No reward - the owner bears the cost, strictly
While the property is still in danger and can be saved
After the casualty, once the wreck is a hazard

blocks.p: The two meet in Article 9, which preserves the owner's right to contract with a salvor or contractor of his own choice for the removal, subject to conditions imposed by the State. So the commercial salvage market still does the work — it is the obligation and the bill that the Convention allocates.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Omitting the fourth category — a ship about to sink or strand — and so defining only what is already on the bottom.
Saying the Convention applies in territorial waters. It applies in the EEZ; the territorial sea is an opt-in under Article 3(2).
Treating every wreck as removable. Without a hazard there is no removal obligation.
Writing limb (c) as one paragraph about pollution, leaving the coastal State's responsibilities unstated.
Confusing the Nairobi regime with salvage. Salvage is a voluntary service for reward; wreck removal is a compulsory duty imposed on the owner.
Failing to name the instrument at all, because this sitting's stem refers only to "the Wreck Removal Convention". Give the full title once.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking which conventions displace Nairobi — CLC 1992, HNS, Bunkers and the nuclear conventions, under Article 11.
Asking whether liability is unlimited. It is not: Article 10(2) expressly preserves limitation under the applicable regime.
Asking for the time limits and expecting only one. There are two — three years and six years, measured from different events.
Asking who reports the wreck. The master or operator of the ship, to the affected State — not the coastal State to the owner.
Asking whether the HNS Convention is in force. At this sitting it is not, which is why Article 11 names it as a displacing regime in principle rather than in current practice.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: What certificate does a ship of 300 GT and above carry under this Convention, and who issues it?
Your ship strands in another State's EEZ. What are your first duties as Chief Engineer and what does the company have to do?
Can the coastal State remove the wreck before the deadline expires?
How does the wreck removal insurance relate to P&I cover?
Which Indian statute governs wreck and salvage, and who is the Receiver of Wreck?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Casualty, then hazard, then four verbs. Nothing is a wreck without a maritime casualty; nothing must be removed unless it is a hazard; and once both are satisfied the Convention is just report, locate, mark, remove. Hang the money on the end: owner strictly liable, 300 GT insurance, direct action, three and six years.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Article 1(1) — Convention area, the exclusive economic zone.
Article 1(4) — definition of wreck, four categories, after a maritime casualty.
Article 1(5) and Article 6 — hazard, and the criteria for determining it.
Article 3(2) — optional extension to the territorial sea.
Articles 5, 7, 8, 9 — reporting, locating, marking, removal.
Article 10 — liability of the registered owner, and the three exceptions.
Article 11 — displacement by CLC, HNS, Bunkers and the nuclear conventions.
Article 12 — compulsory insurance at 300 GT, certificate, direct action.
Article 13 — three-year and six-year time limits.
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 — the Indian statute in force at this sitting.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction notes

blocks.p: The Convention text is a priced treaty-series publication and is held by the MIW corpus as citation and index only. Article effects are stated here and no wording is quoted; the Article numbering is carried as authoritative secondary and should be confirmed against the official text.

The corpus records India as having acceded but flags the date as unverified, so no accession date is stated. The party list is likewise not asserted: it is the one genuinely date-sensitive element of an otherwise stable instrument.

The Indian statute in force at this sitting is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and the exclusion of the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 is unusually clean on this paper. That Act received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026 — so a July 2025 sitting predates not merely its commencement but its existence as law in any sense. If you have read a later MIW answer that cites the 2025 Act, that answer belongs to a later sitting.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A three-stage legal question that moves outward: a definition, then an instrument, then consequences. Limb (a) is pure recall and is where the marks are cheapest - the examiner wants the Article 1(4) definition and its four categories, not a seaman's idea of a wreck. Limb (b) tests whether the candidate knows why the Convention was written at all. Limb (c) is the only limb asking for analysis, and it names two actors, so it must be answered in two named halves or half the marks are unreachable.

questions.understand_first: A wreck is not primarily an environmental problem in this Convention — it is an unallocated bill. Before it entered into force a ship could sink outside a coastal State's territorial sea, in water that State polices but does not own, and there was no clear international power to compel the owner to move it and no certainty that anybody solvent would pay. UNCLOS gave the coastal State rights in the exclusive economic zone but no removal machinery. The Nairobi Convention supplies the machinery, and the whole of it turns on one word: HAZARD. A wreck that endangers nothing is left alone. Once it is a hazard, four things follow mechanically — report it, locate it, mark it, remove it — and the registered owner pays, whether or not anyone was at fault, backed by insurance the State can sue directly. Read the question that way and limb (c) writes itself: the owner carries the cost and the liability, the coastal State carries the judgement and the power to act, and the environment is the reason both exist.

steps.title: The Convention and where it applies
points: Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007 - adopted 18 May 2007, in force 14 April 2015
The printed stem names only 'the Wreck Removal Convention', so supply the full title once
Applies in the Convention area - the exclusive economic zone of a State Party, Article 1(1)
A State Party may extend it to its own territorial sea by declaration under Article 3(2)
At this sitting the domestic Indian statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

steps.title: What "wreck" means - the four categories
points: Article 1(4): a wreck arises only "following upon a maritime casualty"
Category one - a sunken or stranded ship
Category two - any part of a sunken or stranded ship, including an object that is or has been on board
Category three - any object lost at sea from a ship, stranded, sunken or adrift
Category four - a ship about to sink or strand where effective assistance measures are not already being taken

steps.title: Hazard - the switch that turns the Convention on
points: Article 1(5): a danger or impediment to navigation, or a threat of major harmful consequences to the marine environment or to coastal and related interests
Article 6 lists the criteria - depth, proximity to routes, traffic density, type and quantity of cargo and oil, ship type and condition, weather and tidal exposure
No hazard, no removal duty: the Convention does not require every wreck to be lifted

steps.title: Objectives and key provisions
points: Objective one - a uniform international rule for prompt and effective removal beyond the territorial sea, which UNCLOS did not supply
Objective two - the cost falls on the owner and the owner's insurer, not on the coastal State's public purse
Objective three - legal certainty for owners, insurers and States about who does what, and by when
Machinery: report (Art 5), determine hazard (Art 6), locate (Art 7), mark (Art 8), remove (Art 9)
Financial security: strict liability (Art 10), compulsory insurance and direct action (Art 12), time bar (Art 13)

steps.title: The shipowner - strict liability and its limits
points: Article 10 makes the registered owner strictly liable for the cost of locating, marking and removing the wreck

Narrow exceptions only - act of war or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; wholly the act of a third party done with intent to cause damage; wholly the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids
Article 11 stands the Convention down where CLC, HNS, Bunkers or the nuclear conventions govern the same damage
Article 12 - compulsory insurance for ships of 300 GT and above, a certificate to be carried, and direct action against the insurer

Article 10(2) preserves the owner's right to limit under the applicable limitation regime, and Article 13 bars claims after three years from determination of the hazard and in any case six years from the casualty

steps.title: The coastal State - judgement, notice and intervention
points: Determines whether the wreck is a hazard, applying the Article 6 criteria
Informs the flag State and the registered owner, and warns mariners
Sets a reasonable deadline for the owner to remove, and may lay down conditions
May remove the wreck itself - immediately where the hazard is severe - and recover the cost from the owner
Its powers are not open-ended: measures must be proportionate to the hazard and exercised consistently with international law

Outside the Convention area, or in a territorial sea with no Article 3(2) declaration, the State acts under domestic law - in India, the wreck and salvage provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 through the Receiver of Wreck

steps.title: Environmental implications, and what the regime does not reach
points: The wreck itself is a continuing source - bunkers and cargo leaking over years, cargo residues, antifouling and other hazardous materials in the structure
Physical damage to the seabed, reefs and fishing grounds, plus obstruction of ports and routes
An unmarked wreck causes the next casualty, which is why marking sits inside an environmental instrument
Strict liability plus compulsory insurance is what converts an environmental risk into a funded removal
Limits: only wrecks that are hazards; only in the Convention area unless extended; liability is capped by the applicable limitation regime, so a very expensive removal can still exceed the fund

questions.memory_cue: Four categories, three actors, two numbers. CASUALTY then HAZARD (steps 2-3) - nothing happens without both. Then REPORT - LOCATE - MARK - REMOVE (4). Then OWNER PAYS (5), STATE DECIDES (6), SEA SUFFERS (7). The two numbers: 300 GT for insurance and 3 / 6 years for the time bar (5).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Nairobi WRC 2007, in force 14 April 2015. Applies in the EEZ (Art 1(1)); a State may extend it to its territorial sea (Art 3(2)). Wreck, Art 1(4), follows a maritime casualty and covers four things: a sunken or stranded ship; part of one, including anything that was on board; an object lost at sea and stranded, sunken or adrift; and a ship about to sink or strand where help is not already coming. It only bites if the wreck is a hazard (Art 1(5), criteria in Art 6). Then: report, locate, mark, remove. Article 10 makes the registered owner strictly liable; Article 12 requires insurance at 300 GT and allows direct action; Article 13 bars claims after 3 years from determination and 6 years from the casualty. Domestically at this sitting: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
critical_numbers: Adopted 18 May 2007; entered into force 14 April 2015
Four categories of wreck in Article 1(4)
Compulsory insurance for ships of 300 GT and above (Article 12)
Time bar: three years from determination of the hazard, and never later than six years from the maritime casualty (Article 13)
Convention area: the exclusive economic zone, or an equivalent zone not extending beyond 200 nautical miles (Article 1(1))
quick_revision.critical_regulation: Nairobi WRC Article 1(4) for the definition and the four categories, read with Article 1(5) 'hazard' - the definition is useless without the trigger. Article 10 then makes the registered owner strictly liable, and Article 12 backs that with compulsory insurance and direct action.
quick_revision.major_trap: Omitting the fourth category — a ship that is about to sink or strand — because it is not a wreck in ordinary speech. Second trap: saying the Convention applies in territorial waters. It applies in the exclusive economic zone; territorial sea coverage exists only where the State has opted in under Article 3(2). Third trap, specific to an Indian paper at this sitting: reaching for the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 for the domestic wreck provisions. That Act had not even received assent in July 2025 — the governing statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the wreck removal question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Convention and where it applies. 2 The four categories of wreck. 3 Hazard, the switch. 4 Objectives and provisions. 5 The shipowner. 6 The coastal State. 7 Environmental implications and limits. Sections 1-3 are limb (a), 4 is limb (b), 5-7 are limb (c).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (c) names two actors, so the route splits them; without that split half of the six marks has nowhere to land.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define "wreck" under the Nairobi Convention and list the categories.
retrieval_cards.answer: Following upon a maritime casualty: a sunken or stranded ship; any part of one, including any object that is or has been on board; any object lost at sea from a ship and stranded, sunken or adrift; and a ship that is about, or may reasonably be expected, to sink or strand where effective assistance measures are not already being taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Article 1(4). The last category is the one candidates lose the mark on.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a "hazard", and why does it matter more than the definition of wreck?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 1(5): a condition or threat that poses a danger or impediment to navigation, or that may reasonably be expected to result in major harmful consequences to the marine environment or damage to coastal and related interests. It matters more because the reporting, locating, marking, removal and liability machinery all hang off the hazard determination under Article 6 — a wreck that is not a hazard carries no removal duty at all.
retrieval_cards.why: Answering 'define wreck' without 'hazard' gives a correct definition that explains nothing about how the Convention works.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is liable under the Nairobi Convention, on what basis, and with what exceptions?
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 10 makes the registered owner strictly liable for the costs of locating, marking and removing the wreck — no proof of fault. Three narrow exceptions: act of war or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party acting with intent; damage wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids.
retrieval_cards.why: Strict is not absolute, and the word 'wholly' is what defeats most attempts to rely on the third-party defence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the insurance threshold and the two time limits.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 12: ships of 300 GT and above must maintain insurance or other financial security at least equal to the applicable limitation limits, carry a certificate, and the claim may be brought directly against the insurer. Article 13: claims are barred more than three years after the hazard was determined, and in no case later than six years after the maritime casualty.
retrieval_cards.why: Two time limits measured from two different events; expecting only one is the standard error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish Article 10 exceptions from Article 11 displacement.
retrieval_cards.answer: Article 10: the Convention applies but the owner is not liable on those particular facts, so the State may act and recovers nothing from this owner. Article 11: the Convention stands down because another liability regime — CLC 1992, HNS, Bunkers or the nuclear conventions — governs the same damage, so the State recovers under that regime instead and is not left uncovered.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates blur them, but one removes the remedy and the other relocates it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does wreck removal differ from salvage?
retrieval_cards.answer: Salvage is a voluntary service to property in danger, initiated by the salvor, rewarded on no-cure-no-pay, while the property can still be saved. Wreck removal is a compulsory duty on the registered owner, initiated by the affected State's hazard determination and deadline, carrying no reward — the owner bears the cost strictly. Article 9 lets the owner still contract with a salvor of his choice, so the market does the work; the Convention allocates the obligation and the bill.
retrieval_cards.why: A standard confusion, and Article 9 is what reconciles the two regimes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian statute governs wreck and salvage at a July 2025 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, administered through the Receiver of Wreck. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026 — so at this sitting it had not even been enacted, let alone commenced, and it is not the law for this paper.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the paper's standing statute trap, and on this sitting the exclusion is unusually clean: July 2025 predates the assent, not merely the commencement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A hazardous wreck lies in a State Party's EEZ. Set out the sequence of steps.
retrieval_cards.answer: Master and operator report the wreck to the affected State (Art 5). The State determines whether it is a hazard on the Article 6 criteria, and informs the flag State and the registered owner. The State locates it and warns mariners (Art 7) and marks it under the accepted buoyage system (Art 8). The owner removes it within a reasonable deadline; failing that — or immediately where the hazard is severe — the State removes it and recovers the cost (Art 9).
retrieval_cards.why: The Articles run in the order a real casualty unfolds, which is why learning them in sequence is worth more than learning them as a list.

blocks.h: 1. The problem that makes life-cycle accounting necessary

blocks.p: Every mandatory greenhouse gas measure in force at this examination — the EEXI, the CII and the fuel oil Data Collection System — counts emissions at the funnel. That is simple to administer and it produces a serious distortion. A ship burning ammonia or hydrogen emits no carbon dioxide, because there is no carbon in the molecule, whether the fuel was made from natural gas with the carbon vented or from renewable electricity. Measured at the funnel the two are identical.

The emissions have not gone; they have moved ashore, into a production plant the shipowner does not own and the regulation does not see. That is carbon leakage, and a rule that permits it does not merely fail to reduce emissions — it directs investment towards the wrong technology. Funnel-only accounting also mis-ranks the real candidates: LNG looks better than it is because methane slip and upstream leakage are invisible, and a biofuel looks the same whatever its feedstock.

blocks.h: 2. What life cycle analysis of a marine fuel is

blocks.p: Life Cycle Analysis is the systematic, quantified assessment of the greenhouse gas emissions associated with a fuel across its entire life, from the resource in the ground or the field through to its conversion in the ship's engine. Its output is a single comparable figure: the fuel's GHG intensity, in grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule of energy delivered. It is equivalent because methane and nitrous oxide are converted to a carbon dioxide basis at their global warming potentials, which matters greatly for gas fuels.

The IMO basis at this sitting. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80), requires its levels of ambition and checkpoints to take account of well-to-wake emissions as addressed in the LCA guidelines. The operative guidelines are the 2024 Guidelines on Life Cycle GHG Intensity of Marine Fuels, resolution MEPC.391(81), adopted 22 March 2024, whose paragraph 5 expressly revokes the earlier LCA Guidelines in MEPC.376(80). Cite the 2024 edition; the 2023 edition is revoked, not merely superseded. Note what these instruments are: a strategy and a set of guidelines. Neither is mandatory on a ship.

blocks.h: 3. The four methodological stages of an assessment

blocks.p: An assessment is conducted in four stages, iterative rather than strictly sequential:

rows: Why the study is being done and for whom; the functional unit — here, one megajoule of energy delivered for propulsion; the system boundary; and the assumptions and allocation rules
Quantify every input and output crossing the boundary at each stage — energy consumed, feedstock used, emissions released, co-products generated

Convert the inventory into impact categories. For fuels the dominant category is global warming potential, with methane and nitrous oxide expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent over a stated time horizon
Test the sensitivity of the result to the assumptions, state the uncertainty, check completeness and consistency, and draw conclusions honest about their limits

blocks.h: 4. The physical stages of a marine fuel pathway

blocks.p: Alongside the method, the fuel chain has stages, and these are what the inventory is built on:

ul: Feedstock — extraction, recovery or cultivation. Fugitive methane from gas production, and land-use change where a crop is grown for fuel, both enter here.
Processing and conversion — refining, liquefaction, synthesis or electrolysis. The electricity mix is decisive for hydrogen and its derivatives, and any carbon capture is credited here.
Transport, storage and distribution — moving the fuel to the bunkering port, including boil-off and handling losses.
Bunkering — transfer to the ship.
Onboard conversion — combustion in the engine or conversion in a fuel cell, including methane slip, nitrous oxide and the pilot fuel in a dual-fuel engine.

blocks.p: Cutting across all five are accounting decisions that decide the answer as much as the physics does: allocation between a process's main product and its co-products, the treatment of biogenic carbon, and end-of-life.

blocks.h: 5. Well-to-Tank, Tank-to-Wake and Well-to-Wake

rows: Feedstock, production, distribution and bunkering — ending when the fuel is in the ship's tank
The fuel producer and supplier. The shipowner buys it
Conversion onboard — combustion or fuel-cell operation, including methane slip, nitrous oxide and pilot fuel
The sum of the two — the complete figure
Nobody alone, which is the administrative difficulty

blocks.p: The relationship is arithmetic: WtW = WtT + TtW. Well-to-tank is therefore a component of well-to-wake rather than a rival to it, and the choice the question poses is really between the whole and one of its parts. Say so before choosing.

blocks.h: 6. Why well-to-wake is the feasible basis

ul: Well-to-tank alone is not usable for shipping at all. It measures the fuel supply chain and says nothing about the ship — two ships burning the same fuel at entirely different efficiency would carry the same figure.

Tank-to-wake alone is measurable but incentivises the wrong thing. It is easy to administer, which is exactly why CII was built that way — but it permits carbon leakage and treats grey and green ammonia as the same fuel.

Well-to-wake is the only defensible basis. It closes leakage, because an emission can leave the boundary only by not occurring; it ranks the candidate fuels correctly; and it captures both ends of the methane problem — upstream leakage and onboard slip — which neither half does alone.

blocks.p: It is also the basis the Organization has already chosen: MEPC.377(80) states the ambitions on a well-to-wake footing and MEPC.391(81) exists to make that operable. At MEPC 83 in April 2025 the Committee approved a draft new MARPOL Annex VI chapter with a well-to-wake GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism — approved only; it has not been adopted and is not law. The first binding well-to-wake regime is regional: FuelEU Maritime, Regulation (EU) 2023/1805, applying since 1 January 2025 to ships calling at European ports.

Conclusion. Well-to-wake is the feasible methodology. Well-to-tank is indispensable as its upstream half but is not a metric for a ship, and tank-to-wake alone would reward the appearance of decarbonisation over the fact of it.

blocks.h: 7. What makes it hard, and how the difficulty is managed

ul: The shipowner does not control, observe or audit the upstream half of his own fuel's emissions.
Upstream figures vary with feedstock, plant, electricity grid mix, season and route, and much of the data is commercially confidential.
Allocation between co-products and the treatment of land-use change are methodological choices that can change the result by more than the technology does.
Verification requires certification schemes and audited chains of custody, with a real risk of double counting where regional and global regimes overlap.

blocks.p: The practical resolution is a two-part system. The upstream half uses conservative default values for each pathway, which any supplier may improve upon by certifying an actual value through an audited scheme — so the burden of proof sits with the party who benefits from the better number. The onboard half uses measured consumption, which ships already record. That is why the guidelines matter as much as the strategy: without an agreed method for the well-to-tank half, a well-to-wake obligation could be declared but not administered.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The limbs are 8 and 8, so the answer gives them equal weight: three sections each, with section 1 as a shared opening. Two decisions inside that matter. First, limb (a) asks what LCA is and its stages, and "stages" is genuinely ambiguous between the four methodological stages of an assessment and the physical stages of the fuel chain. Giving both costs one extra section and removes the risk entirely. Second, limb (b) asks for a justification, not a description. An answer that defines WtW and WtT beautifully and never chooses between them forfeits half of an 8-mark limb.

blocks.h: The one sentence the whole question turns on

blocks.p: Resolution MEPC.377(80), paragraph 3.2: the levels of ambition and checkpoints take account of well-to-wake greenhouse gas emissions as addressed in the LCA guidelines. If you can attribute the well-to-wake basis to the Strategy and name the guidelines it points at, limb (b) has a regulatory backbone rather than being an opinion.

blocks.h: Which LCA guidelines are current, and the word that matters

blocks.p: The commonly cited resolution is MEPC.376(80), the 2023 LCA Guidelines, because the 2023 Strategy is what made the subject famous. It is not the operative instrument. Resolution MEPC.391(81), adopted 22 March 2024, carries the 2024 Guidelines on Life Cycle GHG Intensity of Marine Fuels, and its operative paragraph 5 revokes the LCA Guidelines adopted by MEPC.376(80).

Revoked, not superseded — and the distinction is worth a mark. A superseded instrument is displaced by a later edition but still describes a state of the world. A revoked one has been withdrawn by the body that made it. Citing MEPC.376(80) as the current LCA framework in a 2025 answer is citing an instrument that had been revoked for more than a year.

blocks.h: Why the fuels rank differently under the two bases

rows: No carbon in the molecule — zero CO2 at the funnel
Everything. The entire burden sits in production, and depends on whether the pathway is fossil-based, fossil-based with capture, or renewable
Lower CO2 than fuel oil, but methane slip from the engine
Upstream fugitive methane from extraction, processing and liquefaction — which can offset much of the funnel advantage
Biogenic carbon, so a low net figure at the funnel
Cultivation, fertiliser, processing and above all land-use change, which varies enormously by feedstock
Extraction, refining and distribution — a real but comparatively stable addition

blocks.p: This table is the answer to "justify your choice" in compact form: four fuels whose ranking changes when the boundary moves.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing the four methodological stages and calling them the fuel life cycle, or the reverse.
Treating WtT as an alternative to WtW rather than as part of it.
Forgetting tank-to-wake because the printed stem does not name it. WtW minus WtT is exactly TtW.
Omitting methane slip and pilot fuel from the onboard stage.
Citing MEPC.376(80) as the current LCA guidelines. It was revoked by MEPC.391(81) on 22 March 2024.
Describing the LCA guidelines as mandatory. They are guidelines, and the Strategy is a strategy.
Calling FuelEU Maritime an IMO measure.
Answering limb (b) without ever choosing a methodology.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking what zero-carbon fuel means. It means no carbon in the molecule, not zero emissions — lifecycle emissions depend on the production pathway.
Asking why CII does not solve this. Because it is a funnel measurement and sees nothing upstream of the bunker manifold.
Asking what a functional unit is, and why it must be energy delivered rather than tonnes of fuel. Fuels differ in calorific value, so mass is not comparable.
Asking who verifies the upstream figure — a certification scheme, not the ship.
Asking which is bigger, well-to-tank or tank-to-wake. It depends entirely on the fuel: for conventional fuel oil the onboard half dominates; for green hydrogen almost the whole burden is upstream.

Asking about the status of the GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism. At this sitting it is approved and not adopted. Saying "in force", or even "pending entry into force", is wrong — an instrument that has not been adopted has no entry into force to be pending.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your owner is considering ammonia. What questions would you ask the supplier?
What is methane slip and at what engine load is it worst?
Why does a bunker delivery note not tell you the fuel's GHG intensity?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: One number, two halves, four stages, five links. The number is gCO2eq/MJ; the halves are well-to-tank and tank-to-wake; the four stages are the method — goal, inventory, impact, interpretation; the five links are the chain — feedstock, production, distribution, bunkering, combustion. The verdict is well-to-wake, because leakage, and it is paid for by defaults plus certification.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency - what this sitting fixes and what it does not

blocks.p: This question sits on a moving instrument, and July 2025 is a clean place on it. Nothing this question engages moves inside July 2025. MEPC 83 closed on 11 April, and the amendments deemed accepted for the Data Collection System, MEPC.385(81), enter into force on 1 August 2025 — one day after the month closes, so they are not in force on any day of this sitting and are not relied on.

The guidelines edition is settled and is settled on primary evidence. MEPC.391(81) was read at source, so its identity, its adoption date and its revocation of MEPC.376(80) are primary-verified rather than carried. The answer to the same question at the January 2025 sitting carried that resolution at P2 with the express note that it had not been read; that limitation is discharged here. What was not read is the guidelines' default-value tables, and consistently with that no default value, emission factor or gCO2eq/MJ figure is quoted anywhere in this answer.

The Net-Zero Framework is the boundary to hold precisely. Its GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism was approved at MEPC 83 on 11 April 2025 — three months before this sitting, so approval is a safe historical fact and stating it scores. It was not adopted, and it may not be described as adopted, as in force, or as "pending entry into force". If you are reading a later MIW answer that describes GFI tiers and remedial unit prices as operative, that answer belongs to a later sitting.

The MIW True Source corpus does not hold MEPC.391(81) and its GHG instrument log presents the revoked MEPC.376(80) as current guidance. This answer departs from the corpus deliberately, on primary evidence, and the corpus defect has been raised as a correction request rather than fixed.

notes: NO BOUNDARY THIS QUESTION ENGAGES MOVES INSIDE JULY 2025. MEPC 83 closed 11 April 2025; MEPC.385(81) enters into force 1 August 2025, one day after the month closes. The answer is therefore day-independent within the sitting month, and that is a property of the calendar rather than an assumption.

THE OPERATIVE LCA EDITION IS MEPC.391(81) AND MEPC.376(80) IS REVOKED, NOT SUPERSEDED. MEPC.391(81) was adopted 22 March 2024 - BEFORE BOTH the January donor sitting and this one - and its operative paragraph 5 revokes MEPC.376(80). Because the change predates both sittings there is NO donor temporal delta on the guidelines edition; what changed is the EVIDENCE, from P2 not-read to P1 read at source.

THE NET-ZERO FRAMEWORK PROHIBITION NARROWS BETWEEN THE DONOR AND THIS PAPER, AND THAT IS THE ONE SUBSTANTIVE TEMPORAL DELTA. At January 2025 the April approval had not happened and could not be mentioned at all. At July 2025 the approval at MEPC 83 on 11 April 2025 is a statable historical fact. What remains absolutely prohibited is unchanged: adopted, in force, or 'pending entry into force'. MEPC/ES.2 (October 2025) is post-sitting and is excluded.

FUELEU MARITIME PHRASING RE-ANCHORED. The donor says it 'began to apply in the sitting month itself' - true of January 2025 and false of July 2025. Restated as applying SINCE 1 January 2025. It remains labelled a REGIONAL European Union instrument; calling it an IMO measure is the second available error on this question.

THE IMO WELL-TO-WAKE MANDATE AT THIS SITTING IS STILL A STRATEGY PLUS GUIDELINES, NOT A MANDATORY MEASURE. The mandatory MARPOL Annex VI measures in force are EEXI, SEEMP, DCS and CII - and CII is measured at the funnel, which is precisely the gap this question is about.

CORPUS DEFECT ENGAGED AND NOT FOLLOWED. The corpus GHG instrument log routes LCA demand to MEPC.376(80) and marks it GUIDANCE with no supersession note. Following the corpus here would have produced a confident, well-structured answer citing an instrument revoked in March 2024. TRUE_SOURCE_CORRECTION_REQUEST raised; corpus not modified.

MEPC.328(76) IS NOT ENGAGED. The open correction request about that resolution's entry-into-force date concerns the revised Annex VI itself, not the LCA guideline layer. Referenced and left open; not reopened and not duplicated.

technical_ambiguities: 'Stages of Life Cycle Analysis' is ambiguous. It can mean the four methodological stages of an assessment - goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment, interpretation - or the physical stages of the fuel pathway. The answer gives BOTH, in that order, and says why.

questions.understand_first: The whole subject exists because of one accounting mistake that was easy to make and expensive to keep. If you measure a ship's greenhouse gas emissions at the funnel — which is what every operational measure in force at this sitting does — then a ship burning ammonia scores zero for carbon dioxide, whether that ammonia was made from natural gas with the carbon vented to atmosphere or from renewable electricity. The emissions did not disappear; they moved ashore, into a plant the shipowner does not own and the regulation does not see. That is carbon leakage, and a decarbonisation rule that rewards it is worse than no rule, because it funds the wrong technology with real money. Life cycle analysis is the fix. Count the emissions of the fuel from the well or the field, through production, transport and bunkering, and on through combustion in the engine — and express the result as one number, the greenhouse gas intensity of the energy the ship actually uses. The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy adopted exactly that basis, and the 2024 LCA Guidelines are the method for computing it. Everything else in this question — the stages, the boundaries, the well-to-tank and tank-to-wake split, and the argument about feasibility — is machinery for producing that one number honestly.

steps.title: The problem that makes life-cycle accounting necessary
points: Every mandatory measure in force at this sitting - EEXI, CII, the Data Collection System - counts emissions at the funnel
A zero-carbon fuel at the funnel is not necessarily a low-carbon fuel: ammonia and hydrogen carry the emissions of their production pathway
Counting only at the funnel therefore permits CARBON LEAKAGE - the emission is moved ashore rather than removed
It also mis-ranks fuels: LNG loses on methane slip, biofuels win or lose on feedstock and land use, and none of that is visible at the funnel

steps.title: What life cycle analysis of a marine fuel is
points: A systematic, quantified assessment of the greenhouse gas emissions of a fuel across its entire life, from resource to use
The output is a GHG INTENSITY: mass of carbon dioxide equivalent per unit of energy delivered, in grams of CO2 equivalent per megajoule
Carbon dioxide equivalent because methane and nitrous oxide are converted at their global warming potentials
The IMO basis at this sitting: the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80), requires the ambitions and checkpoints to take account of WELL-TO-WAKE emissions as addressed in the LCA guidelines

The operative guidelines are the 2024 Guidelines on Life Cycle GHG Intensity of Marine Fuels, resolution MEPC.391(81), adopted 22 March 2024, whose paragraph 5 REVOKES the LCA Guidelines adopted by MEPC.376(80)
Both are GUIDELINES - recommendatory, not mandatory on a ship

steps.title: The four methodological stages of an assessment
points: GOAL AND SCOPE DEFINITION - why the study is being done, the functional unit (one megajoule of energy delivered), and the system boundary
INVENTORY ANALYSIS - quantify every input and output across the boundary: energy, feedstock, emissions, co-products
IMPACT ASSESSMENT - convert the inventory into impact categories, principally global warming potential expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent
INTERPRETATION - test sensitivity and uncertainty, check completeness and consistency, and state the conclusions and their limits
The stages are iterative: an inventory result routinely sends the analyst back to the boundary

steps.title: The physical stages of a marine fuel pathway
points: FEEDSTOCK - extraction, recovery or cultivation, including any land-use change for a biofuel and any fugitive methane from gas production
PROCESSING AND CONVERSION - refining, liquefaction, synthesis or electrolysis, including the electricity mix used and any carbon capture
TRANSPORT, STORAGE AND DISTRIBUTION - moving the fuel to the bunkering port, with boil-off and losses
BUNKERING - transfer to the ship
ONBOARD CONVERSION - combustion or fuel-cell conversion in service, including methane slip, nitrous oxide and pilot fuel
Plus the accounting questions that cut across them: allocation between co-products, end-of-life, and the treatment of biogenic carbon

steps.title: Well-to-Tank, Tank-to-Wake and Well-to-Wake
points: WELL-TO-TANK is everything upstream - feedstock, production, distribution and bunkering - ending when the fuel is in the ship's tank
TANK-TO-WAKE is everything onboard - conversion in the engine or fuel cell, including slip and pilot fuel
WELL-TO-WAKE is the sum of the two, and is the complete figure
So WtT is a COMPONENT of WtW, not an alternative to it - the choice the question poses is really between the whole and one of its parts
The two parts differ in who controls them: the shipowner controls tank-to-wake and buys well-to-tank from someone else

steps.title: Why well-to-wake is the feasible basis
points: It is the only basis that closes carbon leakage - the emission cannot be moved out of the boundary, only out of existence
It is the basis the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy adopted for its ambitions and checkpoints, and MEPC.391(81) exists to make it operable
Only WtW ranks the candidate fuels correctly: green, blue and grey ammonia are the same fuel at the funnel and entirely different fuels over the life cycle
It captures both ends of the methane problem - upstream leakage and onboard slip - which neither half does alone
Well-to-tank alone is not a usable metric for a ship: it says nothing about the ship's own operation
Tank-to-wake alone is measurable and enforceable but incentivises the wrong thing, which is why CII being a funnel measure is a known limitation rather than a model
At MEPC 83 in April 2025 the Committee APPROVED a draft new MARPOL Annex VI chapter carrying a well-to-wake GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism - approved only, NOT adopted and not law
The first binding well-to-wake regime is regional, not IMO: FuelEU Maritime has applied since 1 January 2025 to energy used by ships calling at European ports

steps.title: What makes it hard, and how the difficulty is managed
points: The shipowner does not control, observe or audit the upstream half of his own fuel's emissions
Upstream data varies with feedstock, plant, electricity grid mix and season, and is commercially sensitive
Allocation between co-products, and the treatment of land-use change, are methodological choices that materially change the answer
Verification, certification and the risk of double counting across regimes all add administrative burden

The practical answer is a two-part system: CONSERVATIVE DEFAULT VALUES for the upstream half, which any supplier may improve upon by CERTIFYING an actual value, combined with MEASURED consumption onboard
That is why the guidelines matter as much as the strategy: without an agreed method for the well-to-tank half, a well-to-wake obligation could not be administered

questions.memory_cue: One number, two halves, four stages, five links. The number is GRAMS CO2 EQUIVALENT PER MEGAJOULE (2). The halves are WELL TO TANK and TANK TO WAKE, and their sum is WELL TO WAKE (5). The four stages are the method (3); the five links are the fuel chain - FEEDSTOCK, PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION, BUNKERING, COMBUSTION (4). The verdict is WELL TO WAKE, because leakage (6), paid for by DEFAULTS AND CERTIFICATION (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: LCA counts a fuel's greenhouse gases from resource to funnel and reports one number - gCO2eq per MJ. Method has four stages: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment, interpretation. The fuel chain has five links: feedstock, production, distribution, bunkering, onboard conversion. WtT is everything up to the ship's tank; TtW is everything onboard including methane slip; WtW = WtT + TtW. The feasible basis is well-to-wake, because funnel-only accounting permits carbon leakage and makes grey and green ammonia identical. IMO adopted that basis in the 2023 GHG Strategy, MEPC.377(80); the operative method is the 2024 LCA Guidelines, MEPC.391(81), which revoked MEPC.376(80) - both guidelines, not mandatory. The GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 and NOT adopted. The only binding well-to-wake regime is regional: FuelEU Maritime, since 1 January 2025. The difficulty is upstream data, solved by default values plus certified actual values.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Resolution MEPC.377(80) paragraph 3.2 - the ambitions and checkpoints take account of well-to-wake emissions as addressed in the LCA guidelines. Those guidelines are the 2024 edition, resolution MEPC.391(81), whose paragraph 5 revokes MEPC.376(80). Together those two sentences give limb (b) a regulatory backbone and fix the edition.
quick_revision.major_trap: Citing MEPC.376(80) as the current LCA framework. It was revoked by MEPC.391(81) paragraph 5 on 22 March 2024, more than a year before this sitting - and much circulating material, including instrument indexes, still presents it as current. Second trap: over-stating the Net-Zero Framework. Its GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism was approved at MEPC 83 in April 2025 and was not adopted; describing it as adopted, in force, or 'pending entry into force' is wrong, because an instrument that has not been adopted has no entry into force to be pending. Third trap: calling FuelEU Maritime an IMO measure - it is a European Union regulation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the life cycle analysis question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Why funnel-only accounting fails. 2 What LCA is and the IMO basis. 3 The four methodological stages. 4 The five physical fuel-chain stages. 5 WtT, TtW and WtW defined. 6 Why well-to-wake is the feasible basis. 7 What makes it hard and how that is managed. Sections 2-4 are limb (a), 5-7 limb (b).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) asks what LCA is AND its stages, and "stages" is ambiguous - the answer gives the methodological four and the physical five.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define well-to-tank, tank-to-wake and well-to-wake.
retrieval_cards.answer: Well-to-tank is every emission from feedstock extraction or cultivation through production, transport, storage and bunkering, ending when the fuel is in the ship's tank. Tank-to-wake is every emission from conversion onboard, including methane slip, nitrous oxide and pilot fuel. Well-to-wake is the sum of the two.
retrieval_cards.why: WtT is a component of WtW, not an alternative - saying so is what makes the limb (b) comparison coherent.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the four methodological stages of a life cycle assessment.
retrieval_cards.answer: Goal and scope definition, including the functional unit and system boundary; inventory analysis of all inputs and outputs; impact assessment converting the inventory into impact categories, principally global warming potential; and interpretation, with sensitivity, uncertainty and the limits of the conclusion.
retrieval_cards.why: The stages are iterative - an inventory result routinely sends the analyst back to the boundary.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is tank-to-wake accounting alone unacceptable?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because it permits carbon leakage. A fuel with no carbon in the molecule scores zero at the funnel regardless of how it was made, so grey and green ammonia are indistinguishable and the emission is moved ashore rather than removed. It also mis-ranks fuels whose upstream burden differs sharply, such as biofuels and LNG.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the justification limb (b) actually asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which LCA guidelines resolution is operative, and what happened to its predecessor?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2024 Guidelines on Life Cycle GHG Intensity of Marine Fuels, resolution MEPC.391(81), adopted 22 March 2024. Its operative paragraph 5 revokes the LCA Guidelines adopted by resolution MEPC.376(80). Revoked, not merely superseded - MEPC.376(80) was withdrawn by the Committee that made it.
retrieval_cards.why: MEPC.376(80) is the famous one and is still widely cited as current. Naming the 2024 edition, and the verb 'revokes', is a checkable mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the status of the GHG Fuel Intensity mechanism at a July 2025 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Approved and not adopted. MEPC 83 approved a draft new MARPOL Annex VI chapter carrying it on 11 April 2025. Approval is a statable fact at this sitting. It is not adopted, not in force, and not 'pending entry into force' - an instrument that has not been adopted has no entry into force to be pending.
retrieval_cards.why: Approved, adopted and in force are three states with three dates, and this is the question on the paper where collapsing them is easiest.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which binding well-to-wake regime applied at this sitting, and from when?
retrieval_cards.answer: FuelEU Maritime, Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 - a regional European Union instrument applying since 1 January 2025 to the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used by ships calling at European ports. It is not an IMO measure.
retrieval_cards.why: The IMO instruments at this sitting are a strategy and guidelines; the only binding well-to-wake obligation is regional, and its character is the trap.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the upstream data problem managed in practice?
retrieval_cards.answer: By a two-part system: conservative default values for the well-to-tank half, which any supplier may improve upon by certifying an actual value through an audited scheme, combined with measured fuel consumption onboard for the tank-to-wake half.
retrieval_cards.why: It is why the guidelines matter as much as the strategy - a well-to-wake obligation with no agreed upstream method could not be administered.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does CII relate to life cycle analysis?
retrieval_cards.answer: It does not measure the same thing. CII is an operational carbon intensity measure computed from fuel consumed and distance sailed - a funnel measurement - so it sees nothing upstream of the bunker manifold. That gap is precisely what life cycle accounting exists to close.
retrieval_cards.why: Contrasting the mandatory measure in force with the basis the strategy adopts shows why the subject is live rather than theoretical.

blocks.h: (a) Standard charter parties and their advantages — 4 marks
1. What a standard charter party is

blocks.p: A charter party is the contract by which a shipowner places a ship, or her carrying capacity, at a charterer's disposal. A standard charter party is one written on a pre-printed industry form published by a recognised body — shipowner and charterer associations, trade bodies and the oil and dry-bulk majors — whose wording has been negotiated between representative interests and settled by long use, rather than drafted from scratch for the fixture.

In practice the parties take the printed form and add a rider of additional clauses and amendments, so a fixture is the standard form as amended. Three families answer three different commercial questions:

ul: Voyage charter — the ship is engaged for a stated voyage with a stated cargo. Dry-cargo and tanker voyage forms are the everyday examples, and freight, laytime and demurrage are the commercial heart of them.

Time charter — the ship is at the charterer's disposal for a period, the charterer directing employment and paying hire and, ordinarily, for bunkers and port charges. The New York Produce Exchange form and the oil-major time forms are the standard examples.

Bareboat or demise charter — the charterer takes possession, mans and operates the ship as if owner for the period. This is the form that matters most for limbs (c) and (d), because the demise charterer steps into the owner's shoes.

blocks.h: 2. The advantages of using a standard form

ol: Certainty of meaning. The wording has been litigated and arbitrated for decades, so both parties know what it means before they argue about it. That is the single largest advantage and it cannot be bought any other way.
Speed and cost of fixing. A fixture can be concluded on a form and a short rider in hours. Negotiating a bespoke contract for each voyage would make the chartering market unworkable.

Balance. The forms are drafted or approved by bodies representing both owners and charterers, so the printed allocation of risk starts from a recognised middle rather than from whichever party drafted first.

Compatibility with the rest of the industry. Brokers, P&I clubs, underwriters, banks, arbitrators and courts all know the forms. Cover, security and finance attach to them without special explanation, and standard clause sets for war risks, sanctions, security and emissions can be bolted on as published.
Completeness. A printed form covers the unglamorous eventualities — off-hire, lien, general average, arbitration, notices — that a hurriedly drafted contract omits and then has to litigate.
Fewer disputes, and cheaper ones. Where a dispute does arise, the issue is usually confined to the rider clause the parties actually negotiated rather than to the whole contract.

blocks.p: The corresponding caution, worth one line: the printed form is a starting point. Riders routinely reverse the printed allocation of risk, and it is the amended contract, not the form's reputation, that governs.

blocks.h: (b) Risks covered under charterer's liability insurance — 4 marks
3. What the cover is, and what it reaches

blocks.p: A charterer is not the owner of the ship, so the hull and machinery policy is not his and the owner's P&I entry does not answer for his liabilities. Charterer's liability insurance — written as a charterer's entry with a P&I club or by the fixed-premium market — is the cover that fills that gap. The risks it customarily reaches are these.

ul: Damage to the chartered ship herself. Ordinarily the charterer's largest single exposure, and the one candidates miss. It arises from breach of the safe port and safe berth warranty, from unsafe or damaging cargo, and from bunkers supplied off-specification or contaminated where the charterer supplies them.

Cargo liability — claims by cargo interests where the charterer is the contracting carrier under the bill of lading, and claims passed to him through the charterparty indemnity chain. See limbs (c) below.
Pollution liability arising from the charterer's own operations, including a spill during a bunkering he arranged and pollution from the cargo he ordered carried.
Third-party liabilities — damage to fixed and floating objects such as berths, cranes, buoys and pipelines; and contributions towards wreck removal.
Personal injury, illness and death claims where the charterer's own act, order or operation gives rise to liability.
General average and salvage contributions on interests the charterer owns — his bunkers and, where he carries the risk, freight.
Loss of or damage to the charterer's bunkers on board.
Fines and penalties — customs, immigration and pollution penalties attributable to the charterer's operation, so far as insurable.

Defence cover — the legal costs of pursuing and defending charterparty disputes: hire and off-hire, laytime and demurrage, speed and consumption, bunker quality and cargo claims. This is usually a separate but closely allied cover and it is where most charterers actually use their insurers.

blocks.p: Two limits should be stated. The cover answers for liabilities, not for the charterer's own commercial losses — an unprofitable fixture or unpaid hire is a credit risk, not an insured peril. And it responds to the charterer's legal liability, so it does not reach loss caused by his own wilful misconduct or by trading in breach of a warranty of the entry.

blocks.h: (c) The charterer and cargo loss or damage under the bill of lading — 4 marks
4. The answer turns on who the carrier is

blocks.p: Yes, a charterer can be liable — but not because he is a charterer. He is liable if, and only if, he is the carrier under the bill of lading, because the bill is a contract of carriage between the holder and the carrier and it is the carrier who answers to the holder for cargo loss or damage.
So the question is who is the carrier on this bill, and that is decided by the bill itself rather than by the charterparty, to which the cargo holder is a stranger.

ol: An owner's bill. Where the bill is signed by the master, or by an agent expressly for and on behalf of the master, it is ordinarily the shipowner's contract. The shipowner is the carrier, and the cargo claimant sues him. The charterer is not liable to the holder.

A charterer's bill. Where the charterer or his agent signs in his own name as carrier, or the form identifies the charterer as carrier, the charterer is the contracting carrier and is liable to the holder for cargo loss or damage.
A bareboat charter. The demise charterer possesses and operates the ship as if owner, so bills issued for her are ordinarily his contracts and he is the carrier.

Identity-of-carrier and demise provisions. Many forms carry printed provisions designed to identify the shipowner as carrier whoever signed. Their effect is a matter of construction of the particular bill.

blocks.p: Where the charterer is the carrier, his liability is governed by the applicable cargo regime — the Hague or Hague-Visby Rules as given effect by the applicable law, and in India by the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 for carriage covered by a bill of lading. He then owes the carrier's obligations: to exercise due diligence to make the ship seaworthy before and at the beginning of the voyage, and properly and carefully to load, handle, stow, carry, keep, care for and discharge the cargo. He has the carrier's defences — the catalogue of excepted perils — and the carrier's limitation per package or unit.

blocks.h: 5. And the indemnity chain can put the claim back on him anyway

blocks.p: This is the part that turns a competent answer into a good one. Even where the bill is an owner's bill, so that the shipowner is sued by the cargo interest, the loss frequently ends with the charterer, by two routes:

ul: The employment and indemnity obligation. A time charterer directs the ship's employment and requires the master to sign bills as presented; in return the owner is entitled to be indemnified against the consequences of complying with those orders. If the charterer's orders produced the exposure, the charterer bears it.

Inter-club apportionment. Time charters on the New York Produce Exchange form customarily incorporate an inter-club agreement under which cargo claims are apportioned between owner and charterer by the cause of the loss — unseaworthiness on one side, loading, stowage, handling and discharge operations on the other, with a residual split for everything else. It is a mechanical allocation designed to settle claims without litigating fault.

blocks.p: Conclusion for limb (c). The charterer is liable to the cargo holder where he is the carrier on the bill — a charterer's bill, or a demise charter. Where he is not, he is not liable to the holder; but he may still end up paying, through the indemnity and apportionment machinery of the charterparty.

blocks.h: (d) Charterers and oil pollution compensation under the IMO conventions — 4 marks
6. Channelling, and the one convention whose definition reaches a charterer

blocks.p: Here the answer is largely no, and the reason is a deliberate design feature of the conventions — but there is one important exception and it must be identified precisely.

CLC 1992 — no. The Convention makes the registered owner strictly liable, and Article III(4) then channels liability to him: claims for pollution damage may not be made against a list of protected persons which expressly includes any charterer, howsoever described, including a bareboat charterer, together with the servants and agents of the owner, the crew, the pilot, the salvor and those taking preventive measures. Channelling is the point of the regime: the cargo claimant gets a single, identifiable, compulsorily insured defendant and does not have to litigate against a chain of commercial parties.

The exception is narrow and is the examinable detail. The protection is lost where the damage resulted from that person's own personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such damage, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result. That is a very high threshold, and ordinary negligence by a charterer does not come near it.

The 2001 Bunkers Convention — yes, but only a bareboat charterer. This is the point most candidates get wrong in both directions. The Bunkers Convention does not channel to the registered owner. Its Article 1(3) defines 'shipowner' widely, to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator of the ship, and those persons are jointly and severally liable for pollution damage caused by bunker oil. So a bareboat charterer is squarely within the liable class. A time or voyage charterer is not, because he is neither bareboat charterer, manager nor operator. Note also that the compulsory insurance duty falls on the registered owner alone, so the certificate is his even though the liability is shared.

The pattern across the family. The Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention likewise makes the registered owner strictly liable. The HNS Convention 2010 would channel similarly, but it was not in force at this sitting and cannot be relied on. So the design is consistent: one identified, insured defendant per casualty, and the Bunkers definition is the deliberate exception because a bunker spill can as easily be the act of the party operating the ship as of the party owning her.

And one honest qualification. Channelling bars claims for pollution damage under the Convention. It does not make a charterer immune from everything: he can still be liable to the owner under the charterparty — for breach of the safe port warranty or for supplying off-specification bunkers — and national liability regimes outside the IMO conventions may reach charterers on their own terms. What the charterer is protected from is the pollution claimant, not from the owner's recourse.

Conclusion for limb (d). Under CLC, no — liability is channelled to the registered owner and charterers are expressly protected, save for intent or recklessness with knowledge. Under the Bunkers Convention, a bareboat charterer yes, jointly and severally with the registered owner, manager and operator; a time or voyage charterer no. Under HNS, the question does not arise at this sitting because the Convention is not in force.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Four limbs of four marks each, and they are not four questions about the same thing — they run from commercial document to insurance to cargo liability to pollution liability. The commonest failure is to spend half the answer on limb (a), which is the cheapest and most familiar, and then to give one thin paragraph each to (c) and (d), which are the two limbs that actually discriminate between candidates. Six sections, weighted so that (c) and (d) get two sections and one long one respectively, prevent that.

Both (c) and (d) begin with the word 'Discuss if'. That is an invitation to give a conditional answer with the condition stated — not a yes and not a no. In (c) the condition is who the carrier is; in (d) it is which convention and which kind of charterer. An answer that says simply 'yes' or simply 'no' to either has missed what was being tested.

blocks.h: The two hinges

blocks.p: Limb (c) hinges on the identity of the carrier. The bill of lading is a contract with the carrier, and the cargo holder is a stranger to the charterparty. So the charterer is liable to the holder only if the bill is his contract — a charterer's bill, or bills under a demise charter. Master's signature, or an agent signing for the master, ordinarily makes it the owner's.

Limb (d) hinges on channelling, and on one definition. CLC channels liability to the registered owner and expressly protects charterers; the Bunkers Convention does not channel and defines 'shipowner' widely enough to catch a bareboat charterer. Hold those two side by side and the limb writes itself.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Spending half the answer on limb (a). It is four marks and it is the easiest four.
Answering (c) with a flat yes or no. The stem says 'discuss if' — state the condition, which is the identity of the carrier.
Saying the charterer is liable under the bill because he chartered the ship. The cargo holder is a stranger to the charterparty; only the bill matters to him.
Saying charterers are never liable for oil pollution. A bareboat charterer is within the liable class under the Bunkers Convention.
Saying charterers are liable under CLC. They are expressly protected by the channelling provision.
Treating the CLC exception as though ordinary negligence defeated the protection. It requires intent, or recklessness with knowledge that such damage would probably result.
Listing the HNS Convention as an operative source of charterer liability. It was not in force at this sitting.
Omitting damage to the chartered ship from limb (b). It is usually the charterer's biggest exposure.
Quoting a clause number or edition of a standard form, or an apportionment percentage. Several editions run concurrently and the agreement has been revised.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: The stem prints 'Charter's Liability Insurance' for 'Charterer's'. Answer the question the examiner set; do not comment on the typography.
'Enumerate' in limb (a) is a command for a list. Give numbered advantages, not a paragraph.
'Discuss if' appears twice, in (c) and (d). Both want a reasoned conditional answer, and both have a clean condition available.
Asking who the carrier is on a bill signed by the port agent. It depends on the capacity in which he signed — for the master, or for the charterer.
Asking whether a time charterer is liable under the Bunkers Convention. No — only a bareboat charterer is within the definition, alongside the manager and the operator.
Asking who holds the Bunkers certificate. The registered owner, even though liability is joint and several.
Asking what the charterer's insurance would not pay. Unpaid hire and an unprofitable fixture — those are commercial losses, not liabilities.
