blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: This is the least corpus-supported question on the paper and the only one with no earlier sitting of the same question to draw on. The True Source corpus holds no charter-party form, no BIMCO document, no P&I club rulebook and no policy wording, and it holds the liability conventions at citation and index level only. Nothing in this answer rests on a document that was read.

The discipline applied is the same one used on the paper's other gapped questions: refuse precision rather than invent it. Accordingly no form edition, revision year or clause number is asserted; no package or unit limitation figure is quoted, because it depends on which version of the regime applies; no apportionment percentage from any inter-club agreement is asserted, because the agreement has been revised and no version is held; no section number of the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 is asserted; and no case authority is cited anywhere, on the identity of the carrier, on demise clauses, or on the reach of the CLC channelling provision.

The two load-bearing legal points — CLC Article III(4) channelling and the Bunkers Article 1(3) wide definition — are stated by Article and by effect rather than by quotation, and they are flagged for confirmation. They are also the two points on which this answer is internally consistent with Q1 of this paper, which applies the same distinction between the registered owner under Nairobi and CLC and the wide class under Bunkers.

Nothing here is sitting-sensitive. The forms are commercial and undated in this answer; the cargo regime and the Indian statute long predate the sitting; CLC and Bunkers were in force and unamended across the window; and the HNS Convention's not-in-force status is stated rather than assumed. Note also that no Merchant Shipping Act is engaged by this question — the statute boundary that governs Q9 of this paper does not reach it.

questions.understand_first: Three of these four limbs are really one question asked three times: when does a commercial party who is not the shipowner end up paying? A charterer hires the ship but does not own her, and the whole of maritime liability law is built around the registered owner as the identified, insured defendant. So the interesting answer in each limb is the exception. In limb (b) it is that the charterer's biggest insured risk is not some third party at all — it is damage to the ship he chartered, caused by sending her to an unsafe berth or filling her with bad bunkers. In limb (c) it is that he answers to a cargo holder only if he is the carrier on the bill, which is decided by who signed it and in what capacity, not by the charterparty the cargo holder has never seen. And in limb (d) it is that CLC deliberately channels him out of pollution liability altogether — the Convention names charterers among the protected persons — while the Bunkers Convention does not channel at all and defines 'shipowner' widely enough to catch a bareboat charterer alongside the manager and the operator. Hold the pattern — owner by default, charterer by exception, and name the exception — and all four limbs have a spine.

steps.title: What a standard charter party is
points: a charter party is the contract by which an owner places the ship, or her capacity, at a charterer's disposal
a STANDARD charter party is a pre-printed industry form published by a recognised body, its wording negotiated between representative interests and settled by long use
in practice the fixture is the printed form AS AMENDED by a rider of additional and amending clauses
VOYAGE charter - a stated voyage with a stated cargo; freight, laytime and demurrage are its commercial heart
TIME charter - the ship at the charterer's disposal for a period, the charterer directing employment and paying hire and ordinarily bunkers and port charges
BAREBOAT or DEMISE charter - the charterer takes possession, mans and operates her as if owner; this is the form that decides limbs (c) and (d)

steps.title: The advantages of using a standard form
points: CERTAINTY OF MEANING - the wording has been litigated and arbitrated for decades, which is the largest advantage and cannot be bought another way
SPEED AND COST - a fixture concludes on a form and a short rider in hours; bespoke drafting per voyage would make the market unworkable
BALANCE - drafted or approved by bodies representing both owners and charterers, so the printed risk allocation starts from a recognised middle
COMPATIBILITY - brokers, clubs, underwriters, banks, arbitrators and courts all know the forms, and published clause sets bolt on
COMPLETENESS - off-hire, lien, general average, arbitration and notices are all covered rather than omitted and litigated
FEWER AND CHEAPER DISPUTES - argument is usually confined to the rider clause the parties actually negotiated
THE CAUTION: the form is a starting point, and riders routinely reverse the printed allocation of risk

steps.title: What the cover is, and what it reaches
points: the hull policy is the owner's and the owner's P&I entry does not answer for the charterer's liabilities - charterer's cover fills that gap, written as a charterer's entry or by the fixed-premium market
DAMAGE TO THE CHARTERED SHIP HERSELF is ordinarily the charterer's largest exposure - unsafe port or berth, damaging cargo, and off-specification or contaminated bunkers he supplied
CARGO LIABILITY where he is the contracting carrier, and cargo claims passed to him through the charterparty indemnity chain
POLLUTION arising from his own operations, including a bunkering he arranged
THIRD-PARTY LIABILITIES - damage to fixed and floating objects, and contributions to wreck removal

personal injury, illness and death claims attributable to his act or order; general average and salvage contributions on his bunkers and freight; loss of or damage to his bunkers; fines and penalties so far as insurable
DEFENCE COVER for charterparty disputes - hire and off-hire, laytime and demurrage, speed and consumption, bunker quality
THE TWO LIMITS: it insures LIABILITIES not commercial losses, so unpaid hire and an unprofitable fixture are outside it; and it does not answer for wilful misconduct or trading in breach of warranty

steps.title: The answer turns on who the carrier is
points: YES - but not because he is a charterer. He is liable to the cargo holder only if he is the CARRIER under the bill
the bill of lading is a contract between holder and carrier, and the holder is a STRANGER to the charterparty
OWNER'S BILL - signed by the master, or by an agent for and on behalf of the master: the shipowner is the carrier
CHARTERER'S BILL - signed by the charterer or his agent in his own name as carrier: the charterer is the carrier and is liable to the holder
BAREBOAT CHARTER - the demise charterer possesses and operates her as if owner, so bills are ordinarily his contracts
identity-of-carrier and demise provisions on the form may identify the shipowner as carrier whoever signed; their effect is a matter of construction

where he IS the carrier his liability is the Hague or Hague-Visby liability - due diligence to make her seaworthy, and proper care of the cargo - with the carrier's defences and package limitation, given domestic effect in India by the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925

steps.title: And the indemnity chain can put the claim back on him anyway
points: even on an OWNER'S bill, where the shipowner is sued, the loss frequently ends with the charterer
EMPLOYMENT AND INDEMNITY - the time charterer directs employment and requires bills to be signed as presented, and the owner is entitled to be indemnified against the consequences of complying

INTER-CLUB APPORTIONMENT - time charters on the New York Produce Exchange form customarily apportion cargo claims between owner and charterer BY THE CAUSE of the loss, mechanically, without litigating fault
CONCLUSION: liable to the holder if he is the carrier; and liable to the owner through the charterparty even if he is not

steps.title: Channelling, and the one convention whose definition reaches a charterer
points: LARGELY NO, and the reason is a deliberate design feature of the conventions - but there is one exception and it must be named precisely

CLC 1992 - MAKES THE REGISTERED OWNER STRICTLY LIABLE, and Article III(4) CHANNELS liability to him, barring claims against a protected list that expressly includes any charterer howsoever described, INCLUDING A BAREBOAT CHARTERER
the point of channelling is that the claimant gets a single identifiable compulsorily insured defendant and need not litigate a chain of commercial parties

THE EXCEPTION IS NARROW: protection is lost only for that person's own act or omission committed WITH INTENT, or RECKLESSLY AND WITH KNOWLEDGE that such damage would probably result - ordinary negligence comes nowhere near it

BUNKERS 2001 - does NOT channel. Article 1(3) defines 'shipowner' WIDELY as the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally liable, so A BAREBOAT CHARTERER IS LIABLE and a time or voyage charterer is not
the compulsory insurance duty under Bunkers still falls on the REGISTERED OWNER alone, so the certificate is his though the liability is shared
THE PATTERN: Nairobi likewise makes the registered owner strictly liable, and HNS 2010 would channel similarly but WAS NOT IN FORCE at this sitting
THE QUALIFICATION: channelling bars the pollution claimant, not the owner's recourse - the charterer can still be liable to the owner under the charterparty for an unsafe port or bad bunkers

questions.memory_cue: Four limbs, four one-line answers. FORM PLUS RIDER, and the advantage is CERTAINTY (1-2). HIS BIGGEST RISK IS THE SHIP HERSELF (3). HE IS LIABLE IF HE IS THE CARRIER (4), and the indemnity may reach him even if he is not (5). CLC CHANNELS HIM OUT; BUNKERS CATCHES THE BAREBOAT CHARTERER (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) A standard charter party is a pre-printed industry form used as amended by a rider — voyage, time or bareboat. Advantages: certainty of meaning, speed and cost of fixing, balanced drafting, compatibility with brokers, clubs and courts, completeness, fewer disputes. (b) Charterer's liability cover reaches damage to the chartered ship (his biggest exposure — unsafe berth, bad bunkers), cargo liability, pollution from his operations, damage to fixed and floating objects, injury claims, GA and salvage on his bunkers, fines, and defence cover for charterparty disputes. It does not insure commercial loss such as unpaid hire. (c) He is liable to the cargo holder only if he is the carrier on the bill — a charterer's bill or a demise charter; a master's signature makes it an owner's bill. If he is the carrier, Hague-Visby obligations, defences and package limitation apply. Even on an owner's bill the claim can reach him by employment and indemnity and inter-club apportionment. (d) CLC 1992 Article III(4) channels liability to the registered owner and expressly protects charterers, save for intent or recklessness with knowledge. The 2001 Bunkers Convention Article 1(3) defines 'shipowner' widely — registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager, operator, jointly and severally — so a bareboat charterer is liable; a time or voyage charterer is not. HNS 2010 was not in force.

The CLC exception: the person's own act or omission with INTENT, or RECKLESSLY AND WITH KNOWLEDGE that such damage would probably result

quick_revision.critical_regulation: The two provisions that decide limb (d), read together. CLC 1992 Article III(4) channels liability for pollution damage to the registered owner and bars claims against a protected list that expressly includes any charterer, howsoever described, including a bareboat charterer, unless the damage resulted from that person's own act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result. Bunkers Convention 2001 Article 1(3) does the opposite: it defines 'shipowner' to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, jointly and severally liable — so the bareboat charterer CLC protects, Bunkers catches.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (d) with a flat 'charterers are not liable, liability is channelled to the owner'. That is right for CLC and wrong for the Bunkers Convention, whose Article 1(3) definition of 'shipowner' expressly includes the bareboat charterer alongside the manager and the operator, jointly and severally liable. The opposite error is equally available: saying charterers are liable for oil pollution generally, when CLC names them among the protected persons. Second trap, in limb (c): saying the charterer is liable to the cargo holder because he chartered the ship. The holder is a stranger to the charterparty — the charterer answers to him only if he is the carrier on the bill. Third trap: listing the HNS Convention as an operative source of liability. It was not in force at this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a standard charter party, and what are the three families?
retrieval_cards.answer: A charter party written on a pre-printed industry form published by a recognised body, its wording negotiated between representative interests and settled by long use, and used in practice as amended by a rider of additional clauses. Three families: voyage (a stated voyage and cargo), time (the ship at the charterer's disposal for a period), and bareboat or demise (the charterer possesses, mans and operates her as if owner).
retrieval_cards.why: The bareboat family is what decides limbs (c) and (d), so naming all three in limb (a) sets up the rest of the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Enumerate the advantages of using a standard charter-party form.
retrieval_cards.answer: Certainty of meaning from wording litigated and arbitrated for decades; speed and low cost of fixing on a form plus a short rider; balance, being drafted or approved by bodies representing both sides; compatibility with brokers, clubs, underwriters, banks and courts, and with published clause sets; completeness on off-hire, lien, general average and arbitration; and fewer, cheaper disputes. Caution: riders routinely reverse the printed allocation of risk.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'enumerate', so a numbered list is the mark and a paragraph is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a charterer's largest single insured exposure?
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage to the chartered ship herself — not a third-party liability at all. It arises from breach of the safe port and safe berth warranty, from damaging cargo, and from off-specification or contaminated bunkers where the charterer supplies them. Candidates routinely list third-party risks and omit the one that costs most.
retrieval_cards.why: It is also the exposure a Chief Engineer's records most directly affect, through bunker sampling and machinery damage evidence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: When is a charterer liable to a cargo holder under a bill of lading?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only when he is the carrier on that bill. The bill is a contract between holder and carrier, and the holder is a stranger to the charterparty. A bill signed by the master, or by an agent for and on behalf of the master, is ordinarily an owner's bill; one signed by the charterer or his agent in his own name as carrier is a charterer's bill; and under a demise charter the bills are ordinarily the demise charterer's.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'discuss if', and the condition is the identity of the carrier - not the existence of the charter.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The bill was an owner's bill. How can the cargo claim still reach the charterer?
retrieval_cards.answer: By two routes in the charterparty. Employment and indemnity: the time charterer directs employment and requires bills to be signed as presented, and the owner is entitled to be indemnified against the consequences of complying. And inter-club apportionment: New York Produce Exchange time charters customarily apportion cargo claims between owner and charterer by the cause of the loss, mechanically, without litigating fault.
retrieval_cards.why: It is how cargo claims actually reach charterers in practice, and it is what separates a competent answer from a good one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a charterer liable for oil pollution damage under CLC 1992?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Liability is strict on the registered owner, and Article III(4) channels it to him by barring claims for pollution damage against a protected list which expressly includes any charterer, howsoever described, including a bareboat charterer. The protection is lost only where the damage resulted from that person's own act or omission committed with intent, or recklessly and with knowledge that such damage would probably result.
retrieval_cards.why: Channelling exists so the claimant has one identifiable, compulsorily insured defendant - and the narrowness of the exception is the examinable detail.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is a charterer liable under the 2001 Bunkers Convention?
retrieval_cards.answer: A bareboat charterer, yes. The Bunkers Convention does not channel. Article 1(3) defines 'shipowner' to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator, who are jointly and severally liable. A time or voyage charterer is not within that definition. The compulsory insurance duty nonetheless falls on the registered owner alone.
retrieval_cards.why: The exact bareboat charterer that CLC protects, Bunkers catches - which is why the two must never be answered together as one rule.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Summarise the charterer's position across the pollution conventions.
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC 1992 — registered owner liable, charterers expressly channelled out. Bunkers 2001 — no channelling; registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally liable. Nairobi WRC 2007 — registered owner strictly liable. HNS 2010 — would channel similarly but was not in force at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: The pattern is one identified, insured defendant per casualty, with the Bunkers definition as the considered exception.

blocks.h: 1. The mechanism - why a solid starts behaving as a liquid

blocks.p: A fine-particled bulk cargo is a solid only because of inter-granular friction and the capillary forces between wet particles. It does not need to be dry, and it does not need to be strong; it needs its grains to be pressing on each other.

Once at sea the cargo is subjected to continuous vibration from the machinery and propeller and to rolling and pitching. Both progressively compact the mass, reducing the void volume between particles. The water occupying those voids cannot drain away at the same rate, so the pore water pressure rises. Rising pore pressure removes, in equal measure, the effective stress — the actual contact force — between adjacent particles. When the effective stress approaches zero the grains are supported by the water rather than by each other, and the mass flows.

Nothing has been added and nothing has escaped. The same material has changed state because the water already inside it moved — which is why the cargo can look perfectly sound at the moment of loading and be a liquid two days later.

blocks.h: 2. The conditions and the contributing factors

blocks.p: Three conditions must coincide.

ol: A cargo of a type that can liquefy — established from the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its current individual schedule in the IMSBC Code, never from the commodity name used in conversation.
A moisture content above the transportable moisture limit for that cargo.
Sufficient ship motion and vibration to compact the mass.

blocks.p: Remove any one and the cargo will not liquefy — which is why the whole regulatory scheme concentrates on the second condition, the only one that can be measured and controlled before the ship sails.

Contributing factors on the supply side: fine particle size with a proportion of clay or very fine material; open stockpiles exposed to weather; rain during storage, transfer or loading; wet mining and washing processes; barge transfer in an open roadstead; poor drainage at the terminal; and loading in the monsoon or wet season. On the ship side: engine and propeller vibration, rolling and pitching, long voyages, and heavy weather. And separately, sampling error: a stockpile is not homogeneous, and a certificate is only as good as the sample behind it.

blocks.h: 3. TML and FMP - the numbers that decide acceptance

rows: The moisture content at which the cargo begins to lose shear strength and behave as a fluid under the prescribed test conditions

The maximum moisture content of the cargo considered safe for carriage. For most cargoes it is ninety per cent of the FMP - but the individual schedule governs, and some cargoes use a different determination

blocks.p: Determination is by laboratory test under Appendix 2 — the flow table test, the penetration test, or the Proctor-Fagerberg test. Two certificates then matter and they are not interchangeable: the TML certificate, which is a property of the material and is valid for a period before loading, and the moisture content certificate, which must be taken much closer to loading because moisture changes with the weather while the TML does not.

The master's can test — a sample in a cylindrical can, struck repeatedly against a hard surface, watched for free moisture or fluid behaviour at the surface — is a complementary check on board. It can raise an alarm and justify stopping loading, but it is not a substitute for the certified laboratory determination and it cannot establish that a cargo is safe.

blocks.h: 4. Liquefaction is not dynamic separation

blocks.p: Two phenomena are routinely confused and it is worth separating them:

ul: In liquefaction, the cargo mass itself loses shear strength and flows.

In dynamic separation, moisture migrates upward through the cargo and forms a liquid slurry above a still-solid mass — a wet base with a free surface — without the bulk of the cargo liquefying at all.

blocks.p: The consequence for the ship is comparable and equally dangerous: a free surface where the design assumed none, and a mobile upper layer that can slop and shift. The distinction matters for two reasons. The bauxite casualty most often cited as a liquefaction case is now generally understood as dynamic separation; and the Code addresses the two through different schedules and provisions, so the correct precautions follow from the correct diagnosis.

blocks.h: 5. The dangers to the ship

blocks.p: The danger is not that the cargo is wet. It is that the ship's stability has been calculated on an assumption that has silently become false.

ul: A free surface appears in a hold designed on the assumption that solid cargo cannot move. The virtual rise in the centre of gravity reduces GM.
The mass shifts to the low side and does not come back. Roll becomes asymmetric and a progressive list develops.
The cargo can re-solidify at the angle of list, locking the ship heeled and removing the reserve she needs for the next sea.
The process compounds. Each shift increases the list; each increase in list makes the next shift larger.
Capsize can follow with very little warning, which is what makes these among the most sudden losses in the bulk trades — and why the survival rate is so poor.

Secondary consequences: loss of steering and manoeuvrability; structural damage as cargo works against bulkheads and hatch coamings; inability to launch survival craft from a heavily heeled ship; and extreme danger to anyone in or near the hold.

blocks.h: 6. What the casualties show

rows: A cluster of three bulk carriers lost within weeks
Nickel ore from Indonesia and the Philippines - the losses that drove the IMSBC work on cargoes which may liquefy
Bauxite - sank in the South China Sea with the loss of eighteen of nineteen crew

blocks.p: The instructive case is Bulk Jupiter, and it is not a simple liquefaction case. Its mechanism is now generally understood as dynamic separation, and the regulatory response was a new schedule and express treatment of that phenomenon — which is precisely why section 4 above matters. The common thread through all of them is the same: fine, moist ores loaded in tropical, rain-affected ports; certificates that did not reflect the cargo actually loaded; and losses that were sudden rather than progressive.

blocks.h: 7. Prevention and the regulatory framework

blocks.p: The instrument. The IMSBC Code, made mandatory through SOLAS, and at the date of this examination as amended by amendment 07-23, which has been mandatory since 1 January 2025 having been available for voluntary application from 1 January 2024. It superseded amendment 06-21, which had been in force since 1 December 2023. Name the amendment state, not merely 'the IMSBC Code'. The relevant provisions are section 4 (assessment of acceptability of consignments), section 7.3 (cargoes which may liquefy), section 8 (test procedures and the complementary can test) and Appendix 2 (laboratory test procedures), read with the individual schedules.
Before and during loading.

ul: The shipper declares the cargo under its Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and supplies the section 4 information, with certificates of TML and of moisture content.
The ship checks the declaration against the individual schedule and the section 7.3 conditions, and checks the dates on both certificates.

The acceptance rule: a cargo which may liquefy is not accepted unless its moisture content is below the TML, or the ship is specially constructed or fitted for such carriage, or the cargo is carried under the specific alternative conditions the Code allows.
Inspect the cargo and the barges: watch for splatter, free water, and a surface that flattens or will not hold a slope.
Carry out the can test as a complementary check.
Suspend loading in rain and close the hatches; trim as the schedule requires.
Refuse or stop loading if the cargo does not match its declaration. This is the master's only real protection, and it exists only before the ship sails.

blocks.p: On passage. Sound bilges and wells regularly and record what is found; watch the roll for the asymmetry that signals a shift; route to avoid heavy weather and reduce motion by adjusting course and speed; and never enter a hold to inspect. If liquefaction or separation is suspected: minimise motion, consider shelter or a port of refuge, inform the company, the flag State and the nearest coastal State, and prepare the crew. The condition is not recoverable at sea.

At discharge. Expect the cargo to have compacted or set, possibly at an angle; brief on the hazards of working a shifted or crusted cargo, including voids and collapse; and record and report what was found, so that the loading terminal, the shipper and the charterer are held to the certificate they issued. Supporting the whole framework are SOLAS chapter VI for cargo information, SOLAS chapter XII for bulk carriers, and the BLU Code for the loading and unloading process itself.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (a) asks for the phenomenon "including the conditions under which it occurs and its contributing factors" — that is an instruction to explain why, not what, and a definition alone cannot satisfy it. Limb (b) expressly asks for "examples of incidents", so the casualties get their own section rather than a parenthesis. Limb (c) carries the largest allocation and names three stages — loading, transportation and discharge — so section 7 is organised on those three stages, in that order, using the examiner's own words.

blocks.h: The one sentence of soil mechanics that carries the question

blocks.p: Effective stress equals total stress minus pore water pressure. Everything else follows: compaction raises pore pressure, pore pressure eats effective stress, effective stress is what makes the cargo a solid. A candidate who writes that one relationship has explained liquefaction; a candidate who writes "the cargo becomes wet and slides" has described it.

blocks.h: Why TML and moisture content are certified separately

blocks.p: The TML is a property of the material and does not change with the weather, so its certificate is valid for a longer period. The moisture content is a property of the consignment on the day, and it changes with every shower — which is why its certificate must be much closer to loading, and why the Code requires re-checking after significant rain. Confusing the two, or accepting a stale moisture certificate, is the documentary failure behind several of the casualties in section 6.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Naming amendment 06-21 as the current amendment. It was superseded by 07-23, mandatory since 1 January 2025 — six months before this sitting.
Naming no amendment at all. 'The IMSBC Code' without its amendment state answers a weaker question than the one set.
Stating a cargo's group from the commodity name. Classification and carriage requirements follow the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its current individual schedule.
Quoting TML as ninety per cent of FMP without the qualification. It is the general rule, not a universal one.
Presenting the can test as the test of acceptability. It is complementary, and a negative result proves nothing.
Describing the danger as "loss of stability" without the free surface and the irreversible shift — which is what distinguishes this from an ordinary stability problem.
Offering no named casualty when the stem asks for examples.
Suggesting that a list from liquefaction can be corrected by ballasting. It cannot; the cargo may simply shift further.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: Asking which amendment of the IMSBC Code is in force. At this sitting it is 07-23, and it has been mandatory since the beginning of the year.
Asking whether a can test can clear a cargo for loading. No.
Asking what the master does if the shipper offers an indemnity for loading a doubtful cargo. An indemnity is not a defence and does not change the Code.
Asking about the difference between liquefaction and dynamic separation.
Asking why the cargo does not simply return to the high side as the ship rolls back. Because it has lost shear strength and can re-solidify at the angle of list.
Asking whether you would open a hold at sea to look. Never.
Asking which SOLAS chapter makes the Code mandatory, and which chapter carries the additional bulk carrier measures.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: You are loading nickel ore in the wet season and it has just rained heavily. What do you do?
Describe the can test and what a positive result looks like.
What entries would you expect in the deck and engine log during a suspected cargo shift?
What does the vibration of your machinery have to do with cargo stability?
Which certificates would you check, and how old may each be?
What is a specially constructed or fitted cargo ship in this context?
Which amendment of the IMSBC Code applies to your ship today, and when did it become mandatory?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Four words of physics: compact, pressure, friction, flow. Three conditions: cargo, moisture, motion. Two certificates and one crude check: TML, moisture content, can test. Two phenomena: liquefaction and dynamic separation. Then the ship: free surface, shift, list, loss. Then the three stages the examiner named: load, carry, discharge.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency - a settled edition on an unassembled chain

blocks.p: The amendment date has passed, and that is what makes this sitting the easy one. IMSBC amendment 07-23 became mandatory on 1 January 2025, six months before this examination. It is simply the operative edition — not a change taking effect during the sitting, and nothing about it is day-dependent within July. The January 2025 paper that prints an identical stem sat in the very month the amendment took effect, and for that paper the date was the sharpest on the whole question; here it is settled history.

What has not changed is the evidence position. The MIW True Source corpus holds the IMSBC chain only as far as amendment 06-21, and its own instrument log records everything after that as an open acquisition item: "amendments after 06-21 (the 07-23 cycle and any 2025 adoption) — unknown, verification required." The corpus is therefore one mandatory edition behind this sitting.

Two consequences follow, and both are deliberate. The adopting resolution number for 07-23 is not cited anywhere in this answer — naming one from memory would be exactly the kind of invented citation this answer refuses to make. And the mandatory date is carried as authoritative secondary with a currency flag rather than as a verified fact.

This does not weaken the answer. Liquefaction is governed by sections 4, 7.3, 8 and Appendix 2, whose substance amendment 07-23 did not rewrite. The amendment matters for which edition the candidate names, and that is exactly what is stated.

Finally, no casualty investigation report is held. The incidents are named as industry reference events, and the characterisation of the January 2015 bauxite casualty as dynamic separation rather than classic liquefaction is stated as the industry understanding rather than as a quoted investigation finding.

questions.understand_first: A solid bulk cargo does not float in water and it does not dissolve. What makes it dangerous is something subtler: it is only a solid because of friction between its particles, and that friction depends on the particles pressing against each other rather than against water. Load a fine, moist ore into a hold and it looks and behaves like rock. Then run the ship for two days: the main engine vibrates the hull, the sea rolls her, and the cargo compacts. As the void spaces between particles shrink, the water that was sitting in them has nowhere to go, so the pore water pressure rises. Every increment of pore pressure takes an equal increment off the contact force between grains. When the contact force reaches zero the grains are no longer touching — they are floating in their own water — and the cargo flows. Nothing was added and nothing was spilled; the same material simply stopped being a solid. That is why the whole regulatory answer is about a number measured before loading — the moisture content against the transportable moisture limit — and why the master's can test, crude as it is, matters: once the ship is at sea there is nothing anyone can do about it.

points: THE INSTRUMENT: the IMSBC Code, mandatory through SOLAS, and at this sitting AS AMENDED BY AMENDMENT 07-23, which has been mandatory since 1 January 2025 and had been available for voluntary application from 1 January 2024, superseding amendment 06-21

BEFORE LOADING: the shipper must declare the cargo under its Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and supply the information required by section 4, with certificates of TML and of moisture content; the ship checks the declaration against the individual schedule and the section 7.3 conditions

ACCEPTANCE RULE: a cargo that may liquefy is not accepted unless its moisture content is below the TML, or the ship is specially constructed or fitted for the purpose, or the cargo is carried under the specific alternative conditions the Code allows

DURING LOADING: inspect the cargo and the barges; watch for splatter, free water, a flat or sloping surface that will not hold; carry out the complementary can test; suspend loading in rain and cover the hatches; trim as the schedule requires; and REFUSE OR STOP if the cargo does not match its declaration

ON PASSAGE: monitor bilges and sound wells for water and pump as permitted; watch the ship's roll behaviour for the asymmetry that signals a shift; avoid heavy weather by routeing; reduce motion by course and speed; and NEVER enter a hold to inspect

IF LIQUEFACTION IS SUSPECTED: minimise ship motion, seek shelter or a port of refuge, inform the company, the flag State and the nearest coastal State, and prepare the crew - the condition is not recoverable at sea

AT DISCHARGE: expect the cargo to have compacted or set at an angle, brief on the hazards of working a shifted cargo, and record and report what was found so that the loading terminal and the charterer are held to the certificate they issued
SUPPORTING FRAMEWORK: SOLAS chapter VI cargo information, SOLAS chapter XII for bulk carriers, and the BLU Code for the loading and unloading process itself

questions.memory_cue: One sentence of physics: COMPACT - PORE PRESSURE UP - FRICTION DOWN - FLOW (1). Three conditions: CARGO TYPE, MOISTURE ABOVE LIMIT, MOTION (2). Two certificates and one crude check: TML, MOISTURE, CAN TEST (3). Two phenomena, not one: LIQUEFACTION and DYNAMIC SEPARATION (4). Then the ship: FREE SURFACE - SHIFT - LIST - LOSS (5), and the three stages LOAD, CARRY, DISCHARGE (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Liquefaction: vibration and rolling compact a fine moist cargo, the voids shrink, pore water pressure rises, effective stress between particles falls to zero and the mass flows. Needs three things together - a cargo whose declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and individual schedule place it in the group that may liquefy, moisture above the TML, and ship motion. FMP is where it starts to flow under test; TML is the safe limit, generally ninety per cent of FMP, but the schedule governs. Tests: flow table, penetration, Proctor-Fagerberg. The master's can test is a complementary check, not a substitute. Dynamic separation is a different phenomenon - a slurry above a solid mass. Dangers: free surface, asymmetric roll, an irreversible progressive list, sudden capsize. Casualties: the 2010 nickel ore cluster, Bulk Jupiter in January 2015, Nur Allya in 2019. Control: IMSBC Code, mandatory through SOLAS and at this sitting as amended by amendment 07-23, mandatory since 1 January 2025 - sections 4, 7.3, 8 and Appendix 2.
critical_numbers: TML is generally ninety per cent of the flow moisture point - but the individual schedule governs and not every cargo uses that relationship
Three conditions must coincide: cargo type, moisture above the TML, and ship motion
IMSBC amendment 07-23 has been mandatory since 1 January 2025, six months before this sitting - flagged for confirmation
Amendment 06-21, resolution MSC.500(105), had been in force since 1 December 2023 and is superseded

quick_revision.critical_regulation: IMSBC Code section 7.3, read with section 4 and Appendix 2 - a cargo that may liquefy is not accepted unless its moisture content is below the transportable moisture limit, or the ship is specially constructed or fitted, or the Code's alternative conditions are met
quick_revision.major_trap: Naming amendment 06-21 as the current amendment, or naming no amendment at all. At this sitting the Code is as amended by amendment 07-23, which has been mandatory since 1 January 2025 - six months before the paper - and 06-21 is its superseded predecessor. Second trap: stating a cargo group from the commodity name in the question. The group and the carriage requirements follow the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its current individual schedule. Third trap: treating the can test as the test of acceptability - it is a complementary check by the master and never replaces the shipper's certified laboratory test.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the liquefaction question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The mechanism. 2 Conditions and contributing factors. 3 TML and FMP. 4 Liquefaction is not dynamic separation. 5 The dangers. 6 What the casualties show. 7 Prevention and the regulatory framework, by stage. Sections 1-4 are limb (a), 5-6 limb (b), 7 limb (c).
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) expressly asks for incident examples, so the casualties get their own section rather than a parenthesis.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Explain the liquefaction mechanism in one sequence.
retrieval_cards.answer: Vibration and rolling compact the cargo; the void volume between particles shrinks; the water in those voids cannot escape fast enough, so pore water pressure rises; rising pore pressure reduces the effective stress between particles by the same amount; when effective stress reaches zero the particles are carried by water instead of by each other and the mass flows.
retrieval_cards.why: Four linked steps. Describing wet cargo without the pore-pressure chain is not an explanation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Relate TML and FMP, and name the tests.
retrieval_cards.answer: The flow moisture point is the moisture content at which the cargo begins to behave as a fluid under test. The transportable moisture limit is the maximum considered safe for carriage - generally ninety per cent of the flow moisture point, though the individual schedule governs and some cargoes use a different determination. Determined by the flow table test, the penetration test or the Proctor-Fagerberg test.
retrieval_cards.why: The qualification matters: quoting ninety per cent as universal is wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you establish whether a cargo may liquefy?
retrieval_cards.answer: From the declared Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and its current individual schedule in the IMSBC Code - never from the commodity name used in conversation or in the question. If the declaration and the schedule do not match what is being loaded, that is itself the finding.
retrieval_cards.why: Founder policy and a recorded trap: classification and carriage requirements follow the declared name and schedule, not the casual commodity word.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish liquefaction from dynamic separation.
retrieval_cards.answer: In liquefaction the cargo mass itself loses shear strength and flows. In dynamic separation moisture migrates upward and forms a liquid slurry above a still-solid mass, producing a free surface without the bulk of the cargo liquefying. Both are dangerous to stability; the Code addresses them through different schedules and provisions.
retrieval_cards.why: The bauxite casualty most often cited as a liquefaction case is now generally understood as dynamic separation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the master check before accepting a cargo that may liquefy?
retrieval_cards.answer: The shipper's declaration under the Bulk Cargo Shipping Name and the section 4 information; the certificate of transportable moisture limit and the certificate of moisture content, with their dates; the individual schedule and the section 7.3 conditions; the physical appearance of the cargo and the barges; and a complementary can test. If the cargo does not match its declaration, refuse or stop loading.
retrieval_cards.why: The right to refuse is the master's only real protection - once the cargo is aboard and the ship is at sea, nothing can be done about it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the dangers to the ship, in sequence?
retrieval_cards.answer: A free surface appears where the design assumed none, so the effective centre of gravity rises and GM falls. The liquefied mass shifts to the low side and does not return, so the roll becomes asymmetric and a progressive list develops. The cargo can re-solidify at that angle. Each shift increases the list and each list increases the shift, and capsize can follow suddenly.
retrieval_cards.why: The irreversibility is the point. This is not a list that can be corrected by ballasting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which amendment state of the IMSBC Code applies at a July 2025 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code as amended by amendment 07-23, which has been mandatory since 1 January 2025 - six months before the sitting - having been available for voluntary application from 1 January 2024. It superseded amendment 06-21, which had been in force since 1 December 2023.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming 06-21, or naming no amendment at all, answers a weaker question than the one set.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the can test, and what is it not?
retrieval_cards.answer: A complementary check by the master: a sample is placed in a cylindrical can and the can struck repeatedly against a hard surface, and free moisture or fluid behaviour at the surface indicates the cargo may be too wet. It can raise an alarm and justify stopping loading. It is not a substitute for the shipper's certified laboratory determination and it cannot establish that a cargo is safe.
retrieval_cards.why: A negative can test proves nothing; a positive one is decisive. That asymmetry is the examinable point.

blocks.h: 1. What 'perils of the sea' actually means

blocks.p: The phrase is far narrower than candidates expect, and the whole question turns on that narrowness.

The statutory definition, carried in the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, is that the term 'perils of the seas' refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas, and does not include the ordinary action of the winds and waves.
Two tests follow, and both must be satisfied.

ol: Fortuity. The loss must be accidental — not inevitable, not certain, not the natural consequence of the ship going to sea. Deterioration that was bound to happen is not a peril; it is the passage of time.

Of the sea, not merely at sea. The sea must be the cause, not just the location. A fire in the engine room is not a peril of the seas even though it happens at sea — which is exactly why fire is listed separately in every policy.

blocks.p: What is therefore covered as a peril of the seas: stranding and grounding; sinking and foundering; collision with another vessel; striking a submerged or floating object; heavy weather damage beyond the ordinary action of wind and sea; entry of seawater through an accidental opening; capsizing; and damage from an accidental incursion of the sea into the ship.

What is excluded, and this list earns as many marks as the first: ordinary wear and tear; ordinary leakage and breakage; inherent vice of the subject matter; the ordinary action of the winds and waves; corrosion and gradual deterioration; damage by rats or vermin; and injury to machinery not proximately caused by a maritime peril.

blocks.h: 2. The maritime perils that are covered but are NOT perils of the sea

blocks.p: This section is what makes the rest of the question intelligible, and most candidates omit it.

A hull and machinery policy does not insure 'perils of the sea' alone. Perils of the seas is only the first item in a list, and the other items are there precisely because they would otherwise fall outside it. The perils clause of the standard hull form covers, in substance:

ul: Perils of the seas, rivers, lakes or other navigable waters
Fire and explosion
Violent theft by persons from outside the vessel
Jettison
Piracy
Contact with land conveyance, dock or harbour equipment or installation
Earthquake, volcanic eruption or lightning
Accidents in loading, discharging or shifting cargo or fuel

blocks.p: So the correct answer to 'what perils of the sea are covered' is: the fortuitous casualties of the sea itself — and the policy then adds, by express words, a series of other perils that are not perils of the sea at all.

blocks.h: 3. How an insured covers a peril that is not an insured peril - with examples

blocks.p: The stem's second question presupposes that a shipowner faces exposures the perils clause does not reach. Four routes are available, and a good answer gives an example of each.

ol: Extend the existing policy by an additional clause. The risk is written into the policy for an additional premium, usually against warranties or a higher deductible. Example: the additional perils cover that buys back the exclusion on the cost of repairing or replacing a part found to be defective, where the ordinary latent-defect cover pays for the resulting damage but not for the faulty part itself.

Buy a separate policy for the excluded risk. Some risks are excluded from the hull policy as a matter of market structure and are insured elsewhere. Examples: war, strikes, terrorism and confiscation, excluded by the hull policy and bought back by a war risks policy or an association entry; loss of hire, for the owner's own trading loss during repairs, which no hull policy covers; increased value and hull interest, above the sum insured; and freight insurance.

Cover it mutually, through a P&I club. The hull policy insures the ship; it does not insure the owner's liabilities to third parties. Examples: pollution liability, cargo claims, crew injury, illness, death and repatriation, wreck removal, damage to fixed and floating objects, stowaways and fines. This is the single most important route and the one most often left out.

Adjust the terms rather than the perils. Where the problem is quantum rather than scope, the answer is a higher sum insured, a lower deductible, or removal of a restrictive warranty — again for premium.

blocks.p: Two limits should be stated, because they show the routes are not unlimited. An insurer will not write back a loss that is inevitable rather than fortuitous — wear and tear is a maintenance cost, not an insurable risk. And cover for a known existing defect is not available on ordinary terms; that is not insurance, it is a repair bill.

blocks.h: 4. The perils whose cover is qualified by due diligence

blocks.p: This is the third demand and it is the one that decides the mark. Alongside the perils in section 2, the hull form covers a second group, and every item in it is expressly qualified. The group is known in the market as the Inchmaree clause, after the nineteenth-century case in which a donkey-engine casualty was held not to be a peril of the seas — which is precisely why the clause had to be written.
The perils in the qualified group are:

ol: Bursting of boilers
Breakage of shafts
Latent defect in the machinery or hull
Negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots
Negligence of repairers or charterers, provided they are not an assured under the policy
Barratry of Master, Officers or Crew

blocks.p: The qualification is that the loss or damage is covered provided it has not resulted from want of due diligence by the Assured, Owners, Managers or Superintendents or any of their onshore management.
Three points of precision, and each is examinable.

ul: The Master, Officers and Crew are NOT in the due-diligence list. Their negligence is an insured peril, not a defence. The proviso reaches shore management. This is the most misunderstood feature of the clause: an engineer's mistake is covered; a superintendent's failure to act on a reported defect may not be.

Latent defect cover pays for the damage, not for the defect. The consequential damage is recoverable; the cost of renewing the defective part itself is conventionally excluded, and buying that back is exactly what the additional perils cover in section 3 does.
Barratry is a wrongful act wilfully committed by Master or crew to the prejudice of the owner. It is covered because it is a peril to the owner, and it necessarily involves no privity of the owner.

blocks.h: 5. Where the onus of proof lies, and why it matters

blocks.p: The general rule is settled and follows the structure of the policy.

ul: The assured must prove that the loss was caused by a peril insured against. That is his affirmative case, and it is his burden.
The insurer must prove any exception, exclusion or proviso on which it relies to reduce or defeat a claim that otherwise falls within the cover.

blocks.p: The due-diligence provision is a proviso limiting the insurer's liability, not a condition precedent that the assured must satisfy before he can claim. It follows — and this is the express point of the question — that once the assured has proved a loss falling within the qualified group, the onus of proving want of due diligence lies on the underwriters. The assured does not have to prove that he was diligent; the insurer has to prove that he was not.

Why the allocation matters in practice. Want of due diligence is a negative, it concerns the internal conduct of the owner's own organisation, and the evidence of it sits in the owner's records. Placing the burden on the insurer therefore makes it a demanding one, and it is why claims in this group are fought on documents: the planned maintenance system, defect reports, superintendent's reports and correspondence, class survey records and conditions of class, the safety management system's maintenance and non-conformity records, and the record of what shore management was told and what it did about it.

So the direct answer to the stem's third demand is: bursting of boilers, breakage of shafts, latent defect, negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots, negligence of repairers or charterers, and barratry — covered, but subject to a due-diligence proviso which the insurer must prove is engaged.

blocks.h: 6. The Indian frame, and what it means on board

blocks.p: The statute. The governing law for a policy subject to Indian law is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. The UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 is its model and is often quoted in coaching material, but it is not the operative statute here, and the later UK reform of the avoidance remedy does not apply to Indian law. Under the 1963 Act a contract of marine insurance is a contract of utmost good faith (section 19), and the assured must disclose every material circumstance known to him before the contract is concluded (section 20); section 66 defines a general average loss.

The clause layer. The perils themselves are not in the statute. They are in the policy, and Indian hull policies are ordinarily written on the London market forms, so the perils clause and the Inchmaree clause described above are the operative wording. The Act supplies the framework of the contract; the clauses supply the cover.
What this means for a Chief Engineer, which is why the question is set in this paper at all:

ul: Your negligence is insured. The claim is not defeated because an engineer made a mistake.
The claim is put at risk by shore management's failure to act — and the evidence of that failure, or of its absence, is the paperwork you generate.
A defect reported and not repaired is the single most dangerous document in a machinery casualty file, because it converts a fortuitous loss into an argument about diligence.
Maintain the records: planned maintenance, defect reports, spares ordered and chased, class conditions and their clearance, and what you told the office and when.

Report and preserve. On a casualty, notify promptly, preserve the failed component, photograph the evidence and do not dismantle beyond necessity before the surveyor attends — because the burden the insurer must discharge can only be resisted with evidence.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem contains three questions and a fourth hidden one. It asks what perils of the sea are covered; what an insured can do about a peril that is not covered; and which perils are covered subject to a due-diligence burden on the insurer. The hidden question is the one in section 2: which covered perils are not perils of the sea at all. Without it the second and third demands make no sense, because both are about the parts of the policy that exist precisely because perils of the seas is narrow.

The structure also puts the burden analysis in a section of its own. That is deliberate: the stem's own words are 'the onus of proof is upon the insurers', so the examiner has told the candidate where the marks are, and an answer that mentions it in a clause rather than developing it has ignored an instruction.

blocks.h: The two tests, and why fire is listed separately

blocks.p: Fortuitous, and of the sea rather than merely at sea. Both must hold.

The best single illustration is fire. A fire on board happens at sea, damages the ship and is plainly accidental — and it is not a peril of the seas, because the sea did not cause it. That is why every hull policy lists fire and explosion separately. Give that example and the definition is proved rather than asserted.

The second best is the Inchmaree case itself: a donkey engine damaged by a blocked valve was held not to be a peril of the seas, and the market responded by writing the clause that now bears the ship's name. The whole of the qualified group in section 4 exists because the definition in section 1 is narrow.

blocks.h: The policy in three layers

blocks.h: The distinction that most candidates get wrong

blocks.p: The due-diligence proviso names the Assured, Owners, Managers or Superintendents or any of their onshore management. It does not name the Master, Officers or Crew — whose negligence is an insured peril in the very same clause.

Read those two facts together and the commercial logic is clear. The policy accepts the risk of human error by the people operating the ship, because that is what the owner is insuring against. It does not accept the risk of the owner's own organisation failing to run the ship properly, because that would be insuring the owner against himself.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906. The Indian statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
Treating perils of the sea as meaning 'anything that happens at sea'. It is a narrow term with two tests.
Forgetting that the loss must be fortuitous, and so listing wear and tear, corrosion or inherent vice among the covered perils.
Answering the second demand with only 'take out another policy' and missing the P&I club, which is how third-party liabilities are actually covered.
Getting the burden backwards and saying the assured must prove he exercised due diligence. He must prove the peril; the insurer must prove want of diligence.
Putting the Master and crew into the due-diligence list. Their negligence is the insured peril.
Saying latent defect cover pays for renewing the defective part. It pays for the resulting damage; the part itself is bought back by additional perils cover.
Quoting an Institute clause number. Several editions run concurrently and their numbering differs; enumerate the perils by substance.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Also, enumerate' in the third sentence is a command for a list. Six items, named. A discursive paragraph on due diligence without the enumeration loses the marks the word 'enumerate' was protecting.
'Explain with examples' in the second sentence is likewise a command. Each route in section 3 must carry a concrete example.
The stem's phrase 'the onus of proof is upon the insurers' tells the candidate the answer to half the third demand. Restate it, justify it and use it — do not treat it as background.
The word barratry in the qualified group is a favourite oral follow-up, and it needs the phrase 'to the prejudice of the owner' to be defined correctly.
This is an Engineering Management paper, so the record-keeping consequences in section 6 are properly part of the answer, not an afterthought.

blocks.p: The corpus holds neither the statute nor the clauses. The Marine Insurance Act, 1963 is not held; the corpus carries a concept-level note supporting only sections 19, 20 and 66, and a subrogation section it marks 'VERIFY section'. Those limits are respected literally: no other section number is asserted anywhere in this answer, and the flagged section is not cited at all.

The statutory definition of perils of the seas lives in the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Act. The rule is stated as law because it is settled; its rule number is not asserted, because no held source fixes it and a wrong address is worse than none.

The Institute clause layer is industry documentation, and INDUSTRY_SOURCES.md classifies the whole insurance area as citation and index only. No clause number and no edition is asserted, and the perils are enumerated by substance and grouping — which is also what an examiner wants, since several editions run concurrently in the market with different numbering.
No case authority is cited. The Inchmaree case is named only as the origin of the market's label for the clause, which is a matter of nomenclature rather than of precedent.

Nothing here is sitting-sensitive, and the reason is structural. The statute dates from 1963, the doctrine is long settled, and because no clause edition is asserted anywhere there is no edition boundary that could have moved. Note in particular that the Merchant Shipping Act boundary does not reach this question: marine insurance in India is governed by its own statute, and neither the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 nor the Act of 2025 touches it.

questions.understand_first: The whole question rests on one fact: 'perils of the sea' is a narrow legal term, not a description of everything that can go wrong on a voyage. It means fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas — so the loss must be accidental rather than inevitable, and it must be caused by the sea rather than merely happening at sea. Fire proves the point: it is accidental, it happens at sea, and it is not a peril of the seas, which is why every policy lists it separately. Once that narrowness is seen, the rest of the question explains itself. The policy adds a list of other perils by express words because the first head is so narrow. Where even that list does not reach, the owner buys cover elsewhere — extension, separate policy, P&I entry, better terms. And for the machinery perils that the courts had held were not perils of the seas — a broken shaft, a burst boiler, a latent defect, an engineer's mistake — the market wrote the Inchmaree clause, and attached to it the one qualification that makes this an examinable question: the cover is lost if the loss resulted from want of due diligence by shore management, and it is the underwriters, not the owner, who must prove that it did.

Its Rules for Construction of Policy define perils of the seas as fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas, excluding the ordinary action of the winds and waves. quick_revision.major_trap: Getting the burden backwards. retrieval_cards.prompt: Define 'perils of the seas' and give the two tests.
retrieval_cards.answer: Under the Rules for Construction of Policy in the Schedule to the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, the term refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas and does not include the ordinary action of the winds and waves. Two tests: the loss must be fortuitous — accidental, not inevitable; and it must be of the sea, not merely at sea — the sea must be the cause.
retrieval_cards.why: The narrowness of the term is what generates every other part of the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is fire on board a peril of the seas?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. It is accidental and it happens at sea, but the sea did not cause it, so it fails the second test. That is exactly why fire and explosion are listed separately in the perils clause of every hull policy.
retrieval_cards.why: The cleanest single proof of the definition, and it converts a memorised sentence into demonstrated understanding.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Enumerate the perils covered subject to a due-diligence proviso.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Inchmaree clause group: bursting of boilers; breakage of shafts; latent defect in the machinery or hull; negligence of Master, Officers, Crew or Pilots; negligence of repairers or charterers not assured under the policy; and barratry of Master, Officers or Crew. Covered provided the loss has not resulted from want of due diligence by the Assured, Owners, Managers or Superintendents or any of their onshore management.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'enumerate'. Six named items are the marks; a paragraph about diligence is not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In a broken-shaft claim, who must prove what?
retrieval_cards.answer: The assured proves that the loss was caused by a peril insured against — here, breakage of shafts. The due-diligence provision is a proviso limiting the insurer's liability, not a condition precedent, so the underwriters must prove want of due diligence by the owners, managers, superintendents or onshore management. The assured never has to prove that he was diligent.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the express point of the stem's third demand, and getting it backwards is the standard error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The Second Engineer's mistake wrecked a bearing. The superintendent ignored a reported defect. Same answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Negligence of the Master, Officers and Crew is an insured peril in the Inchmaree clause, so the engineer's mistake is covered. The due-diligence proviso names the Assured, Owners, Managers, Superintendents and onshore management — the crew are not in it. So the superintendent's failure to act on a reported defect is the fact that can defeat the claim.
retrieval_cards.why: The commercial logic is that a policy insures the owner against operational human error but not against his own organisation's failure to run the ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Four routes to cover a peril the policy does not insure. Give an example of each.
retrieval_cards.answer: Extend the policy by an additional clause — additional perils cover buying back the defective part itself. Buy a separate policy — war and strikes, loss of hire, increased value, freight. Enter a P&I club — pollution, cargo claims, crew injury and repatriation, wreck removal, damage to fixed and floating objects. Adjust the terms — higher sum insured, lower deductible, removal of a restrictive warranty.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem says 'explain with examples', and the P&I route is the one candidates most often omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is barratry, and why is it insured?
retrieval_cards.answer: A wrongful act wilfully committed by the Master, Officers or Crew to the prejudice of the owner — scuttling, wilful deviation, smuggling that leads to seizure. It is insured because from the owner's point of view it is a genuine fortuity, and by definition it is done without his privity.
retrieval_cards.why: A favourite oral follow-up, and the phrase 'to the prejudice of the owner' is what makes the definition correct.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Latent defect is found in a casting. Who pays for the new casting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Ordinarily the owner. Latent defect cover under the Inchmaree clause pays for the damage resulting from the defect, not for renewing the defective part itself. Buying back the cost of the part is precisely what an additional perils extension does, for extra premium.
retrieval_cards.why: A precise and commonly-missed limit on a cover candidates assume is complete.
