blocks.h: (a) The importance of gender diversity, and the challenges women face — 8 marks
1. Where gender equality sits, and why it reaches shipping

blocks.p: Sustainable Development Goal 5 — gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls — is one of the seventeen goals of the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted in 2015. It is a cross-cutting goal: it is not a sector programme, it is a condition the other sixteen are expected to be pursued under.
Shipping is caught by it more sharply than most industries for three structural reasons, and naming them is a better opening than repeating the goal.

ul: It is one of the most male-dominated occupations in the world of work, and by a very wide margin at sea.
It is internationally regulated, so a global norm can be given effect through IMO and ILO instruments in a way that a purely national industry could not achieve.
It faces a structural officer shortage. An industry short of qualified officers that recruits effectively from half the population has a supply problem it has partly created.

blocks.h: 2. Why gender diversity matters to the industry

blocks.p: The case is worth making as an argument rather than as a slogan, because the examiner is testing management reasoning.

ol: Labour supply. The industry projects a persistent shortfall of certificated officers. Recruiting from the whole talent pool rather than half of it is the largest single untapped source, and it is available without any change to training capacity.

Quality of selection. If a profession draws from half the population it is, on average, taking the median of that half rather than the top of the whole. Widening the pool raises the standard of entry at no cost.

Decision quality and safety culture. Diverse teams are less prone to the group conformity that sits behind a recognisable class of maritime casualty — the bridge or engine-room team in which nobody challenges the person in charge. Diversity of background supports the willingness to speak up that safety management systems depend on and cannot mandate.

Retention and the shore pipeline. Sea-going experience feeds the shore side — superintendents, surveyors, DPAs, port and flag administrations, class. A sea-going population that excludes women produces a shore management population that excludes them a decade later, which is why the effect compounds.

Commercial and reputational expectation. Charterers, financiers and cargo interests increasingly report on workforce composition under environmental, social and governance frameworks, so it has become a commercial fact and not only an ethical one.
Legitimacy. An industry that carries the great majority of world trade and asks for public and regulatory trust is weakened by a workforce profile that no other technical profession would now defend.

blocks.h: 3. The challenges women actually face

blocks.p: Separate these into three groups. Running them together produces a list; separating them produces an analysis, and the second scores.
Structural and institutional.

ul: Recruitment and cadet-berth allocation, where sponsorship depends on operators who may be reluctant to place a lone woman on a ship.
Family, social and cultural expectation about a sea career, which in many labour-supplying countries operates before any employer is involved.
The absence of visible role models and of senior women in a position to sponsor juniors — a self-perpetuating shortage.
Employer concern about the cost or complexity of accommodating a mixed crew, which is a management problem presented as an operational one.

blocks.p: Shipboard and physical.

ul: Personal protective equipment and workwear sized for the average male body. This is not a comfort issue; ill-fitting PPE is a safety defect, and it is precisely the point the MLC now addresses — see section 5.
Accommodation, sanitary arrangements and privacy on ships designed and built for a single-sex crew.
Isolation: being the only woman on board, often for months, with no peer and no informal support.

Harassment, bullying and sexual harassment, aggravated by the closed community, the confined environment, the impossibility of leaving, and a reporting line that may run through the person complained of.
Access to medical care and to gender-specific health provision at sea.
Manual handling and equipment design based on assumed male anthropometry — a genuine ergonomic issue and one an engineer should identify as a design problem rather than a personal one.

blocks.p: Career and progression.

ul: Interrupted sea time around maternity, in a certification system whose revalidation depends on recent sea service.
Lack of shore-based career paths that would retain trained women who leave the deep sea.
Perception of competence, and the burden of being treated as representative of a category rather than as an individual.
Higher attrition at the first-command and first-chief-engineer stage — the point at which the shore pipeline is actually fed.

blocks.h: (b) The IMO's role, and India's initiatives — 8 marks
4. The IMO's role - the programme, the mechanism, and its limits

blocks.p: The IMO's contribution is real and it is worth being precise about what kind of contribution it is.

ol: The Women in Maritime Programme. Established within the Organization's technical co-operation work in the late 1980s, its purpose is to improve women's access to maritime training and to technical and senior positions in the sector, principally through fellowships, training places and institutional support in developing member States.

The regional Women in Maritime Associations. The programme's most durable structure: regional networks that give women in the sector professional contact, mentoring and visibility across national boundaries.

Agenda-setting. The Organization made 'Empowering Women in the Maritime Community' the World Maritime Day theme for 2019, and established an annual International Day for Women in Maritime on 18 May. These are not law, and the value of naming them correctly is that they show the mechanism — the IMO's principal lever here is convening and visibility.

Measurement. The joint IMO and WISTA International Women in Maritime Survey is the industry's principal attempt to measure participation. Measurement matters because in the absence of it the debate runs on anecdote.
Gender mainstreaming in its own work, including in the Strategic Plan and in the technical co-operation programme, and encouragement of member States to report on it.

The competence framework is already neutral. STCW sets standards of competence and makes no distinction of sex. That is worth stating, because it locates the problem correctly: the barrier is not the certification regime, it is access, conditions and retention.

blocks.p: The limit is the honest part of this limb. Almost all of the IMO's gender work is promotional and capacity-building rather than mandatory. There is no IMO convention requirement that a company employ women, and none is proposed. The hardest law in this field is not an IMO instrument at all — which is the next section.

blocks.h: 5. The hard legal layer, and exactly where it stood at this sitting

blocks.p: The Maritime Labour Convention, 2006 is an ILO instrument, amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII by the Convention's own simplified procedure — not by IMO tacit acceptance. It is where gender equality in shipping stops being aspiration and becomes an enforceable requirement inspectable by port State control.

The 2022 amendments entered into force on 23 December 2024, and are therefore fully operative at this sitting. Among them, Standard A4.3, paragraph 1(b) now requires that the measures a Member adopts for occupational safety and health include 'reasonable precautions to prevent occupational accidents, injuries and diseases on board ship, including through the provision of all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment'.

That single word — appropriately-sized — is the most concrete gender-equality provision in the whole of maritime law, and a candidate who reaches it has answered this question at a different level from one who has not. PPE designed for the average male body does not protect a smaller person; it is a hazard. The obligation is express, it is in Part A of the Code and therefore mandatory, it takes effect through each Member's national law, and it is verifiable at inspection.

The 2016 amendments, in force 8 January 2019, strengthened protection against shipboard harassment and bullying, and the Convention's guidance directs competent authorities to take harassment and bullying into account in national occupational safety and health guidelines and to have regard to the joint ICS and ITF guidance on eliminating it.

And there is a further set, whose status must be stated exactly. The International Labour Conference, at its 113th Session in June 2025, approved a further set of amendments to the Convention. That approval is a fact and it precedes this examination. But the amendments are not in force, and nothing turns on them yet: under the Convention's own procedure an approved amendment takes effect only after the prescribed period and acceptance conditions. Approved is not in force, and an answer that describes the 2025 amendments as operative law is wrong — as is an answer that omits their approval altogether, now that it has happened.

blocks.h: 6. India's initiatives to reduce the gender gap

blocks.p: India is one of the largest suppliers of seafarers in the world, so its policy has effect out of proportion to its own fleet. The measures fall into four groups, and they are stated here at the level the evidence supports.

ol: Regulatory and institutional. The Directorate General of Shipping is the competent authority under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and administers seafarer training, certification and welfare. India has ratified the MLC, and its obligations — including Standard A4.3 — take domestic effect through the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour) Rules made under the 1958 Act. The competent authority is therefore the route by which the appropriately-sized PPE obligation reaches an Indian ship.

Training access. Pre-sea and post-sea training at DG Shipping-approved maritime training institutes is open to women across the deck, engine and electro-technical streams, and the Indian Maritime University, established by the Indian Maritime University Act, 2008, provides the degree-level route on the same basis. Access to training is the necessary first condition and India's system does not restrict it.

Employment and placement. The persistent Indian bottleneck is not admission to training but the cadet berth — the shipboard training placement without which a certificate cannot be completed. Administrative measures directed at training-berth availability, at conditions for women on board Indian ships and at grievance and harassment redressal are the operative levers, and they are exercised through the Directorate's circulars and orders.

Policy and advocacy. India's national maritime policy documents carry commitments to increase women's participation in the maritime workforce, and India supports the IMO's Women in Maritime work including through the regional association for its area.

blocks.p: A closing judgement, which the command word 'discuss' invites. The regulatory barrier has largely gone: STCW is neutral, Indian training is open, and the MLC now requires equipment that actually fits. What remains is berth allocation, shipboard conditions and retention — and those are decided by shipowners and by senior officers on board, not by regulators. That places the responsibility squarely on the management-level officer this examination is certifying.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: This is the question on the paper most likely to be answered in generalities, and generalities score badly at Class I. The structure defends against that in three ways. Section 2 gives six numbered reasons rather than a paragraph of sentiment. Section 3 splits the challenges into structural, shipboard and career, which turns a list into an analysis and lets an engineer speak about PPE and ergonomics as design problems. And section 5 supplies a hard, dated, checkable legal fact, which is what separates a first-class answer from a competent one.

The other structural decision worth understanding is that section 4 states the limit of the IMO's role. Examiners reward a candidate who can say what an organisation cannot do. It also sets up section 5, because the reason the IMO's role is promotional is that the mandatory instrument in this field belongs to the ILO.

blocks.h: The one fact that lifts this answer

blocks.p: MLC Standard A4.3(1)(b), as amended in 2022, in force 23 December 2024: 'all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment'.

Three reasons it is worth more than anything else you could write here. It is mandatory — Part A of the Code, not a guideline. It is recent — in force just over half a year before this sitting, so it is current in a way the examiner will notice. And it converts an abstract topic into an engineering one: PPE sized for the average male body does not protect a smaller person, so this is a safety defect and not a comfort complaint.

blocks.h: Approved, in force, and the three MLC amendment sets

blocks.p: This question now carries three amendment sets at three different statuses, and getting the third right is what distinguishes a July 2025 answer from an earlier one.

rows: Operative law; the load-bearing fact of the answer
State the approval as fact. Do not state or imply that it is operative

blocks.p: Approved, adopted and in force are three states with three dates, and collapsing them is the standard failure in any question about an instrument in motion. An approval by the Conference is a real event that has happened; it is not law until the Convention's own procedure has run.

blocks.h: Locating the law correctly

rows: Women in Maritime Programme, regional associations
World Maritime Day 2019 theme; International Day for Women in Maritime, 18 May
Mandatory, and already gender-neutral on its face

blocks.p: The MLC is amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII, by the Convention's own simplified procedure. It is not an IMO instrument and does not travel by IMO tacit acceptance. Saying so in limb (b) shows the two regimes are held apart.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing limb (a) as advocacy rather than as management argument. The examiner wants reasons an owner would accept, not sentiment.
Quoting a participation percentage. The circulating figures differ by base and by date, and a wrong one is worse than none. Every mark in this answer is available without a number.
Inventing an IMO resolution number for the gender programme or the International Day. Name the act; do not number it.
Inventing a DG Shipping circular number. Same discipline.
Treating the IMO as the source of mandatory gender law. Its role here is promotional; the mandatory instrument is the ILO's.
Missing the MLC 2022 amendment entirely, which is the difference between a pass and a strong answer.

Describing the 2025 MLC amendments as in force. They were approved in June 2025 and are not in force. Omitting the approval altogether is the opposite error and also costs, because it happened before this sitting.
Treating PPE fit as a comfort issue rather than a safety defect — an engineering error, not just a rhetorical one.
Answering only the IMO half of limb (b) and leaving the Indian half thin. It is explicitly asked for and carries half the limb.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: The stem prints 'the international Maritime Organization' with a lower-case initial. It is a printing error in the source and the answer neither reproduces nor remarks on it.
'Elaborate on the initiatives taken by the Indian government' is a specific demand for national content in an otherwise international question. A generic answer forfeits four marks.
'Discuss' in limb (a) requires a position, not a survey. The closing judgement in section 6 supplies one.
The SDG opening sentence is a frame, not the question. Spending two marks' worth of writing on the 2030 Agenda is the commonest way to run out of time on this question.
Asking about the status of the newest MLC amendments. The correct answer at this sitting is approved, not in force — and that is a better answer than either silence or an overstatement.

The question is set in an Engineering Management paper. The strongest material is therefore the material an engineer owns: PPE, equipment design, anthropometry, habitability and the safety-culture argument.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which SDG is gender equality, and is it binding on your company?
Name one mandatory requirement in maritime law that exists because of gender. When did it come into force?
Is that an IMO or an ILO instrument, and how is it amended?
Has the MLC been amended since? What is the status of the newest set?
Your company sends you PPE in one size. What is your obligation?
You are the Chief Engineer and the only woman on board is in your department. What do you actually do differently?
Does STCW distinguish between men and women?
Who is the competent authority in India, and under which Act?
What is the practical bottleneck for an Indian woman cadet, and is it a regulatory one?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Limb (a) is WHY then WHAT: six reasons the industry needs it (2), then three families of barrier — structural, shipboard, career (3).

Limb (b) is SOFT, HARD, HOME: the IMO's promotional work (4), the MLC's mandatory requirement (5), then India (6). The pivot sentence between the first two is that the IMO convenes and the ILO compels.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and evidence limits

blocks.p: The corpus holds no gender material at all. There is no Women in Maritime document, no SDG document and no DG Shipping circular in True Source — the DGS-circulars directory carries an instrument log and a manifest and no document. Everything in sections 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 is therefore authoritative secondary or management judgement, and is labelled as such.

The consequence has been applied strictly rather than noted and ignored. No participation statistic appears anywhere in this answer, no IMO resolution number is asserted for the gender programme or the International Day, and no DG Shipping circular number is asserted. The qualitative case is complete without any of them, and this is the question on the paper where invented precision would be easiest and most damaging.

The one hard anchor — the MLC 2022 amendment — is correspondingly strong: it was proved by reading the paragraph in both the pre-2022 and the consolidated held texts and observing that the PPE clause is absent from the first.

On the 2025 amendments, only two facts are stated and neither is exceeded: that the International Labour Conference approved them at its 113th Session in June 2025, and that they are not in force. Their content is not described, because the corpus segregates them as not yet in force and holds no consolidated text incorporating them. The temptation on a question like this is to describe what a newly approved instrument will require; at this sitting that would be describing law that does not exist.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two eight-mark limbs. Limb (a) is a management-argument question wearing a social-policy coat: it asks why gender diversity MATTERS to the industry and what actually obstructs it, and it rewards reasons an owner would accept rather than sentiment. Limb (b) is two questions in one - the IMO's role, which is largely promotional, and India's initiatives, which is a specific national demand that a generic answer forfeits. The hidden demand in limb (b) is to locate the mandatory law correctly, which means recognising that it is an ILO instrument and not an IMO one.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, printed as 8 + 8. Limb (a) takes three sections - the SDG frame kept short, six numbered reasons, and the barriers in three families. Limb (b) takes three - the IMO's mechanism and its limit, the hard MLC layer with its three amendment statuses, and India in four groups. The MLC section is where a strong answer separates itself, so it is given full weight despite sitting in the middle of the second limb.

questions.understand_first: The examiner has set a social-policy question in an Engineering Management paper, and that is the key to answering it well. The marks are not for sympathy; they are for argument and for law. The argument half is a management case an owner would accept — an industry with a structural officer shortage that recruits from half the population has a supply problem it created, and a crew in which nobody challenges the person in charge is a safety problem before it is a diversity one. The law half turns on a distinction most candidates miss: the IMO is not where the hard law is. Its gender work is a technical co-operation programme, some regional associations and a day in the calendar — real, useful, and not binding on anybody. The one genuinely mandatory, port-State-inspectable, gender-specific requirement in maritime law belongs to the ILO: the Maritime Labour Convention, whose 2022 amendments were already in force at this sitting, requires appropriately-sized personal protective equipment. One adjective, in Part A of the Code, converts the whole subject from aspiration into a defect a surveyor can write up. Find that provision, place India's Directorate General of Shipping correctly as the competent authority that brings it home under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and the answer writes itself.

steps.title: Where gender equality sits, and why it reaches shipping
points: SDG 5 - gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls - within the UN 2030 Agenda adopted in 2015
it is a CROSS-CUTTING goal, a condition the other sixteen are pursued under, not a sector programme
shipping is caught sharply because it is among the most male-dominated occupations in the world of work
because it is internationally regulated, so a global norm can be given effect through IMO and ILO instruments
and because it faces a structural officer shortage while recruiting from half the population

steps.title: Why gender diversity matters to the industry
points: LABOUR SUPPLY - the largest untapped source of certificated officers, available without new training capacity
QUALITY OF SELECTION - drawing from the whole population raises the standard of entry at no cost
DECISION QUALITY AND SAFETY CULTURE - diverse teams resist the group conformity behind a recognisable class of casualty
RETENTION AND THE SHORE PIPELINE - a sea-going population that excludes women produces a shore management that excludes them a decade later
COMMERCIAL AND REPUTATIONAL EXPECTATION - charterers, financiers and cargo interests report on workforce composition
LEGITIMACY - an industry carrying most of world trade cannot defend a profile no other technical profession would defend

steps.title: The challenges women actually face
points: STRUCTURAL - cadet-berth allocation and sponsorship, social and family expectation, absence of role models and sponsors, employer reluctance framed as an operational problem
SHIPBOARD - PPE and workwear sized for the average male body, which is a SAFETY DEFECT and not a comfort issue
SHIPBOARD - accommodation, sanitary arrangements and privacy on ships designed for a single-sex crew; isolation as the only woman on board
SHIPBOARD - harassment, bullying and sexual harassment, aggravated by a closed community and a reporting line that may run through the person complained of
SHIPBOARD - equipment and manual-handling design based on assumed male anthropometry, which an engineer should identify as a DESIGN problem
CAREER - interrupted sea time around maternity in a system whose revalidation depends on recent sea service; attrition at the first-command and first-chief-engineer stage

steps.title: The IMO's role - the programme, the mechanism, and its limits
points: the Women in Maritime Programme, established in the late 1980s in the technical co-operation work - fellowships, training places, institutional support
the regional Women in Maritime Associations, the programme's most durable structure
agenda-setting - the World Maritime Day theme for 2019 and the International Day for Women in Maritime on 18 May
measurement - the joint IMO and WISTA International Women in Maritime Survey
gender mainstreaming in the Strategic Plan and the technical co-operation programme
STCW is already gender-neutral on its face, which locates the barrier at access, conditions and retention rather than certification
THE LIMIT - almost all of it is promotional and capacity-building rather than mandatory; the hardest law in this field is not an IMO instrument at all

steps.title: The hard legal layer, and exactly where it stood at this sitting
points: the MLC 2006 is an ILO instrument, amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII, not by IMO tacit acceptance
the 2022 amendments are IN FORCE from 23 December 2024 - seven months before this sitting
Standard A4.3(1)(b) now requires all necessary APPROPRIATELY-SIZED personal protective equipment - Part A, therefore mandatory and inspectable
PPE sized for the average male body does not protect a smaller person: this is a safety defect, not a comfort complaint
the 2016 amendments, in force 8 January 2019, strengthened protection against shipboard harassment and bullying
the 2025 amendments were APPROVED by the International Labour Conference at its 113th Session in June 2025 - one month before this sitting - and are NOT IN FORCE
APPROVED IS NOT IN FORCE: state the approval, refuse the operative status, and do not describe their content

steps.title: India's initiatives to reduce the gender gap
points: REGULATORY - the Directorate General of Shipping as competent authority under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, with MLC obligations taking domestic effect through the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour) Rules
TRAINING - DG Shipping-approved institutes open to women across deck, engine and electro-technical streams, and the Indian Maritime University under the Act of 2008
PLACEMENT - the real bottleneck is the CADET BERTH, not admission to training; administrative measures address berth availability, shipboard conditions and harassment redressal
POLICY - national maritime policy commitments to women's participation, and support for the IMO's regional Women in Maritime association

THE CLOSING JUDGEMENT - the regulatory barrier has largely gone; what remains is berth allocation, shipboard conditions and retention, which are decided by owners and by senior officers on board rather than by regulators

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is WHY then WHAT — six management reasons (2), then three families of barrier: structural, shipboard, career (3). Limb (b) is SOFT, HARD, HOME — the IMO convenes (4), the ILO compels (5), then India (6). The one fact that lifts it: APPROPRIATELY-SIZED PPE (5).

quick_revision.recall_15s: SDG 5 is gender equality, within the UN 2030 Agenda. Shipping is caught because it is the most male-dominated trade, it is internationally regulated, and it is short of officers. Make the case as management argument: labour supply, quality of selection, safety culture, the shore pipeline, commercial expectation, legitimacy. Barriers come in three families — structural (cadet berths, sponsorship, role models), shipboard (PPE fit, accommodation, isolation, harassment, anthropometry) and career (interrupted sea time, attrition at first command). The IMO convenes: Women in Maritime Programme, regional associations, World Maritime Day 2019, International Day 18 May, the IMO-WISTA survey — all promotional. The ILO compels: MLC Standard A4.3(1)(b), as amended in 2022 and in force 23 December 2024, requires appropriately-sized PPE — mandatory and inspectable. The 2025 amendments were approved in June 2025 and are NOT in force. India: DG Shipping under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, approved training institutes, the Indian Maritime University, and the cadet berth as the real bottleneck.

critical_numbers: SDG 5 of 17 goals, within the 2030 Agenda adopted 2015
MLC 2016 amendments - harassment and bullying - in force 8 January 2019

MLC 2025 amendments - approved at the 113th Session, June 2025 - APPROVED, NOT IN FORCE

quick_revision.critical_regulation: MLC 2006, Standard A4.3, paragraph 1(b), as amended in 2022 and in force from 23 December 2024: the measures adopted must include reasonable precautions to prevent occupational accidents, injuries and diseases on board ship, including through the provision of all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment. It is in Part A of the Code, so it is mandatory; it is an ILO instrument amended under Article XIII by the Special Tripartite Committee, not an IMO one; and it reaches an Indian ship through the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour) Rules made under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
quick_revision.major_trap: Treating the IMO as the source of mandatory gender law. Its gender work is promotional and capacity-building; the one hard, inspectable, gender-specific requirement is the ILO's MLC Standard A4.3(1)(b). Second trap, and the one specific to this sitting: mis-stating the newest MLC amendments. They were approved by the International Labour Conference in June 2025, one month before this examination, and they are not in force — so describing them as operative is wrong, and omitting the approval altogether is also wrong now that it has happened. Third trap: quoting a participation percentage. The circulating figures differ by base and by date, and every mark in this answer is available without one.

Barriers in three families: structural, shipboard, career
The IMO convenes - programme, associations, agenda, measurement - and its limit
The ILO compels - MLC A4.3(1)(b), appropriately-sized PPE, and the status of all three amendment sets
India - DG Shipping under the 1958 Act, training, the cadet berth, policy - and a stated judgement

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the gender equality question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 SDG 5 and why shipping is caught by it. 2 Six management reasons diversity matters. 3 The barriers in three families. (b) 4 The IMO's role and its limit. 5 The hard MLC layer and the status of each amendment set. 6 India's initiatives and a closing judgement.
retrieval_cards.why: Three sections per limb match the 8 + 8 split, and section 4's statement of the IMO's limit is what sets up section 5.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name one mandatory requirement in maritime law that exists because of gender, and date it.
retrieval_cards.answer: MLC 2006, Standard A4.3, paragraph 1(b), as amended in 2022 and in force from 23 December 2024: reasonable precautions must include the provision of all necessary appropriately-sized personal protective equipment. It sits in Part A of the Code, so it is mandatory and port-State inspectable.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable fact in the answer, and the one that converts an abstract topic into an engineering requirement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the hard gender law in shipping an IMO or an ILO instrument, and why does it matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: ILO. The MLC 2006 is amended by the Special Tripartite Committee under Article XIII by the Convention's own simplified procedure, not by IMO tacit acceptance. It matters because the IMO's gender work is promotional - a technical co-operation programme, regional associations and an international day - while the MLC is mandatory and inspectable.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) asks about the IMO, so saying plainly what the IMO cannot do is the mark rather than an evasion.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the status of the newest MLC amendments at a July 2025 sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Approved, not in force. The International Labour Conference approved them at its 113th Session in June 2025, one month before the examination. Under the Convention's own procedure an approved amendment takes effect only after the prescribed period and acceptance conditions. State the approval; do not state or imply that it is operative, and do not describe its content.
retrieval_cards.why: Approved, adopted and in force are three states with three dates, and this is the question on the paper where they are easiest to collapse.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is ill-fitting PPE an engineering issue rather than a comfort one?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because protective equipment sized for the average male body does not protect a smaller person - a harness, respirator, glove or boot that does not fit is a defeated control, not an inconvenience. That is why the 2022 MLC amendment uses the word appropriately-sized and why the point belongs in an Engineering Management answer.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the bridge between the social topic and the technical paper it is set in, and it is where an engineer can outscore a policy answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the three families of barrier women face at sea.
retrieval_cards.answer: Structural - cadet-berth allocation and sponsorship, social and family expectation, absence of role models, employer reluctance. Shipboard - PPE and workwear fit, accommodation and privacy, isolation, harassment and bullying, medical access, equipment designed for male anthropometry. Career - interrupted sea time around maternity against revalidation requirements, few shore paths, and attrition at the first-command and first-chief-engineer stage.
retrieval_cards.why: Separating them turns a list into an analysis, which is what 'discuss' is asking for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the IMO actually do about gender, and what can it not do?
retrieval_cards.answer: It runs the Women in Maritime Programme within its technical co-operation work, supports regional Women in Maritime Associations, sets the agenda through the 2019 World Maritime Day theme and the International Day for Women in Maritime on 18 May, and measures participation jointly with WISTA. What it does not do is impose any mandatory requirement that a company employ women - no IMO convention does.
retrieval_cards.why: The limit is the honest part of the limb, and it explains why the mandatory instrument belongs to the ILO.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who is India's competent authority, under which Act, and how does the MLC reach an Indian ship?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Directorate General of Shipping, under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. India has ratified the MLC, and its obligations - including Standard A4.3 - take domestic effect through the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour) Rules made under the 1958 Act. Training runs through DG Shipping-approved institutes and the Indian Maritime University under its Act of 2008.
retrieval_cards.why: The Indian limb is expressly demanded and a generic answer forfeits half the limb; naming the Act correctly also fixes the sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the real bottleneck for an Indian woman cadet, and is it regulatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The cadet berth - the shipboard training placement without which a certificate cannot be completed. It is not a regulatory barrier: STCW is gender-neutral, and admission to DG Shipping-approved training is open. The obstacle is allocation by owners and operators, which is a commercial and management decision rather than a legal one.
retrieval_cards.why: It supports the closing judgement that the remaining barriers are decided by owners and senior officers rather than by regulators.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.2.8: 'Suspect areas are locations showing substantial corrosion and/or are considered by the surveyor to be prone to rapid wastage.' The definition is the link between a measurement and a future survey obligation.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.2.11, coating condition, defined in three grades: GOOD - only minor spot rusting; FAIR - local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections and/or light rusting over 20 per cent or more of areas under consideration, but less than POOR; POOR - general breakdown of coating over 20 per cent or more of areas, or hard scale at 10 per cent or more of areas.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.2.10: a corrosion prevention system is normally considered a full hard protective coating, usually epoxy or equivalent; other systems that are neither soft nor semi-hard may be acceptable if applied and maintained to the manufacturer's specification.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.1.3: the Code contains the minimum extent of examination, thickness measurements and tank testing, and 'the survey should be extended when substantial corrosion and/or structural defects are found and include additional close-up survey when necessary'.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.5: in any kind of survey, thickness measurements of structures in areas where close-up surveys are required should be carried out simultaneously with the close-up surveys.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.2.5: close-up survey is a survey where the details of structural components are within the close visual inspection range of the surveyor, normally within reach of hand. Paragraph 1.2.6 defines the transverse section; 1.2.7 defines representative spaces.

PRIMARY - ESP Code paragraph 1.2.2: a space used for both cargo and salt water ballast is treated as a ballast tank when substantial corrosion has been found in it. A finding of substantial corrosion therefore changes the survey regime that applies to the space.

PRIMARY - ESP Code section 2.2, dry-dock survey: a survey in dry-dock is part of the renewal survey; a minimum of two bottom inspections in the five-year certificate period, maximum interval 36 months; for ships of 15 years and over the bottom inspection is in dry-dock.

THE ESP CODE AMENDMENT CHAIN AFTER A.1049(27) IS NOT ASSEMBLED (RQ-26). The Code is amended at almost every MSC session. Everything cited here is read from the base text of A.1049(27) and no amendment is asserted, so a later renumbering or revision of a cited paragraph cannot be excluded.

THE ANNEX NUMBERS DIFFER BETWEEN ANNEX A AND ANNEX B. The Code carries a separate annex set for bulk carriers and for oil tankers, and the extended-measurement annex is not the same number in both. The answer names the annex by its FUNCTION - the requirements for the extent of thickness measurements at areas of substantial corrosion - and does not assert a single number across both ship types.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA FOR DOUBLER PLATES, AND THE CIRCUMSTANCES IN WHICH A SOCIETY WILL PERMIT THEM AS OTHER THAN A TEMPORARY MEASURE, ARE SOCIETY-SPECIFIC. Described as practice, not asserted as a rule.

The ESP Code applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers. Substantial corrosion as a concept is used more widely in class practice, but the Code definition quoted here is the ESP definition and the answer says so rather than generalising it silently.

cross_links.label: QP2507 Q8 - the classification framework and the survey cycle within which this renewal survey sits

blocks.h: 1. The definition - and it is printed twice, not once

blocks.p: Substantial corrosion is defined in the 2011 ESP Code (resolution A.1049(27), mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/2), at paragraph 1.2.9. The Code gives two definitions and a Class I answer gives both.

ol: The general definition. Substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits.

The Common Structural Rules definition. For ships built under the IACS Common Structural Rules, substantial corrosion is an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates a gauged (or measured) thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net.

blocks.p: Read the general definition carefully, because both halves of it are examinable. 'In excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins' means most — but not all — of the corrosion allowance is gone. 'But within acceptable limits' means the structure is still acceptable. Substantial corrosion is therefore not a defect requiring immediate renewal. It is a warning state: a declaration that this location is close to its limit and must now be watched more closely and measured more widely.

The CSR definition says the same thing in a different currency. Under CSR the scantling is expressed as a net thickness plus a corrosion addition; substantial corrosion is the last 0.5 mm above the net thickness. Below t-net the steel is no longer acceptable at all.

blocks.h: 2. Where the concept sits, and the model it presupposes

blocks.p: The definition only makes sense against the corrosion-allowance model of hull scantlings, and stating that model first is what converts a memorised sentence into an answer.

ul: A rule scantling is a net thickness required for strength, plus a corrosion addition for the wastage expected over the ship's life.
Allowable margin is that addition. Renewal thickness is the point at which it is exhausted and the steel must be renewed.
Wastage is therefore measured not as a percentage of the original plate but as a proportion of the margin. Substantial corrosion is 75 per cent of the way through it.

blocks.p: The Code is deliberate about its own status. Paragraph 1.1.3 states that it contains the minimum extent of examination, thickness measurement and tank testing, and that 'the survey should be extended when substantial corrosion and/or structural defects are found and include additional close-up survey when necessary'. That sentence is the engine of the whole question: a finding of substantial corrosion is the trigger that enlarges the survey.

One further consequence is easy to miss. Paragraph 1.2.2 provides that a space used for both cargo and salt water ballast is treated as a ballast tank when substantial corrosion has been found in it. A finding does not merely add measurements — it can change the survey regime the space falls under.

blocks.h: 3. The criteria used to assess it during inspections

blocks.p: The surveyor is not applying one criterion but a small set, and the Code supplies the vocabulary for each.

ol: The measured wastage against the allowable margin. The primary criterion. The gauged thickness is compared with the rule renewal thickness taken from the society's rules and the ship's approved scantling drawings; the result is expressed as a proportion of the margin, and 75 per cent is the threshold.

The corrosion pattern, not a single reading. The Code says 'assessment of the corrosion pattern'. A single low point is not the test. General diminution, grooving, pitting and edge and weld-line wastage are read together across the member.

Coating condition, graded by paragraph 1.2.11 as GOOD (only minor spot rusting), FAIR (local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections, and/or light rusting over 20 per cent or more of the areas under consideration, but less than POOR) or POOR (general breakdown of coating over 20 per cent or more of areas, or hard scale at 10 per cent or more). Coating condition is what tells the surveyor where corrosion will appear next.

Whether a corrosion prevention system is in place and effective. Paragraph 1.2.10 treats a corrosion prevention system as normally a full hard protective coating, usually epoxy or equivalent. A tank with no effective system attracts a heavier survey regardless of today's measurements.

Whether the location is a suspect area. Paragraph 1.2.8: suspect areas are locations showing substantial corrosion and/or considered by the surveyor to be prone to rapid wastage. Note the 'and/or' — the surveyor's judgement is an independent route into the category.

The ship's history. Paragraph 1.2.7 requires that in selecting representative spaces, account be taken of the service and repair history and of identifiable critical or suspect areas. Previous findings drive present scope.

blocks.h: 4. Inspection techniques - how it is actually found

blocks.p: The techniques run from the general to the particular, and the Code's own sequence is the right order to write them in.

ol: Preparation. The space must be cleaned, de-scaled, ventilated, gas-freed, illuminated and made safe for access. A poorly prepared tank is the commonest reason a survey cannot be credited.
Overall survey — a survey to report on the overall condition of the hull structure and to determine the extent of additional close-up surveys required.

Close-up survey — defined at paragraph 1.2.5 as a survey where the details of structural components are within the close visual inspection range of the surveyor, normally within reach of hand. Achieved by staging, rafting, cherry-picker, rope access or remote inspection techniques as the society accepts.

Thickness measurement by ultrasonic gauging, carried out by a company certified for the purpose — the Code carries a dedicated annex of procedures for certification of a company engaged in thickness measurement of hull structures — and witnessed by the attending surveyor.

Simultaneity. Paragraph 1.5 requires that, in any kind of survey, thickness measurements of structures in areas where close-up surveys are required be carried out simultaneously with the close-up surveys. Measuring after the staging has come down is not compliance.

Supplementary techniques where the visual and gauged evidence points to cracking rather than wastage: magnetic particle or dye-penetrant inspection at weld toes and hard spots, and hammer testing to identify heavily scaled or grooved material.
Tank pressure testing of boundaries, and internal examination of the spaces the Code lists.
Recording. Thickness measurement reports on the Code's reporting format, the survey report, and the Condition Evaluation Report which summarises the ship's structural condition at the renewal survey.

blocks.h: 5. What a finding does to the renewal survey

blocks.p: The renewal survey is the five-yearly hull survey that re-establishes fitness for the next period of validity of the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate. Its shape is fixed before substantial corrosion is found, and is then enlarged by the finding.

The baseline. Under section 2, the renewal survey may commence at the fourth annual survey and be progressed during the succeeding year with a view to completion by the fifth anniversary date (2.1.1); the survey programme is dealt with in advance and thickness measurement is not to be held before the fourth annual survey (2.1.2); all cargo holds, ballast tanks, pipe tunnels, cofferdams and void spaces bounding cargo holds, decks and the outer hull are examined and the examination supplemented by thickness measurement and testing, sufficient to discover substantial corrosion, significant deformation, fractures, damage or other structural deterioration (2.1.4); a dry-dock survey forms part of it, with a minimum of two bottom inspections in the five-year period and a maximum interval of 36 months, in dry-dock for ships of 15 years and over (2.2.1–2.2.2); and concurrent crediting to both the intermediate and the renewal survey is not acceptable (2.1.7).
The steps once substantial corrosion is found:

ol: Extend the thickness measurements to the increased extent the Code's dedicated annex prescribes for areas of substantial corrosion. The Code is express, in the corresponding intermediate-survey provision, that these extended measurements must be carried out before the survey is credited as completed — the survey is not closed on a promise.
Extend the close-up survey where necessary, per paragraph 1.1.3, to establish the extent of the affected structure rather than the extent of the first sample.

Record the locations as suspect areas, so that they are examined at every subsequent survey and gauged again. This is the mechanism by which a single finding follows the ship for the rest of her life.
Re-classify the space where 1.2.2 applies, so that a combined cargo and ballast space is thereafter surveyed as a ballast tank.

Assess against renewal thickness. Where measurements are within the substantial-corrosion band the steel is acceptable but monitored; where they are at or below renewal thickness the material must be dealt with now.
Repair or renew, to an approved scheme — section 6 below.

Deal with the cause, not only the symptom. Coating condition graded POOR, a failed or absent corrosion prevention system, or defective anodes are addressed as part of the same event, because renewing steel into a failed coating simply restarts the clock.
Complete the records — thickness measurement reports, survey report and Condition Evaluation Report — and only then credit the survey.

blocks.h: 6. Repair methods and their acceptance

blocks.p: This part of the answer is class practice and the IACS framework, not Convention text, and should be written as such. What the ESP Code supplies is the trigger and the record; what the society's rules supply is the acceptance.

ul: Cropping and renewal of wasted plating and stiffening is the primary and permanent remedy: the wasted material is cut out and replaced with new material of at least the original rule thickness, of approved grade, with approved welding procedures, qualified welders and approved consumables, and with post-weld NDT.
Partial renewal — renewing the wasted strake, face plate, web or bracket rather than the whole member — where the wastage is local and the surrounding structure is sound.
Insert plates with full penetration butt welds, sized and positioned so that seams do not fall in high-stress locations or coincide with existing welds.

Doubler plates are a temporary and conditional measure only, accepted at the society's discretion, usually with a time limit and a condition of class requiring permanent repair. A doubler conceals the parent material and traps moisture behind it, which is precisely why it is not a repair.
Weld repair and build-up for grooving corrosion along weld lines, within the limits the society allows — it is easy to do more harm than good by heat input into thin material.
Renewal of the corrosion prevention system: surface preparation, coating to the maker's specification, and renewal of sacrificial anodes.
Reinforcement or redesign where wastage is recurrent in the same location, because a repeated failure is a design or drainage problem rather than a maintenance one.

blocks.p: Two conditions govern all of it. First, a repair affecting classed structure requires the society's prior approval of the repair scheme and survey of the completed work. Second, the work must be recorded, because the next surveyor's scope depends on knowing what was done.

blocks.h: 7. The role of the classification society

blocks.p: The society is present at every stage of what has just been described, and it is worth naming the roles separately because they are different.

ol: Rule-maker. It sets the scantlings, the corrosion additions and the renewal thicknesses against which everything is measured, and adopts the IACS Unified Requirements and the Common Structural Rules into its own rules.
Survey planner. It agrees the survey programme in advance with the owner, and it determines the extent of close-up survey and thickness measurement — including the extension the finding requires.
Attending surveyor. It carries out the overall and close-up surveys, witnesses the gauging and applies the assessment criteria in section 3.
Approver of the repair. It approves the repair scheme, the materials, the welding procedures and the welders, and surveys the completed repair.
Keeper of the record. It maintains the survey status, the thickness measurement records, the Condition Evaluation Report and the suspect-area register that determines future survey scope.

Enforcer. Where compliance is impaired it imposes a condition of class with a due date; if that is not cleared, class is suspended. Because the Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate is normally issued by the same organisation acting as the flag State's Recognized Organization, the practical consequence reaches the ship's statutory certification too — but through the flag State's delegation, not through class itself.

Certifier of the measuring company. The Code's own annex requires the thickness-measurement company to be certified, and that certification is a class function — a point almost no candidate makes and one that shows the whole chain has been understood.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem asks four things in one sentence — define, criteria, steps at renewal survey, and within that inspection techniques, repair methods and the role of class. The commonest failure is to write a good definition and then a vague paragraph about surveys, which collects perhaps five of sixteen marks. Seven sections in the printed order of the demands guarantee that every demand has a home, and the definition section is deliberately short so that the procedural sections can be full.

The single most valuable thing in this answer is the observation in section 1 that substantial corrosion is a warning state, not a defect. It follows straight from the Code's own words 'but within acceptable limits', and it explains why the correct response is to measure more rather than to renew. A candidate who writes 'substantial corrosion means the plate must be renewed' has contradicted the definition he just quoted.

blocks.h: The two definitions, side by side

rows: Wastage in excess of 75% of allowable margins
Gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net
A proportion of the corrosion allowance
An absolute band above the net thickness
At or below renewal thickness: renew

blocks.p: Both are printed in ESP Code paragraph 1.2.9. Quoting only the first is the commonest incompleteness in this answer, and the CSR limb is the more likely one on a modern bulk carrier or tanker.

blocks.h: The corrosion-allowance model, in one line

blocks.p: Rule scantling = net thickness + corrosion addition. The addition is the allowable margin. Substantial corrosion is 75 per cent of the way through the addition — not 75 per cent of the plate. A candidate who says 'more than 75 per cent of the plate thickness is gone' has described a hole, not substantial corrosion, and has lost the definition mark.

blocks.h: What triggers what

rows: Thickness measurements extended to the annex extent; close-up survey extended as necessary (1.1.3)
Survey not credited as completed until they are done
Becomes a suspect area (1.2.8) - examined and gauged at every later survey
Combined cargo/ballast space with substantial corrosion
Treated as a ballast tank thereafter (1.2.2)
Heavier survey regime; the coating itself must be dealt with
No longer substantial corrosion - the steel is unacceptable and must be renewed

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Giving only one of the two definitions in paragraph 1.2.9.
Saying substantial corrosion means 75 per cent of the plate thickness is lost, rather than 75 per cent of the allowable margin.
Treating substantial corrosion as a defect requiring immediate renewal, which contradicts 'but within acceptable limits'.
Describing the renewal survey generically and never saying what the finding changes — which is the actual question.
Omitting that extended measurements must be completed before the survey is credited.
Offering doubler plates as a repair method without saying they are temporary, conditional and normally attract a condition of class.
Attributing the ESP Code to SOLAS chapter II-1. It is made mandatory by SOLAS XI-1/2.
Presenting repair acceptance criteria as Convention requirements. They are class rules.
Quoting a numeric renewal thickness. It is rule- and ship-specific and inventing one is worse than giving the method.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Define' is the first word of the stem. An approximate paraphrase will not do; the two-limb definition is the cheapest three marks on the paper and the most commonly half-taken.

'What criteria are used' is plural and is not a repeat of the definition. It wants the assessment framework: pattern rather than point, coating condition, corrosion prevention system, suspect-area status and survey history.

'Including inspection techniques, repair methods, and the role of the classification society' is a three-part instruction embedded in a clause. Each of the three is worth marks and each needs its own section.
The ESP Code applies to bulk carriers and oil tankers. Saying so is a mark; silently generalising the definition to all ships is a small error a strong examiner will notice.

The Code's language is 'should' throughout, because it is a code applied through class and made mandatory by SOLAS XI-1/2 rather than drafted as SOLAS text. Reproducing it as 'shall' misstates the instrument.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Define substantial corrosion. Now give the Common Structural Rules definition.
Is a plate in substantial corrosion acceptable? Then why does it matter?
You find substantial corrosion in a topside tank at the fourth annual survey. What happens to the scope of the renewal survey?
What is a suspect area, and how does a location become one?
Grade this coating: local breakdown at stiffener edges with light rusting over about a quarter of the area.
Who is allowed to take the thickness measurements, and who witnesses them?
Your owner asks for a doubler plate over a wasted strake. What do you tell him?
Which instrument makes the ESP Code mandatory?
What is in the Condition Evaluation Report, and why does the next surveyor want it?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The answer is the surveyor's own working day: DEFINE → MODEL → CRITERIA → FIND → EXTEND → FIX → CLASS. Seven words, seven sections.
For the definition itself, one sentence: seventy-five per cent of the margin, still acceptable, so measure more. It contains the number, the caveat and the consequence.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The corpus holds the base 2011 ESP Code and its instrument log records expressly that the amendment chain after A.1049(27) is not assembled (RQ-26), the Code being amended at almost every MSC session. Everything cited in this answer is read from the base text and no amendment is asserted. For a definition-and-procedure question that is sufficient; for an edition-precise citation it would not be, and the log says so.

The annex that carries the extended measurement extent is numbered differently in the bulk carrier and oil tanker annexes of the Code, so it is named here by its function rather than by a number that would be right for only one ship type.

No numeric renewal thickness, corrosion addition or acceptance criterion for doubler plates is quoted. Those are rule- and ship-specific, the corpus holds no class rulebook, and the method is worth more to a candidate than a figure that would be wrong for his ship.

Nothing in this question is sitting-sensitive, and that is a verified result rather than an assumption. The governing instrument predates this sitting by thirteen years, and it was tested for movement across the four months between the March 2025 sitting that shares this stem and this one — because an identical stem is not an identical answer, a lesson learned when SIRE 2.0 superseded VIQ7 between two otherwise identical questions. questions.understand_first: The examiner is testing whether you understand that substantial corrosion is a warning, not a failure. The ESP Code's own words are 'wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits' — the steel is still good. What has been consumed is most of the corrosion allowance, the margin deliberately added to the net scantling to be eaten over the ship's life. So the correct response to a finding is not to cut plate out; it is to find out how far it goes. That is why the Code makes the finding a trigger that enlarges the survey — more thickness measurement, more close-up survey, and the location placed on a suspect-area register that follows the ship for the rest of her life. Renewal only enters when the measurements reach the renewal thickness, at which point the material is no longer in substantial corrosion at all: it is simply unacceptable. Hold that logic and the whole answer — criteria, techniques, steps, repairs and the society's role — falls out of it in order.

points: the baseline - may commence at the fourth annual and complete by the fifth anniversary (2.1.1)
scope under 2.1.4, sufficient to DISCOVER substantial corrosion; dry-dock survey part of it; no concurrent crediting (2.1.7)
extend thickness measurement to the annex extent, and complete it BEFORE the survey is credited
extend close-up survey to establish the true extent of the affected structure
record the locations as suspect areas so they follow the ship
assess against renewal thickness, and deal with the cause - coating and anodes - not only the symptom

steps.title: Repair methods and their acceptance
points: cropping and renewal as the primary permanent remedy, with approved procedures, welders and consumables and post-weld NDT
partial renewal and insert plates with full penetration welds, sited clear of high-stress locations
doubler plates as a TEMPORARY and CONDITIONAL measure only, normally with a condition of class
weld repair and build-up for grooving corrosion, within the society's limits
renewal of the corrosion prevention system and anodes
prior approval of the repair scheme and survey of the completed work

steps.title: The role of the classification society
points: rule-maker - scantlings, corrosion additions, renewal thicknesses, and adoption of IACS URs and CSR
survey planner - the survey programme agreed in advance, and the extent of close-up survey and gauging
attending surveyor - overall and close-up survey, witnessing the gauging, applying the criteria
approver of the repair scheme, materials, welding procedures and welders
keeper of the survey status, thickness records, Condition Evaluation Report and suspect-area register
enforcer - condition of class, then suspension; and separately, as the flag's RO, the statutory certificate
certifier of the thickness-measurement company under the Code's own annex

questions.memory_cue: The surveyor's working day, in seven words — DEFINE (1), MODEL (2), CRITERIA (3), FIND (4), EXTEND (5), FIX (6), CLASS (7). For the definition itself: seventy-five per cent of the margin, still acceptable, so measure more.

quick_revision.recall_15s: ESP Code A.1049(27) para 1.2.9, mandatory via SOLAS XI-1/2. Substantial corrosion = wastage in excess of 75% of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits; under IACS CSR, gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net. It is a warning state, not a defect. Consequence: extend thickness measurement and close-up survey (1.1.3), complete the extension before crediting the survey, and record the location as a suspect area (1.2.8). Renew only at renewal thickness. Coating graded GOOD / FAIR / POOR (1.2.11).
critical_numbers: Substantial corrosion: wastage in excess of 75% of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits
IACS CSR form: gauged thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net
Coating POOR: general breakdown over 20% or more of areas, or hard scale at 10% or more
Coating FAIR: local breakdown at stiffener edges and weld connections and/or light rusting over 20% or more, but less than POOR
Renewal survey may commence at the 4th annual survey and complete by the 5th anniversary; thickness measurement not before the 4th annual
Dry-dock: minimum 2 bottom inspections in the 5-year period, maximum interval 36 months; in dry-dock for ships 15 years and over
quick_revision.critical_regulation: 2011 ESP Code, resolution A.1049(27), made mandatory by SOLAS regulation XI-1/2. Paragraph 1.2.9 carries both definitions; paragraph 1.1.3 makes the Code a minimum and requires the survey to be extended when substantial corrosion is found; paragraph 1.2.8 turns the location into a suspect area for every later survey.
quick_revision.major_trap: Saying that substantial corrosion means the plate must be renewed, or that 75 per cent of the plate thickness has been lost. Neither is what the Code says. It is 75 per cent of the allowable margin — the corrosion addition, not the plate — and the Code adds 'but within acceptable limits', so the steel is still acceptable. The required response is to measure more widely, not to cut it out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define substantial corrosion, in both forms the ESP Code prints.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP Code paragraph 1.2.9. General: an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates wastage in excess of 75 per cent of allowable margins, but within acceptable limits. For ships built under the IACS Common Structural Rules: an extent of corrosion such that assessment of the corrosion pattern indicates a gauged (or measured) thickness between t-net + 0.5 mm and t-net.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem opens with 'Define'. Giving only the general limb is the commonest incompleteness, and the CSR limb is the more likely one on a modern bulk carrier or tanker.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Substantial corrosion has been found. Must the plate be renewed?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The definition ends 'but within acceptable limits' — the steel is still acceptable. The required response is to extend the thickness measurements and, where necessary, the close-up survey, and to record the location as a suspect area. Renewal is required only when measurements reach the renewal thickness, at which point the material is no longer in substantial corrosion but simply unacceptable.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most valuable point in the answer, and it follows from the definition the candidate has just quoted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the three coating condition grades and their numeric thresholds.
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP Code 1.2.11. GOOD — only minor spot rusting. FAIR — local breakdown at edges of stiffeners and weld connections and/or light rusting over 20 per cent or more of areas under consideration, but less than POOR. POOR — general breakdown of coating over 20 per cent or more of areas, or hard scale at 10 per cent or more of areas.
retrieval_cards.why: Two checkable numbers in one definition, and coating condition is one of the assessment criteria the stem asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a suspect area, and how does a location become one?
retrieval_cards.answer: ESP Code 1.2.8: locations showing substantial corrosion and/or considered by the surveyor to be prone to rapid wastage. Note the 'and/or' — the surveyor's judgement is an independent route in, without any measurement. Once recorded, the location is examined and gauged at every subsequent survey.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the mechanism by which one finding follows the ship for life, and the 'and/or' is a precise point most candidates miss.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What changes at a renewal survey once substantial corrosion is found?
retrieval_cards.answer: Extend the thickness measurements to the extent the Code's dedicated annex prescribes, and complete them before the survey is credited. Extend the close-up survey as necessary (1.1.3). Record the locations as suspect areas (1.2.8). Re-classify a combined cargo/ballast space as a ballast tank (1.2.2). Assess against renewal thickness, repair or renew where it is reached, and deal with the coating and anodes as well as the steel.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the core of the stem's third demand and the part most often answered generically.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instrument makes the ESP Code mandatory, and what is the Code's own status?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS regulation XI-1/2 makes the 2011 ESP Code (resolution A.1049(27)) mandatory. The Code itself is written in 'should' language and sets the minimum extent of examination, thickness measurement and tank testing — paragraph 1.1.3 — which is why the survey is extended, not reduced, when substantial corrosion is found.
retrieval_cards.why: Attributing the ESP Code to SOLAS chapter II-1 is a common and avoidable error, and the 'minimum' point sets up the whole answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your owner proposes a doubler plate over a wasted strake. What is the correct answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: A doubler is a temporary and conditional measure only, accepted at the society's discretion, normally time-limited and normally attracting a condition of class requiring permanent repair. It conceals the parent material from inspection and traps moisture behind it. The permanent remedy is cropping and renewal to approved procedures with post-weld NDT.
retrieval_cards.why: Offering doublers as a repair method without that qualification is a standard mark-loser and a genuine engineering error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who takes the thickness measurements, who witnesses them, and when must they be taken?
retrieval_cards.answer: By a company certified for the purpose — the Code carries a dedicated annex of procedures for certifying a company engaged in thickness measurement of hull structures — and witnessed by the attending surveyor. Paragraph 1.5 requires that in any survey the measurements in areas requiring close-up survey be taken simultaneously with the close-up survey.
retrieval_cards.why: The certification requirement and the simultaneity rule are two precise, checkable points that show the whole chain has been understood.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the substantial corrosion question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Define — both limbs. 2 The corrosion-allowance model and the extension trigger. 3 The assessment criteria. 4 Inspection techniques. 5 What the finding changes at the renewal survey. 6 Repair methods. 7 The society's role.
retrieval_cards.why: Seven sections in the printed order of the stem's four demands, so nothing the examiner asked for is left without a home.
