blocks.h: (a) Requirements for classification, and the role of the society — 8 marks
1. What classification is, and the line between class and statutory work

blocks.p: Classification is a private, contractual certification of technical fitness against a society's own published rules. A classification society develops rules for the structure, machinery and electrical installations of a ship, approves the design against them, surveys the ship during construction and then surveys her periodically in service. If she complies, the society assigns and maintains class and issues a Certificate of Class.
Two consequences follow immediately, and a Class I answer states both.

ul: Class is not law. It is a contract between the owner and the society. The society's remedy for non-compliance is to impose a condition, suspend or withdraw class — not to detain the ship.

Class is nevertheless commercially compulsory. Hull and machinery underwriters, P&I clubs, charterers, financiers and flag Administrations all require it, so a ship out of class is effectively unemployable and uninsurable. Withdrawal of class is the sharpest sanction in the industry precisely because it is not a legal one.

blocks.p: The statutory work — SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line, Tonnage, ISM, ISPS, MLC — belongs to the flag Administration. It only reaches a classification society because the Administration delegates it. Keeping those two ideas apart is what limb (b) then tests.

blocks.h: 2. The requirements a ship must satisfy to be assigned class

blocks.p: Classification is not a single event. It is a sequence of requirements running from the drawing board to the end of the ship's life, and the marks in this limb are in that sequence.

ol: Application and rule selection. The owner applies to the society; the applicable rule set is fixed by ship type, size, service and intended notations — and for bulk carriers and oil tankers by the IACS Common Structural Rules.

Plan approval. Structural drawings, midship section, scantlings, shafting and propeller, main and auxiliary machinery, piping, electrical single-line diagrams and control systems are submitted and approved against the rules before construction.

Approval and certification of materials and components. Steel, castings, forgings, welding consumables, main engine, boilers, pressure vessels, shafting, anchors and chain cables are made at approved works under survey and issued with certificates.

Survey during construction. The society's surveyor attends the yard to verify that the ship is being built to the approved plans — alignment, welding and NDT, tank testing, sea trials and machinery trials.

Assignment of class. On satisfactory completion the society assigns a class notation and issues the Certificate of Class. The notations record the basis on which she was built — hull and machinery character marks, service restriction, ice class, UMS, and any special notation.

Maintenance of class in service. Class is retained only by a continuing survey regime: annual, intermediate and five-yearly renewal surveys, docking or in-water surveys, tailshaft and boiler surveys, and machinery surveyed either at renewal or on a rolling continuous-survey or approved planned-maintenance basis.

Reporting of damage and of change. The owner must report damage, grounding, defects and repairs affecting class, and must not alter classed items without approval. Failure to do so is itself a breach.

Conditions of Class. Where a defect impairs compliance, the surveyor imposes a time-bound requirement to rectify. Class continues meanwhile; if the condition is not cleared by its due date, class is suspended.

blocks.p: All of that is class practice and the IACS framework. It is not a SOLAS requirement, and stating it as one is the commonest error in this question.

blocks.h: 3. Where class rules acquire legal force, and how the society ensures compliance

blocks.p: The society becomes legally relevant at two distinct points, and they are different mechanisms.

First, SOLAS adopts class rules as the construction standard. Regulation II-1/3-1 provides that, in addition to the requirements elsewhere in the regulations, ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society which is recognized by the Administration in accordance with regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration which provide an equivalent level of safety. That single regulation is what converts a private rulebook into the operative construction standard for a Convention ship — and note the words designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED, which is why the survey cycle, not just the newbuilding survey, is a SOLAS matter.

Second, the Administration may delegate the statutory work itself. Regulation I/6 places inspection and survey on officers of the Administration, but permits the Administration to entrust them to nominated surveyors or to recognized organizations. Regulation XI-1/1 then requires that authorisation to be given in accordance with the RO Code (resolution MSC.349(92)), whose parts 1 and 2 are mandatory and part 3 recommendatory. The RO Code sets what an organisation must be and must do to be recognised, and how the Administration must oversee it.

So the society ensures compliance in two capacities that must never be confused: as classification society, enforcing its own rules by conditions of class and ultimately withdrawal; and as Recognized Organization, acting for the flag State under a specific delegation, issuing statutory certificates in the Administration's name. Under regulation I/6 the RO must at minimum be empowered to require repairs and to survey at a port State's request, and must notify the Administration where a ship's condition does not correspond substantially with her certificates.

blocks.h: (b) A ship classed by two societies — management and statutory responsibility — 8 marks
4. What dual class means, and why an owner takes it

blocks.p: Dual class — also called joint or double classification — is where a ship is entered with two classification societies simultaneously, and must comply with both societies' rules and hold a Certificate of Class from each. It is not the same as either of the two things candidates confuse it with:

ul: It is not transfer of class, where the ship leaves one society and joins another under the IACS transfer-of-class procedure.
It is not the ordinary and universal split between a class society and a flag Administration.

blocks.p: Owners take dual class for commercial and regulatory access rather than for safety. Typical drivers: a national requirement that ships on a particular register or in a particular domestic trade be classed with the national society; charterer or oil-major preference for a specific society; financiers or the shipyard requiring a society the owner would not otherwise use; retaining an existing society's records on a second-hand purchase while adding the buyer's preferred society; and market access to a trade where one society is dominant.
The cost is real: two rule sets to satisfy, two sets of surveys to arrange and pay for, two sets of records, and the risk that the two societies take different views of the same defect.

blocks.h: 5. How the arrangement is managed in practice

blocks.p: Management is contractual, and it is settled before the ship is entered, not after a dispute. The recurring elements are these.

ol: A joint-class agreement between the two societies and the owner. It records the scope each society takes, how surveys are shared, how findings are exchanged and how disagreement is resolved.

The stricter rule governs. Where the two rule sets differ, the ship must satisfy both, so in practice she is built and maintained to the more demanding requirement in each area. Design approval is normally led by one society with the other reviewing and accepting.

Division of the survey scope. The commonest shape is that each society surveys an agreed part of the ship — for example one taking hull and the other machinery — or that the societies alternate the survey cycle. Each then accepts the other's survey for its own class purposes.

Mutual acceptance of records. Survey reports, thickness measurement reports, conditions of class and the survey status are exchanged so that both societies' records agree. IACS procedural requirements govern this exchange between IACS members; the arrangement between an IACS and a non-IACS society is purely a matter of the agreement.

One survey status on board. The practical requirement is that the ship carries a single coherent picture of what is due and what is outstanding, whichever society raised it. Two divergent survey-status reports is the failure mode this whole arrangement exists to prevent.
Conditions of class are honoured by both. A condition imposed by either society is a condition on the ship. Clearing it with one does not clear it with the other unless the agreement so provides.

blocks.h: 6. Who conducts the statutory surveys and audits, and why this is a flag question

blocks.p: This is the part of the question that decides the mark, and the answer turns on a point of text.

Statutory surveys and audits are the flag Administration's, and only the flag Administration can say who performs them. Under regulation I/6 they are the Administration's own function; a society performs them only where that Administration has recognised and authorised it under regulation XI-1/1 and the RO Code. Dual class does not confer statutory authority on either society. A society may be the ship's classification society and have no delegation from her flag at all.

Regulation II-1/3-1 speaks of the requirements of a classification society — singular and indefinite. The construction standard is satisfied by compliance with one recognised society's requirements; nothing in the regulation contemplates or requires two.
The practical position is therefore:

ul: The Administration nominates one RO to act for it in respect of a given ship — normally one of the two societies, and normally the one it has authorised. That society issues the statutory certificates in the Administration's name.

Statutory certification is not duplicated. A ship holds one Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, not two. Two societies issuing the same statutory certificate would be a defect in the delegation, not a feature of dual class.

ISM and ISPS audits follow the same rule and are separately delegated. The Administration may authorise a different organisation for audits than for surveys, and the DOC and SMC belong to the company and ship respectively, not to a class society.
The Administration may reserve items to itself — commonly initial certification, exemptions, equivalents and detention decisions — and the delegation instrument says which.

Class survey and statutory survey may be carried out by the same surveyor on the same attendance, and usually are. That convenience is exactly what obscures the distinction, and the candidate must state it: the surveyor wears two hats and acts under two different authorities.

blocks.p: Conclusion for limb (b). Dual class doubles the classification obligation and leaves the statutory obligation single. The two societies share the class work by agreement between themselves; the statutory work is performed by whichever of them — or which other organisation, or the Administration's own officers — the flag State has authorised, and by nobody else.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The question is two questions of eight marks and they are not the same kind of question. Limb (a) is a process question — it rewards a sequence, and the sequence is the ship's own life from plan approval to withdrawal of class. Limb (b) is a distinction question, and it rewards one idea held firmly: class is contractual and can be doubled; statutory authority is delegated and cannot.

Section 1 spends a short paragraph establishing that class is not law. That paragraph is what makes sections 3 and 6 scorable, because both turn on the boundary it draws. Candidates who skip it write eight marks of correct description in limb (a) and then cannot answer limb (b) at all.

blocks.h: The three capacities a classification society can occupy

blocks.p: Almost every error in this question comes from collapsing these into one. Hold them apart:

ul: Classification society — acting under its own rules, under a private contract with the owner. Sanction: condition of class, suspension, withdrawal.
Recognized Organization — acting for a flag Administration under a delegation given per SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code. Sanction: the Administration's, exercised through the RO.
Nominated surveyor — an individual, not an organisation, entrusted under regulation I/6.

blocks.p: A society is not automatically an RO, is not an RO for every flag, and is not an RO for every function of a flag that has authorised it. Each of those three is a separate examinable point.

blocks.h: What dual class does and does not double

rows: Parties who can impose a condition of class
The port State's view of her

blocks.h: The textual point most candidates miss

blocks.p: SOLAS II-1/3-1 requires compliance with the requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration. The indefinite singular is doing work: the Convention's construction standard is met by one recognised society. Dual class is therefore a commercial arrangement layered on top of a statutory scheme that neither requires it nor recognises it. Once that is seen, limb (b) writes itself.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Writing that SOLAS requires a ship to be classed. It does not. It requires compliance with a recognised society's structural, mechanical and electrical requirements or with equivalent national standards of the Administration — and the alternative is in the text.

Treating class certificates as statutory certificates. The Certificate of Class is not a Convention certificate and a port State control officer does not detain on it, though he may well ask to see the survey status.
Answering limb (b) as though dual class meant transfer of class, or as though it meant the ordinary class-and-flag split.
Saying that under dual class the two societies each issue statutory certificates. That would mean two flag delegations issuing the same certificate for the same ship.
Listing the survey types in limb (a) and never reaching plan approval, material certification or survey during construction — which is where classification actually begins.
Inventing an IACS PR number for the mutual-recognition procedure. Name the mechanism; the number is not required and a wrong one costs more than an absent one.
Forgetting that II-1/3-1 says maintained, and treating classification as a newbuilding activity that stops at delivery.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Who is responsible?' in limb (b) invites the answer 'the classification society'. The correct answer names the flag Administration first and the society only as its delegate.
The stem prints 'classes by two classification societies' for 'classed by'. Answer the question the examiner set; do not comment on the typography.

The word audits is in the stem alongside surveys. It is there to test whether the candidate knows ISM and ISPS audits are separately delegated and produce company and ship documents. An answer that treats 'surveys and audits' as one phrase leaves marks on the table.

Limb (a) is a process question about how a ship becomes and stays classed, with an explicit sub-demand about how the society ENSURES compliance - that is, its enforcement mechanism, not merely its activities. Limb (b) is a distinction question disguised as a scenario: it asks what happens when the class relationship is doubled, and then asks who does the statutory work - which is the trap, because the answer is that the statutory work was never a class function at all.

questions.understand_first: This question is really about one boundary: the line between what a classification society does for the owner under a private contract, and what it does for the flag State under a delegated statutory authority. Limb (a) is life on the owner's side of that line — how a ship becomes classed and stays classed, and what the society can actually do to an owner who lets her slip. Limb (b) then doubles the owner's side and asks what happens to the flag State's side. The answer is: nothing. Class is contractual, so a ship can have two of them; statutory authority is delegated by an Administration, so it cannot be doubled by a commercial arrangement the Administration is not party to. SOLAS makes the point in its own wording — it requires compliance with the requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration, and one recognised society satisfies it. Everything else in this question is detail hung on that boundary.

steps.title: What classification is, and the line between class and statutory work
points: class is a private contractual certification against the society's own published rules
the society's sanction is condition, suspension and withdrawal - never detention
class is commercially compulsory even though it is not law - insurers, charterers, financiers and flag all require it
statutory work belongs to the flag Administration and reaches a society only by delegation

steps.title: The requirements a ship must satisfy to be assigned class
points: application and selection of the applicable rule set, including CSR for bulk carriers and oil tankers
plan approval of structure, machinery, piping and electrical installations before construction
approval and certification of materials and components at approved works under survey
survey during construction against the approved plans, with NDT, tank testing and trials
assignment of class and the Certificate of Class, with notations recording the basis of build
maintenance of class by annual, intermediate and renewal surveys, docking, tailshaft and machinery surveys
the owner's duty to report damage, defects and repairs affecting class
conditions of class as the time-bound instrument of enforcement short of suspension

steps.title: Where class rules acquire legal force, and how the society ensures compliance
points: SOLAS II-1/3-1 - ships shall be designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED to the requirements of a recognised society, or to equivalent national standards
SOLAS I/6 - survey is the Administration's function, which it may entrust to nominated surveyors or recognized organizations
SOLAS XI-1/1 - that authorisation must follow the RO Code, MSC.349(92), parts 1 and 2 mandatory
the society acts in two capacities - as class under its own rules, and as RO in the Administration's name
the RO's minimum powers under I/6 - require repairs, survey at a port State's request, notify the Administration

steps.title: What dual class means, and why an owner takes it
points: entered with two societies at once; both rule sets must be satisfied and two Certificates of Class held
distinguish sharply from transfer of class and from the ordinary class/flag split
drivers - national register requirements, charterer or oil-major preference, yard or financier requirement, second-hand purchase, market access
costs - two rule sets, two survey programmes, two record sets, and the risk of divergent views

steps.title: How the arrangement is managed in practice
points: a joint-class agreement settled in advance between the two societies and the owner
where the rule sets differ the stricter governs, because both must be satisfied
division of the survey scope - by system, or by alternating the cycle - with each accepting the other's survey
mutual exchange and acceptance of survey reports, thickness measurements and conditions of class
one coherent survey status on board, whichever society raised the item

steps.title: Who conducts the statutory surveys and audits, and why this is a flag question
points: statutory surveys and audits are the Administration's; only it can say who performs them
dual class confers no statutory authority - a society may class the ship and hold no delegation from her flag
SOLAS II-1/3-1 speaks of A classification society - singular and indefinite; one recognised society satisfies it
statutory certification is not duplicated - one Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, not two
ISM and ISPS audits are separately delegated and produce the DOC and SMC and the ISSC
the same surveyor may do both on one attendance, under two different authorities - which is what obscures the distinction

questions.memory_cue: Two sentences carry the whole answer. Limb (a) is the ship's own life — APPLY, APPROVE, CERTIFY, BUILD, ASSIGN, MAINTAIN, REPORT, CONDITION (2), with the law bolted on at step (3). Limb (b) is four words — TWO SOCIETIES, ONE FLAG (6).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Class is a private contract; statutory authority is a flag delegation. Class runs APPLY → APPROVE → CERTIFY → BUILD → ASSIGN → MAINTAIN → REPORT → CONDITION, enforced by condition of class, suspension and withdrawal. SOLAS II-1/3-1 makes a recognised society's rules the construction standard; I/6 makes survey the Administration's; XI-1/1 plus the RO Code (MSC.349(92)) is how it is delegated. Dual class doubles the class side and nothing else — two rule sets, two Certificates of Class, one flag, one set of statutory certificates.
critical_numbers: RO Code MSC.349(92) - parts 1 and 2 MANDATORY, part 3 RECOMMENDATORY
Renewal survey cycle 5 years, with annual and intermediate surveys between
Dual class: 2 rule sets, 2 Certificates of Class, 1 flag Administration, 1 set of statutory certificates
quick_revision.critical_regulation: SOLAS II-1/3-1 read with XI-1/1 and I/6. II-1/3-1 adopts the requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration as the construction standard, and requires the ship to be designed, constructed and maintained to them; I/6 makes inspection and survey the Administration's own function with a power to entrust it; XI-1/1 requires any such authorisation to be given in accordance with the RO Code.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering limb (b) with 'the classification societies do the statutory surveys'. Statutory surveys and audits belong to the flag Administration, and a society performs them only where that Administration has recognised and authorised it. Dual class is an arrangement between the owner and two societies; the flag State is not a party to it and its delegation is unaffected by it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the classification and dual-class question.
retrieval_cards.answer: (a) 1 What class is, and the class/statutory line. 2 The eight-stage classification process. 3 Where class rules acquire legal force, and the enforcement mechanism. (b) 4 What dual class is and why it is taken. 5 How it is managed. 6 Who does the statutory surveys and audits.
retrieval_cards.why: Three sections per limb match the 8 + 8 split, and section 1 is what makes section 6 arguable rather than asserted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which SOLAS regulation makes class rules the construction standard, and what alternative does it allow?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation II-1/3-1. Ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society recognised by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1 - or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety. The alternative is in the text, so SOLAS does not strictly require class.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates routinely write that SOLAS requires classification. It does not, and the exception is examinable.

retrieval_cards.prompt: In what two capacities can a classification society act, and what is the sanction in each?
retrieval_cards.answer: As classification society under its own rules, by private contract with the owner - sanction: condition of class, suspension, withdrawal. As Recognized Organization under a flag Administration's delegation given per SOLAS XI-1/1 and the RO Code - it issues statutory certificates in the Administration's name and exercises the Administration's authority.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole of limb (b) depends on holding these apart, and the same surveyor often performs both on one attendance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is dual class, and what is it not?
retrieval_cards.answer: A ship entered with two classification societies at the same time, complying with both rule sets and holding a Certificate of Class from each. It is not transfer of class - leaving one society for another - and it is not the ordinary split between class society and flag Administration.
retrieval_cards.why: Both confusions are common and either one loses the whole limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A ship is dual classed. Who issues her statutory certificates?
retrieval_cards.answer: Whichever organisation the flag Administration has recognised and authorised for that ship - normally one of the two societies, possibly neither, or the Administration's own officers. Statutory certification is not duplicated: one Cargo Ship Safety Construction Certificate, not two. Dual class confers no statutory authority on either society.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the mark-deciding point of limb (b) and the trap the stem is built around.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a dual-class arrangement managed?
retrieval_cards.answer: By a joint-class agreement settled in advance: the scope each society takes, how surveys are shared, how records are exchanged, how disagreement is resolved. Where the rule sets differ the stricter governs, because both must be satisfied. Survey scope is divided by system or by alternating the cycle, each society accepting the other's survey, with one coherent survey status carried on board.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks 'how is this process managed', which is a procedure demand, not a definition demand.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the stages by which a ship becomes and remains classed.
retrieval_cards.answer: Application and rule selection; plan approval; approval and certification of materials and components; survey during construction; assignment of class with notations and the Certificate of Class; maintenance of class by the survey cycle; reporting of damage, defects and repairs; conditions of class where compliance is impaired.
retrieval_cards.why: Eight stages for eight marks, in the order the ship experiences them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does the RO Code do, and which of its parts are mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: It sets what an organisation must be and must do to be recognised and authorised by an Administration, and how the Administration must oversee it. Resolution MSC.349(92): parts 1 and 2 are mandatory, part 3 is recommendatory. SOLAS XI-1/1 requires authorisation to be given in accordance with it.
retrieval_cards.why: The mandatory/recommendatory split is a precise, checkable fact and is stated in XI-1/1 itself.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The stem says 'statutory surveys and audits'. Why are audits mentioned separately?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because ISM and ISPS verification is delegated separately from survey and produces different documents - the Document of Compliance to the company, the Safety Management Certificate and the International Ship Security Certificate to the ship. An Administration may authorise a different organisation for audits than for surveys.
retrieval_cards.why: Treating 'surveys and audits' as one phrase leaves an examinable distinction unanswered.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - MS Act 1958, the Part dealing with investigations and inquiries into shipping casualties. Named at PART LEVEL ONLY. The machinery is: a duty to report a casualty; a preliminary inquiry conducted by a person appointed for the purpose; and, where the circumstances warrant it, a formal investigation before a court with assessors, which may find fault and may cancel or suspend the certificate of a master, mate or engineer. NO SECTION NUMBER IS ASSERTED, because the Act is not held.

Named at Part level; no section number asserted.

AUTHORITATIVE SECONDARY - the Indian Coast Guard as the authority responsible for the marine pollution response at sea in India's maritime zones, and the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan as the standing national plan under which a spill response is mounted, with tiered response levels. PRIMARY BY IDENTITY - the Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84), mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/6. Held in the corpus's Casualty-Investigation-Code directory. Under it a marine safety investigation is mandatory for a very serious marine casualty - one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment.

MIW STANDING CORRECTION - the Casualty Investigation Code is not engaged by every pollution incident; a mandatory investigation is required only for a very serious marine casualty, and lesser casualties fall under recommended practice. Applied here in the candidate's favour: the printed scenario states loss of lives, so the mandatory limb IS engaged.

MIW STANDING CORRECTION - Merchant Shipping Act 2025 claims are time-sensitive; its section numbers must never be invented and it must not be presented as current for a pre-2026 sitting. Applied by excluding the 2025 Act entirely.

blocks.h: 1. What has happened, and which State the examiner is asking about

blocks.p: Separate the incident into its legal components, because each triggers different machinery and different people:

ol: A collision — engaging the duties of both masters and the law of collision.
Loss of life — which makes this a very serious marine casualty and, as section 6 shows, makes a safety investigation mandatory.
Damage to the vessels — engaging seaworthiness, survey, detention and possibly salvage.
An oil spill — engaging the pollution response machinery, the directions power and the liability conventions.

blocks.p: Now read the stem carefully, because it has been narrowed. It does not ask what steps should be taken generally. It asks what steps should be initiated by the coastal State. India is here wearing two hats at once — she is the flag State of the casualty vessel and she is the coastal State off whose coast the casualty occurred — and the examiner has asked about one of them. An answer built on flag-State machinery answers a different question.

The statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. It governs at this sitting and throughout the response to this casualty. Note the constant that runs through the whole answer: the Act is enabling as much as prohibitory. Most of what follows is the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping being given power to direct, and the owner, master and salvor being obliged to comply.

blocks.h: 2. The coastal State's jurisdiction - why it may act at all

blocks.p: Before listing steps, establish the basis for taking them, because that is what distinguishes coastal-State action from flag-State action.

ul: The casualty is in India's maritime zones. Those zones are established by the Maritime Zones of India Act, 1976, and within them India exercises the jurisdiction a coastal State has over the protection of its marine environment and its coastal interests.

Coastal-State jurisdiction is territorially based, not flag-based. It reaches both ships involved in this collision — including the other vessel, whether she is Indian or foreign flagged. That is the single most important consequence of the narrowing, and it is what flag-State powers cannot do.

The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 supplies the domestic powers, principally the pollution provisions of Part XA and the unseaworthy-and-unsafe-ships power, exercised by the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping.
Intervention is proportionate. The coastal State acts to protect its coastline and related interests from pollution or the threat of it, and its measures must be proportionate to the harm threatened.

blocks.h: 3. What the ship must do, and what the coastal State requires of her

blocks.p: The first steps are the Master's, and they are taken before any authority is involved — but the coastal State's whole response depends on them, which is why they belong in this answer. The order is life, then ship, then environment, then evidence.

ol: Muster, account for all persons, and search for the missing. With loss of life reported, this is the first and overriding duty.

Render assistance to the other vessel and to persons in danger, so far as he can without serious danger to his own ship and those on board, and stand by; exchange identifying particulars. This duty is in the Act's collision Part and is not discretionary.
Sound tanks and compartments, assess damage and stability, and contain flooding before any decision to move.
Stop the source of the spill — isolate the damaged tank, transfer internally where safe, and deploy the ship's SOPEP.

Report. To the Indian Coast Guard and the nearest MRCC or coastal radio station for search and rescue and the pollution response; to the Directorate General of Shipping through the nearest Mercantile Marine Department; to the owner and DPA; to the port and coastal authorities. Alongside these sit a MARPOL Protocol I report and a SOLAS chapter V danger message.
Preserve evidence. Secure the voyage data recorder, charts, logs, engine and alarm records. This is the step candidates omit and it decides both the investigation and the liability.

blocks.h: 4. The coastal State's steps for the safety of the ships

ol: Take charge of the casualty response and coordinate it. Establish a command structure, obtain the picture from both ships, and decide the sequence of operations.

Give directions to the master, owner or salvor. Under Part XA the Central Government and the Director-General may direct a ship to move, to take or refrain from specified action, or to be salved. This is the power that converts a commercial decision into a compellable one, and it is exercisable in respect of either ship.

Detain an unsafe ship. The unseaworthy-and-unsafe-ships provisions — sections 334 to 336 — empower detention of a ship unsafe by reason of defective hull or machinery, undermanning, overloading or improper loading. A damaged ship after a collision is squarely within that power, and the initiator is the Director-General of Shipping or a surveyor acting for him.

Decide on a place of refuge. If a casualty must be moved to sheltered water, the decision is the coastal State's — it is not the owner's and not the flag State's. The current guidance is resolution A.1184(33), Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, adopted by the 33rd Assembly on 6 December 2023 and revoking A.949(23). The decision is taken on an objective analysis of the risks of granting refuge against the risks of refusing it. This is the clearest coastal-State power on the paper and it should be named as such.
Secure navigational safety. Mark the casualty, issue navigational warnings, and establish an exclusion or safety zone where necessary.

Require survey and approve repairs before the ship proceeds, and oversee any salvage. Where the casualty produces wreck, the Act's wreck and salvage Part — sections 390 to 404 — and the Merchant Shipping (Wrecks and Salvage) Rules, 1974 provide the framework and the receiver of wreck's functions.

blocks.h: 5. The coastal State's steps for the marine environment

blocks.p: This is the second object the stem names, and it is where coastal-State responsibility is at its clearest.

ol: The statutory directions power is the legal engine. Under Part XA — prevention and containment of pollution of the sea by oil, at sections 356J, 356K and 356L — the Central Government and the Director-General may give directions to the owner, master or salvor for the prevention or containment of pollution, may take the action themselves where directions are not complied with or the case requires it, and may recover the cost from the owner.

Activate the national response. The National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan is the standing plan, and the Indian Coast Guard is responsible for the response at sea in India's maritime zones. The plan is tiered, escalating from a local response with local resources to national and, where necessary, international mobilisation.

Mount response operations. Aerial and satellite surveillance to establish the extent and drift of the slick; containment with booms; mechanical recovery with skimmers; dispersant application where and only where authorised for those waters and that oil; protection of sensitive shorelines and intakes; shoreline clean-up; and waste reception and disposal.

Protect coastal and related interests. Coordinate with State pollution control boards, fisheries and environment departments and port authorities; close or restrict affected areas; and protect water intakes, aquaculture and amenity shorelines.

Recover the cost. The coastal State is not expected to carry the bill: the Part XA power to act and recover, backed by the owner's P&I cover and the compulsory insurance behind the CLC or Bunkers certificate, is what makes the response fundable — with the certificate supporting direct action against the insurer.

blocks.h: 6. Investigation - which part is the coastal State's, and which is not

blocks.p: There are two parallel systems with different purposes, and the narrowing in the stem makes it important to say which belongs to whom.

The national inquiry under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is administered by India as the Administration for her own ship. Its Part on investigations and inquiries into shipping casualties runs in stages: a report of the casualty; a preliminary inquiry by a person appointed for the purpose; and, where the circumstances warrant it, a formal investigation before a court sitting with assessors, which may find fault and may cancel or suspend the certificate of a master, mate or engineer. Its orientation is partly disciplinary.

The marine safety investigation under the Casualty Investigation Code, resolution MSC.255(84), mandatory through SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, exists not to apportion blame but to prevent recurrence. It is mandatory here, because a very serious marine casualty includes one involving a death — and this scenario states loss of lives. Note that it is engaged by the death, not automatically by the spill: a spill engages it only if the environmental damage is severe.

Where the coastal State stands in all this. Both of those are, in their primary form, flag State functions, and here India happens to be the flag State too. But the coastal State has its own standing, and a July answer should say so: a State whose environment or coastal interests are seriously harmed is a substantially interested State under the Code and is entitled to participate in the investigation; and if the other vessel is foreign flagged, India's coastal-State interest is the basis on which she participates in that ship's investigation, since she is not that ship's flag State. India's coastal-State evidence — surveillance imagery, response records, samples and shoreline survey — is also what the investigation will largely rest on.

blocks.p: The stem asks who as expressly as it asks what, so answer it as a named allocation rather than in passing.

blocks.p: The one-sentence answer. For the coastal State, the responsible authority is the Central Government acting through the Director-General of Shipping, which directs, detains, acts in default and recovers the cost, with the Indian Coast Guard executing the response at sea and the coastal State itself deciding on a place of refuge — and the Master and owner remain the initiators of everything in the first hour, because no State machinery moves before they report.

A closing caution worth a mark. Because the casualty vessel is Indian-flagged, India is both flag State and coastal State and the two sets of powers run together in practice. They are still different powers with different bases, and if the other vessel is foreign flagged the distinction becomes immediately practical — India's reach over her is coastal-State jurisdiction, not flag-State authority.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem is a scenario with two express demands — what steps, and who is responsible for initiating them — a two-part object, the safety of the ships and the marine environment, and one decisive qualifier: by the coastal state. Sections 4 and 5 answer the two objects in the stem's own order and every step in them is attributed. Section 7 answers 'who' as a table, because the examiner asked for it twice and a named allocation cannot be skimmed over.

Section 2 has no counterpart in a general version of this question and it is where a strong answer separates itself. Before listing what a coastal State does, say why it may do it — territorial jurisdiction in India's maritime zones, reaching both ships regardless of flag. That single paragraph is what shows the narrowing has been noticed.

blocks.h: The word in the stem that changes the answer

blocks.p: 'By the coastal state.' India here is both the flag State of the casualty vessel and the coastal State off whose coast it happened, and it is very easy to write a complete, accurate, well-organised answer about the flag State — the casualty report, the preliminary inquiry, the formal investigation, the cancellation of certificates — and score poorly, because none of that is what was asked.

The test to apply to every sentence you write: would this power still exist if the ship were foreign flagged? If yes, it is coastal-State power and it belongs in the answer. If no, it is flag-State power and it belongs only in the boundary discussion in section 6.

blocks.h: The fact in the scenario that changes the law

blocks.p: 'Resulting in the loss of lives.' Under the Casualty Investigation Code a marine safety investigation is mandatory for a very serious marine casualty — total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment. A casualty short of that falls under recommended practice.

So the mandatory limb is engaged here, and it is engaged by the death, not automatically by the oil spill. A spill engages it only if the environmental damage is severe. Getting that reasoning the right way round is the most examinable point in the investigation limb — but keep it in proportion on this sitting, because the investigation is primarily a flag-State function and the stem has asked about the coastal State.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering the flag State's question. The commonest and most expensive error on this sitting: a full account of the casualty report, preliminary inquiry, formal investigation and certificate cancellation, none of which is coastal-State action.
Citing the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. At this sitting it had not received assent. The governing statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
Inventing section numbers of the 1958 Act. Name the Part; a wrong section costs more than an absent one.
Describing procedures without saying who owns each one, when the stem asks 'who is responsible' expressly.
Treating the place of refuge decision as the owner's or the salvor's. It is the coastal State's.
Saying the safety investigation exists to apportion blame. It exists to prevent recurrence and its findings are not to be used to apportion liability.
Forgetting the other vessel. Coastal-State jurisdiction reaches her too, whatever her flag.
Stating that CLC applies without qualification. It turns on whether she is a CLC ship and whether the oil is persistent; otherwise the Bunkers Convention is the relevant regime.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'By the coastal state' is the whole trap. The examiner rewrote this question from an earlier sitting precisely to insert it.
Asking which Act governs. At July 2025 it is the 1958 Act — the 2025 Act had not been enacted.
Asking whether the coastal State can act against the other ship. Yes: coastal-State jurisdiction is territorial, not flag-based.
Asking who decides on a place of refuge, and on what basis — the coastal State, on an objective analysis of the risks of granting against refusing, under A.1184(33).
Asking what makes this a very serious marine casualty. The death, not the spill.
Asking who pays for the response. The owner, through the Part XA cost-recovery power and the compulsory insurance behind the certificate — not the coastal State's public funds.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Which Merchant Shipping Act governs, and how do you know?
Your ship is damaged and leaking off the Indian coast. Who can order you to move, and under what power?
You ask for a place of refuge. Who decides, and what will they weigh?
The other ship is Panamanian. What can India do about her?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: WHOSE QUESTION → WHY → SHIP → SEA → INQUIRY → WHO. Establish that the coastal State is being asked about (1), state the jurisdictional basis (2), what the ship must do (3), then the two objects the stem names — ships (4) and environment (5) — then the investigation boundary (6), then the named allocation (7).

For the coastal State's own powers, four words: DIRECT, DETAIN, REFUGE, RESPOND. Direct under Part XA; detain under the unsafe-ships power; decide refuge under A.1184(33); respond through the Coast Guard and the national plan.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and jurisdiction notes

blocks.p: The statute that governs this question is the one the corpus does not hold. The True Source corpus holds the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 and holds no copy of the Act of 1958. Its own instrument log goes further and instructs that 1958-section-number answers be re-based onto the 2025 Act. That instruction is correct for a 2026 examination and wrong for this one, and it has been deliberately not followed: the 2025 Act received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026, so at a July 2025 sitting it had not been enacted at all. No provision of it appears anywhere in this answer.

The section-number discipline is correspondingly strict. Because the 1958 Act is not held, the only section numbers asserted are three groups already established in this corpus for exactly this machinery — ss.356J–356L in Part XA, ss.390–404 in the wreck and salvage Part, and ss.334–336 for unseaworthy and unsafe ships — and each is carried as authoritative secondary and flagged. The investigations and inquiries Part and the collision Part are named at Part level with no section number asserted, because inventing one is the specific failure this discipline exists to prevent.

The National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan is not held. Its existence, its custodian and its tiered structure are stated; no provision, revision date or tier threshold is asserted. No DG Shipping circular is cited, because the corpus holds none. The Maritime Zones of India Act, 1976 is named by identity only and no zone limit is asserted from it.

Finally, the printed scenario does not say whether the other vessel is Indian or foreign flagged. Both possibilities are addressed, because the coastal State's reach over her and the investigation architecture both differ — and on this sitting that ambiguity is worth engaging rather than resolving silently, since it is the cleanest illustration of what coastal-State jurisdiction does that flag-State authority cannot.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: A scenario question with two express demands and one decisive qualifier. The demands are WHAT steps and WHO is responsible for initiating them; the object is twofold, the safety of the ships and the marine environment; and the qualifier is BY THE COASTAL STATE. The qualifier is the whole difficulty: the vessel is Indian-flagged and the casualty is off India, so India is simultaneously flag State and coastal State, and it is entirely possible to write a complete and accurate flag-State answer that does not address the question asked. The examiner rewrote this question from an earlier sitting precisely to insert that qualifier.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: 16, undivided. The two named objects - ships and environment - take roughly equal weight and are the largest blocks; the jurisdictional basis and the who-is-responsible allocation are each worth real marks because the stem's own words demand them; the investigation limb is kept proportionate rather than expansive, because it is primarily a flag-State function on a question that has asked about the coastal State. Seven sections weight it that way.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate notices the narrowing and answers it: the coastal State's jurisdictional basis in India's maritime zones, reaching both ships regardless of flag; the Part XA directions power with action in default and cost recovery as the legal engine; detention of an unsafe ship; the place-of-refuge decision as an exclusively coastal-State call under A.1184(33); the national pollution response through the Indian Coast Guard and the NOSDCP; navigational safety measures; and a named allocation of responsibility. Then, correctly bounded, the investigation layer - the national inquiry and the mandatory marine safety investigation triggered by the loss of life - with an honest statement of which parts are flag-State functions and where the coastal State's standing lies.

Establish the statute boundary first: confirm the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 assent and commencement dates against the anchor, and confirm that July 2025 precedes even the assent.
Read the corpus's own MS Act 2025 instrument log and its re-basing instruction, so that the decision NOT to follow it is a recorded adjudication rather than an omission.
Fix the section-number discipline before drafting: only the three groups already established in this corpus for this machinery may carry numbers; everything else is Part level.
Confirm A.1184(33) as the operative places-of-refuge edition at this sitting and that no 34th Assembly instrument is engaged.
Apply the standing MIW correction on the Casualty Investigation Code: check whether the printed scenario engages the mandatory limb, and if so say why - the death, not the spill.
Sweep all eight surface classes for the statute, in reverse of the April 2026 regression.
decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: LOW as to the instruments and HIGH as to the evidence environment. Nothing engaged by this question moved between the donor's sitting and this one, and no boundary falls inside July 2025. The risk is not the calendar: it is that the corpus holds the repealing statute and instructs that answers be re-based onto it, so the danger is importing 2026 law into a 2025 sitting from a source that appears authoritative.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: HIGH, and it is the whole question. The examination is Indian, the statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and the stem confines the demand to coastal-State action in a scenario where the same State is also the flag State. Two distinct jurisdictional errors are available: citing the 2025 Act, and answering with flag-State machinery. Both are addressed expressly.

questions.understand_first: Read the stem twice before you write, because it has been narrowed, and the narrowing is the question. An almost identical question was set four months earlier asking simply what steps should be initiated and by whom — and that version is answered perfectly well by flag State machinery: the casualty report, the preliminary inquiry, the formal investigation, the cancellation of a certificate. This version asks what steps should be initiated by the coastal state. India happens to be both here — she is the flag State of the ship and the coastal State off whose coast the collision happened — and that coincidence is exactly what makes the trap effective. The discipline that saves you is a single test applied to every sentence: would this power still exist if the ship were foreign flagged? Directing her to move or be salved, detaining her as unsafe, deciding whether to grant her a place of refuge, putting booms in the water, marking the casualty, recovering the cost of the clean-up — all of those survive the test, because they rest on territorial jurisdiction in India's maritime zones and reach both ships whatever their flags. Cancelling a certificate of competency does not. The statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958: the 2025 Act had not even received assent at this sitting.

steps.title: What has happened, and which State the examiner is asking about
points: Four legal events in one casualty: a collision, loss of life, damage to the vessels, and an oil spill - each with its own machinery
Loss of life makes this a VERY SERIOUS MARINE CASUALTY
THE STEM IS NARROWED: it asks what steps should be initiated BY THE COASTAL STATE, not what steps should be taken generally
India is here BOTH the flag State of the casualty vessel AND the coastal State - and the examiner has asked about one of them
The governing statute is the MERCHANT SHIPPING ACT, 1958; the Act of 2025 had not received assent at this sitting
The Act is enabling as much as prohibitory - most of what follows is a power to DIRECT, and a corresponding duty to comply

steps.title: The coastal State's jurisdiction - why it may act at all
points: The casualty is in India's maritime zones, established by the Maritime Zones of India Act, 1976
Coastal-State jurisdiction is TERRITORIAL, not flag-based, so it reaches BOTH ships - including the other vessel, whatever her flag
The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 supplies the domestic powers, principally Part XA and the unsafe-ships power
Those powers are exercised by the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping
Coastal-State measures must be proportionate to the harm threatened to the coastline and related interests

steps.title: What the ship must do, and what the coastal State requires of her
points: The order on board is LIFE, then SHIP, then ENVIRONMENT, then EVIDENCE
Muster and account for all persons and search for the missing - the overriding duty where life is lost
Render assistance to the other vessel and persons in danger, stand by, and exchange particulars - the Act's collision Part, not discretionary
Assess damage and stability, contain flooding, stop the source of the spill and deploy the SOPEP

Report outward in parallel - Indian Coast Guard and MRCC, DG Shipping through the Mercantile Marine Department, owner and DPA, port and coastal authorities - plus a MARPOL Protocol I report and a SOLAS chapter V danger message
Preserve evidence: voyage data recorder, charts, logs, engine and alarm records

steps.title: The coastal State's steps for the safety of the ships
points: Take charge of and coordinate the casualty response
GIVE DIRECTIONS to the master, owner or salvor under Part XA - to move, to act or refrain, or to be salved - exercisable in respect of EITHER ship
DETAIN an unsafe ship under the unseaworthy-and-unsafe-ships power, sections 334 to 336, on the Director-General's authority
DECIDE ON A PLACE OF REFUGE - exclusively the coastal State's call, under resolution A.1184(33) of 6 December 2023, on an objective analysis of the risks of granting against refusing
Secure navigational safety - mark the casualty, issue warnings, establish an exclusion or safety zone
Require survey and approve repairs before the ship proceeds; oversee salvage, and apply the wreck and salvage Part, sections 390 to 404, where wreck arises

steps.title: The coastal State's steps for the marine environment
points: THE LEGAL ENGINE IS PART XA, sections 356J to 356L - directions to owner, master or salvor for prevention or containment; action in default; and RECOVERY OF THE COST from the owner
Activate the National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan, with the INDIAN COAST GUARD responsible for the response at sea in India's maritime zones
The plan is TIERED - local resources, then national, then international mobilisation
Response operations - surveillance to establish extent and drift, containment booms, mechanical recovery, dispersant only where authorised, shoreline protection and clean-up, waste reception
Protect coastal and related interests with State pollution control boards, fisheries and environment departments and port authorities
Recovery of cost is backed by the owner's P&I cover and the compulsory insurance behind the CLC or Bunkers certificate, with direct action against the insurer

steps.title: Investigation - which part is the coastal State's, and which is not
points: TWO PARALLEL SYSTEMS with different purposes, and they must not be merged

The national inquiry under the MS Act 1958 investigations and inquiries Part - report, preliminary inquiry, then a formal investigation before a court with assessors which may find fault and cancel or suspend a certificate
The marine safety investigation under the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84), mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6, exists to PREVENT RECURRENCE and not to apportion blame
It is MANDATORY here because a very serious marine casualty includes one involving A DEATH - engaged by the death, not automatically by the spill
BOTH are primarily FLAG STATE functions, and here India happens to be the flag State too - say so rather than blurring it

The coastal State's own standing: a State whose environment or coastal interests are seriously harmed is a SUBSTANTIALLY INTERESTED STATE entitled to participate, and if the other vessel is foreign flagged that is the basis of India's participation in her investigation

steps.title: Who is responsible for initiating each step
points: The MASTER initiates everything in the first hour - muster, assistance, damage control, SOPEP and the first reports
The OWNER AND COMPANY initiate the commercial and technical response through the ISM safety management system
The CENTRAL GOVERNMENT, through the DIRECTOR-GENERAL OF SHIPPING, directs, detains, acts in default and recovers the cost
The INDIAN COAST GUARD executes the pollution response at sea under the national plan
The COASTAL STATE decides on a place of refuge
The ADMINISTRATION holds the preliminary inquiry and any formal investigation; the FLAG STATE conducts the marine safety investigation
Closing caution: India wears both hats here, but they are different powers with different bases - and if the other vessel is foreign flagged the distinction becomes immediately practical

quick_revision.recall_15s: The stem is narrowed to the coastal State, and India is also the flag State here — test every power by asking whether it would exist if the ship were foreign flagged. Statute: the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 (the 2025 Act had not received assent). Jurisdiction: territorial, in India's maritime zones, reaching both ships. Coastal-State powers: DIRECT the owner, master or salvor under Part XA, ss.356J-356L, with action in default and cost recovery; DETAIN an unsafe ship under ss.334-336; decide a PLACE OF REFUGE under A.1184(33) — exclusively the coastal State's call; RESPOND through the Indian Coast Guard under the tiered National Oil Spill Disaster Contingency Plan; plus marking, warnings and exclusion zones. Investigation: the national inquiry (report, preliminary inquiry, formal investigation with assessors, may cancel a certificate) and the mandatory marine safety investigation under MSC.255(84) — mandatory because a death makes this a very serious marine casualty — are both primarily flag State functions; the coastal State participates as a substantially interested State. Who: Master first hour, owner through the SMS, Central Government through DG Shipping for compulsion, Coast Guard at sea.

MS Act 1958 sections 334 to 336 - unseaworthy and unsafe ships, detention (flagged)

Resolution A.1184(33), adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.949(23) - places of refuge
Casualty Investigation Code MSC.255(84), mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/6

quick_revision.critical_regulation: Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, Part XA, sections 356J to 356L - the Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping may give directions to the owner, master or salvor of a ship for the prevention or containment of pollution, may take the action themselves where the directions are not complied with, and may recover the cost from the owner. That is the legal engine of the coastal State's whole environmental response and the direct answer to 'who is responsible'.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering the flag State's question. The stem asks what steps should be initiated by the coastal state, and because the vessel is Indian-flagged it is easy to write a full, accurate account of the casualty report, the preliminary inquiry, the formal investigation and the cancellation of certificates — none of which is coastal-State action. Test every power by asking whether it would still exist if the ship were foreign flagged. Second trap: citing the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025. It received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026, so at this July 2025 sitting it had not been enacted at all — the governing statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. Third trap: inventing section numbers of the 1958 Act. Name the Part; a wrong section costs more than an absent one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the collision and coastal-State question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The four legal events, and which State the stem asks about. 2 The coastal State's jurisdictional basis. 3 What the ship must do. 4 Coastal-State steps for the safety of the ships. 5 Coastal-State steps for the marine environment. 6 The investigation boundary between coastal and flag State. 7 Who is responsible, as a named allocation.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem names two objects and asks 'who' expressly, so sections 4, 5 and 7 map straight onto its own words.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The ship is Indian-flagged and the casualty is off India. Why does the stem's phrase 'by the coastal state' matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because India is both flag State and coastal State here, so a complete and accurate flag-State answer — casualty report, preliminary inquiry, formal investigation, cancellation of certificates — can be written without answering the question. Test every power by asking: would it still exist if the ship were foreign flagged? If yes it is coastal-State power; if no it is not.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner rewrote this question from an earlier sitting specifically to insert that qualifier.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which statute governs, and how do you know?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025 and commenced on 15 March 2026 — both after a July 2025 sitting — so at this examination it had not been enacted at all, let alone commenced.
retrieval_cards.why: The single most dangerous error available on this paper, and the assent date is a cleaner test than the commencement date.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the legal engine of the coastal State's pollution response, and what three things does it allow?
retrieval_cards.answer: MS Act 1958 Part XA, sections 356J to 356L. The Central Government and the Director-General of Shipping may (1) give directions to the owner, master or salvor for the prevention or containment of pollution; (2) take the action themselves where directions are not complied with or the case requires it; and (3) recover the cost from the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: It answers 'what steps' and 'who is responsible' in one provision, and the cost-recovery limb is what keeps the bill off public funds.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Who decides whether the casualty is granted a place of refuge, and on what basis?
retrieval_cards.answer: The coastal State — exclusively. Not the owner, not the salvor and not the flag State. The guidance is resolution A.1184(33), Guidelines on places of refuge for ships in need of assistance, adopted 6 December 2023 and revoking A.949(23), and the decision is taken on an objective analysis of the risks of granting refuge against the risks of refusing it.
retrieval_cards.why: The clearest purely coastal-State power in the whole answer, which is why it is worth naming as such on this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What makes this a very serious marine casualty, and what follows?
retrieval_cards.answer: The loss of life. Under the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84), a very serious marine casualty is one involving the total loss of the ship, a death, or severe damage to the environment — and for such a casualty a marine safety investigation is mandatory. It is engaged by the death, not automatically by the oil spill; a spill engages it only if the environmental damage is severe.
retrieval_cards.why: Getting the trigger the right way round is the examinable point, and the word 'lives' is in the stem for exactly that reason.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish the national inquiry from the marine safety investigation.
retrieval_cards.answer: The national inquiry under the MS Act 1958 runs report, preliminary inquiry, then a formal investigation before a court with assessors; it may find fault and may cancel or suspend a certificate, so it is partly disciplinary. The marine safety investigation under MSC.255(84) exists to establish causal factors and prevent recurrence, expressly not to apportion blame, and its report goes to the IMO.
retrieval_cards.why: One can take a certificate away; the other exists so the accident does not happen twice. Merging them loses marks in both directions.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The other vessel is foreign flagged. What can India do about her?
retrieval_cards.answer: A great deal, because coastal-State jurisdiction is territorial rather than flag-based. India may direct her under Part XA, detain her if unsafe, decide whether to grant her a place of refuge, mark her and require her to be salved. What India may not do is exercise flag-State authority over her — cancel her officers' certificates, or conduct her marine safety investigation; there India's standing is as a substantially interested State.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the cleanest illustration of what the narrowing is actually testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name who initiates each stage of the response.
retrieval_cards.answer: Master — muster, assistance, damage control, SOPEP and the first reports. Owner and company — emergency response through the ISM system, salvage and surveyors. Central Government through the Director-General of Shipping — directions, detention, action in default and cost recovery. Indian Coast Guard — the response at sea under the national plan. Coastal State — the place of refuge decision. Flag State — the marine safety investigation.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks 'who is responsible' expressly, so a named allocation is the mark rather than a summary.
